The exponents are common to the JJ-Q2Q_{2} and JJ-Q3Q_{3} models, and in some cases the JJ-Q4Q_{4} model also produces very similar power-law decays, though its first-order tendencies are much stronger.

We further analyze the correlation functions of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model and extract the scaling dimension Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} to unprecedented precision. We implement the trick of taking the distance (rr) derivative C′​(r)C^{\prime}(r) of a correlation function C⁡(r)C(r) as a “filter” [29] to minimize the impact of the eventual long-range order at the weak first-order transitions. With the PQMC method we have converged such calculations to the ground state for system sizes up to L=1024L=1024, where critical scaling is observed up to distances close to 200200. We also fit an appropriate function directly to C⁡(r)C(r) for LL up to 512512, with scaling corrections included, and the results of this approach also agree well with those from the derivatives. All these results lead us to the firm conclusion that Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} is about 4% smaller than the previously used input value for the CFT bootstrap calculation (see Table 1), which may appear to be a minor discrepancy but is an important one when it comes to establishing agreement with the SO(55) CFT. The individual values for Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} obtained from spin and dimer correlations agree with each other to within a statistical error of about 11% and we therefore assume that they really are the same, as required by the SO(55) CFT description.

In Sec. V we use a symmetric multi-spin (singlet) correlator not containing the order parameters in attempts to extract the scaling dimensions Δt\Delta_{t} and Δs\Delta_{s} of the two relevant symmetric perturbations of the critical point. However, while the value of Δt\Delta_{t} is relatively easy to extract from the long-distance correlation decay, giving the value listed in Table 1, it is difficult to distinguish the subleading contributions governed by Δs\Delta_{s} from other expected scaling corrections. We obtain Δs\Delta_{s} in other ways, as explained further below. We further argue that a spatial bond (JJ-term) modulation used to induce a helical VBS phase in Ref. [54] contains the conserved current operator, which allows us to extract its scaling dimension Δj\Delta_{j}. This scaling dimension was already obtained approximately in Ref. [54], but without noting the role of the conserved current operator and with a numerical value 1.90​(2)1.90(2); five error bars off the expected value 22. With improved results for the corresponding correlation function, we now find a value consistent with the general requirement Δj=2\Delta_{j}=2 for a Noether current operator. This result is important in that it demonstrates explicitly that a scaling dimension with a known CFT value can be extracted despite the fact that the systems we study cannot reach the critical point exactly.

The most natural scenario for a multicritical point is that it is attached to a first-order line on which the relevant singlet field ss varies and the SO(55) violating field vanishes (t=0t=0), as in either of the scenarios in Fig. 2(a) and Fig. 2(b). To study such a first-order line in a 2D parameter space, in Sec. VI we study the phase diagram of the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model, keeping J+Q2=1J+Q_{2}=1 and extracting transition values Q2​cQ_{2c} for several values of Q6Q_{6}. As expected, we find that the transition for increasing Q6Q_{6} develops gradually stronger first-order signatures, which we use to further test the multicriticality scenario. Using finite-size scaling of a Binder cumulant, we show consistency with the value in Table 1 of the correlation-length exponent νs=(3−Δs)−1\nu_{s}=(3-\Delta_{s})^{-1} pertaining to the first-order line. Moreover, we extrapolate the order parameters to infinite size, using the common value m2​(L)m^{2}(L) of the two squared order parameters where they cross each other, to ensure that the system is properly in the coexistence state for each LL. We find power-law scaling of the form m2∼(Q6−Q6​c)2​βm^{2}\sim(Q_{6}-Q_{6c})^{2\beta} with β≈0.87​(5)\beta\approx 0.87(5), which agrees with the value computed from the independently extracted scaling dimensions in Table 1; β=Δϕ/(3−Δs)≈0.84\beta=\Delta_{\phi}/(3-\Delta_{s})\approx 0.84. The fitted critical Q6Q_{6} value is negative, Q6​c=−0.07​(2)Q_{6c}=-0.07(2), and cannot be studied directly with sign-free QMC simulations. However, there is now no specific objective reason to doubt that this multicritical point exists in the real model space, in contrast to the common view that only a critical point described by a complex CFT is possible [48, 51, 52, 53, 60].

In Sec. VI we also carry out similar analyses of the first-order lines of the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Z2Z_{2} and JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Z3Z_{3} models, which reveal no detectable changes in the order parameters when Z2Z_{2} or Z3Z_{3} is increased, even though the transition point evolves. This behavior implies that the Z2Z_{2} and Z3Z_{3} operators are dominated by their tt field content, which points to one plausible reason why many models show weak first-order AFM–VBS transitions (beyond the fact that the critical exponents β\beta and νs\nu_{s} imply large critical scaling regions): the overlap of the ss field with typical lattice interactions is small. Extreme operators such as the spatially large Q6Q_{6} terms are required to shift the transition significantly into the coexistence line (increasing the ss field).

In addition to the scaling dimensions of the relevant CFT operators listed in Table 1, in Sec. VII we extract the scaling dimensions of leading irrelevant perturbations of the SO(55) symmetry, using quantities probing the symmetry deformations inherent to the Hamiltonian (instead of analyzing corresponding correlation functions that decay very fast for irrelevant operators, thus being affected by large statistical errors). The leading lattice-induced ℤ4{\mathbb{Z}}_{4} deformation of the emergent U(11) symmetric VBS order parameter is detected in the size dependent distribution P⁡(Dx,Dy)P(D_{x},D_{y}) and corresponds in the SO(55) CFT to an ℓ=0\ell=0 (Lorentz spin), parity-even, rank-44 (internal symmetry) dangerously irrelevant primary operator, for which we obtain the scaling dimension denoted Δ4\Delta_{4}.

Surprisingly, we find that the inherent symmetry deformation involving both AFM and VBS components, detected via P⁡(Mz,Dx)P(M_{z},D_{x}), is not governed by Δ4\Delta_{4} but by a larger scaling dimension Δ2,3≈4.71\Delta_{2,3}\approx 4.71 which satisfies Δ2,3≈Δ4+1\Delta_{2,3}\approx\Delta_{4}+1. Here the subscripts 2,32,3 refer to violation of the symmetry between the 33-component AFM order parameter and the 22-component VBS order parameter. An exact relationship Δ2,3=Δ4+1\Delta_{2,3}=\Delta_{4}+1 would correspond to the first descendant of the rank-44 primary, which, however, is not possible because the symmetries of the Hamiltonian should not allow the presence of this operator. Given the exact SO(33) symmetry of the AFM order parameter 𝐌{\bf M} and the ℤ4\mathbb{Z}_{4} or U(11) symmetry of the VBS order parameter 𝐃{\bf D}, the probed perturbation is really one involving amplitudes, in the simplest form D2​M2D^{2}M^{2}. Decomposing this into its allowed SO(55) operators, the most likely scenario is that the deformation is dominated by the first irrelevant primary operator t′t^{\prime} in the same symmetry sector as the tt field driving the transition (the imposed deformation that is tuned to zero at the critical point), i.e., an irrelevant ℓ=0\ell=0, parity-even, rank-22 operator. Such an operator with scaling dimension ≈4.35\approx 4.35 was identified in the fuzzy sphere calculation [60], which, given the discrepancies in some of the other scaling dimensions in Table 1, is not that far off from our value. We thus posit that actually Δ2,3≡Δt′\Delta_{2,3}\equiv\Delta_{t}^{\prime}. The rank-44 operator with smaller scaling dimension Δ4≈3.7\Delta_{4}\approx 3.7 (≈3.9\approx 3.9 in the fuzzy sphere calculation) may be expected to eventually govern the behavior at the longest length scales but must have a comparably very small amplitude in the JJ-QQ models or, possibly, is completely absent. We will argue that the physical source of the deformation t′t^{\prime} indeed is an effectively repulsive interaction D2​M2D^{2}M^{2} between the AFM and VBS order parameters, which we also illustrate using a simple classical O(55) deformation model, which rules out the phase diagram with coexistence phase and tetracritical point in Fig. 2(c) (which would require an attractive interaction).

Moreover, the scaling dimension Δt′\Delta_{t^{\prime}} is related by Eq. (1) to the observed emergent exponent ν∗\nu_{*} of the pseudocritical (bubble) scale. As discussed above in Sec. II.2, a glaring inconsistency between previous results for JJ-QQ and loop models and potential CFT descriptions of the DQCP phenomenon has been the anomalously small correlation length extracted from various quantities, e.g., Binder cumulants [29, 90]. The value ν≈0.45\nu\approx 0.45 violates a generic CFT bound ν>0.51\nu>0.51 under the assumption of only one relevant perturbation that maintains all the symmetries of the Hamiltonian, i.e., the absence of relevant SO(55) singlet operators [64]. This bound is no longer of concern if there is a relevant singlet in the CFT spectrum, in which case the transition is fine-tuned as proposed in Refs. [54, 74]. However, as seen in Table 1, there is no scaling dimension Δ∗=3−1/ν≈0.80\Delta_{*}=3-1/\nu\approx 0.80 of the right symmetry in the CFT spectrum computed in Ref. [56] and also no operator close to this value in the fuzzy sphere calculation [60]. In Ref. [90] an apparent scaling dimension Δ∗≈0.80\Delta_{*}\approx 0.80 was actually identified in the form of a particular correlation function decaying as r−2​Δ∗r^{-2\Delta_{*}}. This value of Δ∗\Delta_{*} matched very well the correlation length exponent with its estimated value at the time, ν∗≈0.45\nu_{*}\approx 0.45, through the standard relationship 1/ν∗=3−Δ∗≈2.21/\nu_{*}=3-\Delta_{*}\approx 2.2. However, we now have a better way of estimating the pseudocritical exponent, from a scaling behavior of the emergent SO(55) away from the transition, which we investigate in Sec. VII.2 and find 1/ν∗≈2.401/\nu_{*}\approx 2.40. We believe that Δ∗\Delta_{*} (whose value stays close to 0.800.80 in the improved analysis here) is also associated in some way with the phenomenon of pseudocriticality, but we do not know the exact relationship (if any) between Δ∗\Delta_{*} and ν∗\nu_{*}. Δ∗\Delta_{*} has no impact on any other results in this work beyond presenting a lingering mystery. Presumably, a perturbation theory of the SO(55) CFT on the weak first-order line could answer this question, but this undertaking is beyond the scope of the present paper.

A major result of our work is that ν∗\nu_{*} can be derived from a generalization of results for a classical tetracritical point with emergent O(NN) symmetry by Bruce and Aharony [67]. They showed that the shape of phase boundaries of the coexistence phase of two order parameters, schematically drawn in Fig. 2(c), is given by a combination of the crossover exponent, νt\nu_{t} in the present context, and the scaling dimension of the leading irrelevant perturbation of the O(NN) symmetry. The tetracritical point with its adjacent coexistence phase forms in Landau theory as a result of attractive interactions between two order parameters [67], but as already mentioned we have ruled out a coexistence phase in the JJ-QQ model.

In Sec. VIII we will argue that, while there is no new phase induced by repulsive interactions, an associated crossover region nevertheless surrounds the first-order transition; schematically between the dashed and solid curves fanning out from the SO(55) point in Fig. 3. This region is associated with a length scale that we can derive by starting from scaling arguments previously developed for the attractive case. We arrive at the following expression, already presented in a different form as Eq. (1):

1ν∗=1νs​(1νt+|yt′|),\frac{1}{\nu_{*}}=\frac{1}{\nu_{s}}\left(\frac{1}{\nu_{t}}+|y_{t^{\prime}}|\right), (3)

where yt′=3−Δt′y_{t^{\prime}}=3-\Delta_{t^{\prime}}. Given our explicit determination of the scaling dimension of the inherent dangerously irrelevant SO(5)(5) perturbation (which becomes relevant on the first-order line) causing the asymmetry between the critical AFM and VBS order parameters, we will assume that Δt′\Delta_{t^{\prime}} is to be used here, not the smaller dimension Δ4\Delta_{4}, at least on the length scales accessible in practice close to the multicritical point (and note that the divergence of ξ∗\xi_{*} is anyway cut off in a manner similar to conventional first-order transitions when moving even closer to the transition, inside the fan marked by dashed curves in Fig. 3). The value of ν∗\nu_{*} extracted in Sec. VII.2 from a quantity corresponding to the size of the window within which emergent SO(55) symmetry is manifested (the regime where the repulsive order parameter interactions are relevant) is indeed fully consistent with this expression.

By using the extracted value of ν∗\nu_{*} together with our estimates for νt\nu_{t} and yt′y_{t^{\prime}}, we can alternatively solve Eq. (3) for 1/νs=3−Δs1/\nu_{s}=3-\Delta_{s}, which leads to our best value of Δs\Delta_{s} in Table 1. The value is close to the predicted CFT bootstrap value in Table 1 and, in combination with our values of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} and Δt\Delta_{t}, falls very close to previously computed SO(55) CFT bounds [65] (which are believed to be close to the true exponents [56]). In Sec. VI we show that our Δs\Delta_{s} value is also fully compatible with the growth of the coexisting order parameters when moving along the first-order line of the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model, i.e., the exponent β\beta that we extract from the order parameters on the first-order line to a precision of a few percent.

In Sec. VIII we show that a detailed understanding of the observed correlation length (as obtained from correlation functions or from critical data collapse procedures) requires all the relevant length scales, i.e., the three exponents νt\nu_{t}, νs\nu_{s}, and ν∗\nu_{*}. We further explain how the scaling crossover of the correlation length varies as the first-order line is crossed at different distances from the multicritical point as in Fig. 4, using the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model with different values of Q6Q_{6} (corresponding to kk in Fig. 4). The impact of the bubble length scale governed by ν∗\nu_{*} fades away as the critical point is approached, becoming truly extinct at the critical point.

The three length scales governed by νt\nu_{t}, νs\nu_{s}, and ν∗\nu_{*} impact also other physical observables that intrinsically are related to the correlation length. In Sec. IX we discuss the previous ansatz with two length scales (corresponding to νt\nu_{t} and ν∗\nu_{*}) [41] in light of our present understanding, which implies a reinterpretation of the physical nature of the length scales and their exponents assumed in Ref. [41] (but with the same scaling forms). While νt\nu_{t} and ν∗\nu_{*} often dominate scaling properties, accounting for the full finite-size dependence of many observables also requires that νs\nu_{s} is taken into account when the transition is crossed as in Figs. 2(a) and 2(b), where both the fields ss and tt are varied. We demonstrate the resulting intricate behavior using Binder cumulants and the spin stiffness ρs\rho_{s}.

IV Order parameters

Here we begin by precisely defining spin and dimer correlations and their critical exponents in Sec. IV.1. In Sec. IV.2 we present PQMC results for these correlations at distance r=L/2r=L/2 on lattices of size up to L=384L=384 for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model and somewhat smaller, L=320L=320, for the JJ-Q3Q_{3} and JJ-Q4Q_{4} models. The main result here is that the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model undergoes a very weak first-order transition, which is clearly detectable in the correlation functions of the order parameters only with high-quality data (small error bars) for large lattices. For increasing nn, the JJ-QnQ_{n} models host transitions of increasing first-order character, as seen in the magnitude of the coexisting AFM and VBS order parameters.

In Sec. IV.3, we examine the distance dependence of the correlation functions Cs,d​(r)C_{s,d}(r) and their rr derivatives. In the presence of the weak coexisting long-range orders at the transition point, the derivatives show power-law behaviors over longer distances and are useful for extracting the scaling dimension Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}, as was previously found with the 3D loop model [29]. In the case of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model, we present ground-state converged PQMC results for derivatives up to r=256r=256 for a system as large as L=1024L=1024, revealing a significant window of rr for which a scaling dimension Δϕ≈0.61\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.61 effectively governs the behavior of both the spin and dimer derivatives. To complement and confirm the validity of this approach, we also analyze the correlation functions themselves with scaling corrections included, using system sizes up to L=512L=512, which is the largest size for which the correlations are well converged to the ground state (i.e., the derivatives converge faster). The two approaches deliver compatible results for the AFM and VBS values of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}, with the individual scaling dimensions being the same to within statistical errors of less than 1%. Our best estimate of the common value is Δϕ=0.607​(4)\Delta_{\phi}=0.607(4).

IV.1 Spin and dimer correlation functions

We define the staggered spin correlation functions as

Cs​(𝐫)=⟨𝐒𝟎⋅𝐒𝐫⟩​ϵ𝟎​ϵ𝐫,C_{\rm s}({\bf r})=\langle{\bf S}_{\bf 0}\cdot{\bf S}_{\bf r}\rangle\epsilon_{\bf 0}\epsilon_{\bf r}, (4)

where ϵ𝐫=(−1)rx+ry\epsilon_{\bf r}=(-1)^{r_{x}+r_{y}} is the AFM phase factor for the spin at 𝐫=(rx,ry){\bf r}=(r_{x},r_{y}). The dimer correlation function is defined as

Cd​(𝐫)=[⟨(𝐒𝟎⋅𝐒𝐱^)​(𝐒𝐫⋅𝐒𝐫+𝐱^)⟩−⟨𝐒𝟎⋅𝐒𝐱^⟩2]​θ𝟎​θ𝐫C_{\rm d}({\bf r})=[\langle({\bf S}_{\bf 0}\cdot{\bf S}_{\bf\hat{x}})({\bf S}_{\bf r}\cdot{\bf S}_{\bf r+\hat{x}})\rangle-\langle{\bf S}_{\bf 0}\cdot{\bf S}_{\bf\hat{x}}\rangle^{2}]\theta_{\bf 0}\theta_{\bf r} (5)

where x^=(1,0)\hat{x}=(1,0) is the lattice vector in the xx direction and θ𝐫=(−1)rx\theta_{\bf r}=(-1)^{r_{x}} is the appropriate phase factor for a columnar dimer pattern in the ordered state, corresponding to the wave-vector of the dominant critical fluctuations; q=(π,0)q=(\pi,0) and (0,π)(0,\pi) (the latter with x↔yx\leftrightarrow y in the above definitions). In all cases, we average translationally over the reference spin r=0r=0 and also use the reflection and rotation symmetries of the square lattice as appropriate.

In a system with long-range order of a given kind, the corresponding long-distance correlation function should converge to a nonzero value representing the square m2m^{2} of the ordered moment, while in a critical system a power law decay of the form

C⁡(r)∝r−2​Δϕ≡r−(1+ηϕ)C(r)\propto r^{-2\Delta_{\phi}}\equiv r^{-(1+\eta_{\phi})} (6)

should be observed asymptotically. Here Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} is the scaling dimension of the order parameter considered, and its indicated relationship to the critical exponent ηϕ\eta_{\phi} (the anomalous dimension) is

2​Δϕ=d+z−2+ηϕ2\Delta_{\phi}=d+z-2+\eta_{\phi} (7)

for spatial dimensionality d=2d=2 and dynamic exponent z=1z=1. Evidence for z=1z=1 was presented already in the first study of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model [28] and later, e.g., in Ref. [164]. The similarities between the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model and the manifestly space-time invariant classical 3D loop model [29, 33] also supports z=1z=1, as we already discussed in Sec. II.2.

Below we will show both the spin and dimer correlations only for separations along the line 𝐫=(r,0){\bf r}=(r,0). We have also computed the correlations along the lines (r,r)(r,r) and (0,r)(0,r), the latter of which is not equivalent to (r,0)(r,0) in the case of CdC_{d} for the xx-oriented dimer operator. We find the same type of behavior (including the decay exponent that we extract) in all cases in both spin and dimer correlations.

IV.2 Phase coexistence in JJ-QnQ_{n} models

Long-distance correlation functions in finite systems can be studied either by considering distances r≪Lr\ll L for large LL or by taking one of the longest distances in a periodic system, e.g., r=L/2r=L/2. The former approach delivers the true correlation function in the thermodynamic limit, while C⁡(L/2)C(L/2) for large LL extrapolates to the correct squared order parameter in a system with long-range order. In a critical CFT system, the same scaling exponent governs the correlations versus rr and versus LL, while the overall factor is different because of boundary enhancements when r≈L/2r\approx L/2. For the purpose of detecting weak long-range order, investigating C⁡(L/2)C(L/2) versus LL is preferable, as only the behavior versus the single parameter LL has to be monitored.

Figure 5(a) shows both spin and dimer correlations at r=L/2r=L/2 versus 1/L1/L at the value of the critical coupling ratio of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model obtained from Binder cumulant crossings in Ref. [90]. It is certainly clear that any nonzero values for L→∞L\to\infty must be very small, suggesting a critical point or very nearly critical ground state. For system sizes up to about L=100L=100, power laws can describe the behaviors reasonably well, e.g., in Ref. [163] the exponent 1+η≈1.271+\eta\approx 1.27 was found this way for both spin and dimer correlations. However, the exponent drifts significantly for larger systems. For the 3D loop model, system sizes up to L≈500L\approx 500 were considered [29] and it was found that η\eta extracted under the assumption of the critical form Eq. (6) eventually tends toward negative values, while for shorter distances η\eta matches well the value in the JJ-QQ model. Such drifting behavior is also found with the present results in Fig. 5(a).

In Figs. 5(b) and 5(c) we zoom in on the largest system sizes for three different values of JJ (here keeping Q2=1Q_{2}=1) close to the transition point. Comparing the variations in the spin and dimer correlations in this small window of couplings leaves little doubt that there is one value of JJ, or possibly a very small range of values, for which both order parameters extrapolate to nonzero values. Thus, instead of a critical ground state, AFM and VBS long-range orders coexist, as expected at a first-order transition or in a coexistence phase. We will later, in Sec. VII.2, provide strong evidence for no finite coexistence phase, only a first-order AFM–VBS coexistence line (on which we will move by adjusting another coupling in Sec. VI). The present data indicate that the transition value of JJ is between the values 0.045000.04500 and 0.045050.04505; slightly lower than the estimate in Ref. [90] but close to an older estimate based on correlation lengths in Ref. [166].

The dashed curves in Figs. 5(b) and 5(c) are cubic polynomial fits to the data at both J=0.04500J=0.04500 and 0.045050.04505 (i.e., one function was collectively fitted to two data sets) in order for the curve to roughly correspond to the behavior at the transition point. While these curves likely provide reasonably good estimates for the coexistence state located between these two couplings, they are here intended only to illustrate the main qualitative trends. More detailed analysis of the nonzero L→∞L\to\infty order parameters will be deferred to Sec. VI, where we move further into the first-order coexistence state by introducing a third tunable interaction (Q6Q_{6}).

A leading linear correction in 1/L1/L of the order parameter is expected in general for a system breaking O(N>1N>1) symmetry, reflecting gapless Goldstone modes with their associated transverse correlations decaying as 1/r1/r in two spatial dimensions. The AFM order parameter is O(33) symmetric [strictly speaking SO(33), but the lack of reflection symmetry of the AFM state is irrelevant here] and the ultimately ℤ4{\mathbb{Z}}_{4} symmetric VBS order parameter has emergent U(11) symmetry up to some length scale (as discussed further in Sec. VII.1) in a near-critical VBS phase. Moreover, the two order parameters develop emergent SO(55) symmetry (discussed in Sec. VII.2), and so the 1/L1/L behavior with corrections in the form of higher powers in Figs. 5(b) and 5(c) is expected for both order parameters over some range of system sizes, both inside the respective ordered phases and at the transition point. As will be shown in detail in Sec. IV.3, the distance dependence of the correlations is characterized by a crossover from critical power-law decay to the nonzero squared ordered moment of the coexistence state.

In Fig. 6 we show results for the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model close to its AFM–VBS transition. Here we only draw straight lines in 1/L1/L through the data points for the largest systems. We note that the dimer correlation for the largest size (L=320L=320) deviates slightly upward from the linear behavior, and there is also a less apparent downtrend in the spin correlation. These behaviors suggest that the value of JJ used here is marginally inside the VBS phase. Focusing on the AFM order parameter, where linear behavior exactly at the transition should persist when L→∞L\to\infty both inside the AFM phase and on the coexistence line (which is in practice close enough to the JJ value used here), we see that the extrapolated correlation function is roughly twice that of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model in Fig. 5(b), i.e., the first-order discontinuity is stronger in the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model, though not very dramatically so. The VBS order parameter actually appears to be a bit smaller, but it should be kept in mind that the extrapolation is likely not quantitatively reliable.

Moving on to the JJ-Q4Q_{4} model, in Fig. 7 we show data for values of the QQ coupling (here with J+Q=1J+Q=1) close to the transition as well as further inside the ordered phases. The roughly extrapolated order parameters of the coexistence state are clearly significantly higher than those of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} and JJ-Q3Q_{3} models.

In Fig. 7(b) we observe nonmonotonic behavior of the dimer order parameter inside the VBS phase, close to the transition point. Such behavior is natural in the neighborhood of a first-order transition (another example was discussed in Ref. [191]), where a small system effectively is in the coexistence state and the order parameter that eventually is stabilized is averaged together with its much smaller value pertaining when the system fluctuates into the other phase. Once the system is large enough, it no longer fluctuates between the two phases, and the computed order parameter therefore represents, in the limit of infinite system size, the actual value in the ordered phase. The nonmonotonic behavior is only completely observable in Fig. 7(b) at Q=0.4140Q=0.4140, but the upward trend is clear also at Q=0.4130Q=0.4130 and Q=0.4127Q=0.4127. A precursor to the increasing behavior is seen at Q=0.4126Q=0.4126. The maximum seen at L≈150L\approx 150 at Q=0.4140Q=0.4140 gradually diminishes as QQ is increased further and eventually (data not shown here) a completely monotonic behavior sets in, with Cd​(L/2)C_{d}(L/2) rapidly approaching (on account of the gapped VBS state with finite correlation length) its L→∞L\to\infty value from above.

In Fig. 7(a) the spin correlations do not exhibit nonmonotonicity for the available system sizes, though likely a maximum followed by convergence from above would also set in here for larger system sizes. Precursors similar to those preceding the upturn with increasing LL in Fig. 7(b) are seen, and the same arguments for nonmonotonicity apply in the AFM phase as well. The less pronounced nonmonotonic behavior here should follow because the AFM order parameter has three components with exact SO(33) symmetry, representing a larger phase space compared to the eventually discrete four-fold degenerate VBS pattern. The fluctuations out of the AFM phase, even relatively close to the transition point, will therefore be weaker.

Clearly, in both phases, the nonmonotonic behaviors will shift to larger systems upon moving closer to the transition point, and exactly at the transition the crossover out of the coexistence phase never takes place; thus a monotonic behavior is expected at the transition point. It is very difficult (computationally expensive) to locate the transition point to sufficient precision to follow the coexisting order parameters for large LL. The transition window shrinks rapidly with increasing system size—in classical dd-dimensional systems as L−dL^{-d} and, correspondingly in quantum systems as L−d−zL^{-d-z}, where zz is the dynamic exponent (which likely should be taken as z=2z=2 for long-ranged order parameters with continuous symmetry [34]). The relative probability of either of the two phases changes smoothly from close to 00 to close to 11 when traversing this narrow window.

The curves fitted in Fig. 7 can represent the size dependence when the coexisting order parameters have developed the emergent SO(55) symmetry. This symmetry must eventually break down (as discussed further in Sec. VII.2), which should be accompanied by a crossover of the order parameters versus 1/L1/L also at the transition point. The SO(33) symmetric AFM order parameter should still approach its infinite-size limit as 1/L1/L, but with a different constant of proportionality. Due to its ultimate discrete nature, the VBS order parameter will asymptotically converge exponentially. Such crossovers, which require very large sizes to be observed in these models, make it essentially impossible to extract the discontinuities in the order parameters at the transition. For scaling purposes, we have nevertheless found a practically useful method for extrapolating the strength of the coexisting order parameters, which we do on the first-order line of the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model in Sec. VI.

IV.3 Scaling dimension of the order parameters

In the first study of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model [28], in PQMC simulations of system sizes up to L=32L=32 it was found that the critical decay of the AFM and VBS order parameters was similar, with an exponent η=0.26​(3)\eta=0.26(3), or Δϕ≈0.630​(15)\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.630(15) by Eq. (6). Later studies for larger lattices found consistent results, e.g., in Ref. [163] η≈0.27\eta\approx 0.27 described both order parameters for LL up to 9696. These results were based on the distance integrated correlation functions, which scale with the system size in the same way as the r≪Lr\ll L correlator with rr. For a generic correlation function C⁡(r)C(r) the squared order parameter is

m2=1N​∑𝐫|C⁡(𝐫)|,m^{2}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf r}|C({\bf r})|, (8)

and if C⁡(r)∼r−2​ΔϕC(r)\sim r^{-2\Delta_{\phi}} then m2​(L)∼L−2​Δϕm^{2}(L)\sim L^{-2\Delta_{\phi}}.

In the 3D loop model [29], a study of much larger system sizes revealed that η\eta extracted from correlation functions at r=L/2r=L/2 drifts toward smaller values with increasing LL, eventually turning negative. For small to moderate values of rr, up to r≈20r\approx 20, the above quoted values of η\eta still describe the behavior, however, thus lending support to the loop and JJ-QQ models hosting the same kind of critical fluctuations. The behavior of η\eta turning negative (with 1+η1+\eta eventually tending to 00 at the first-order transition that is now without doubt) can clearly be understood as arising from the small ordered moment of a coexistence state, which dominates the correlation function for large distances; C⁡(r)→m2C(r)\to m^{2} for r→∞r\to\infty, while not affecting much the critical fluctuations for small rr.

Nahum et al. [29] further made a very interesting and useful observation: the first discrete rr derivative of the correlation functions exhibited good power-law scaling, C′​(r)∼r−2−ηC^{\prime}(r)\sim r^{-2-\eta}, up to much larger distances than C⁡(r)∼r−1−ηC(r)\sim r^{-1-\eta}. For L=512L=512, power law decays were observed for distances up to r≈200r\approx 200, with ηs=0.256​(6)\eta_{s}=0.256(6) and ηd=0.25​(3)\eta_{d}=0.25(3), respectively, for the AFM and VBS correlations (with the larger error bar on the VBS result explained by much larger statistical errors of the dimer correlations). This much extended scaling behavior of the derivatives can be explained by writing the correlation function (spin or dimer) for a finite system as

C⁡(r,L)=C1​(r)+C2​(L)+C3​(r,L),C(r,L)=C_{1}(r)+C_{2}(L)+C_{3}(r,L), (9)

which clearly can always be done, with non-uniqueness circumvented by (in principle) minimizing C3C_{3}. In the case at hand, one would suspect that C1​(r)C_{1}(r) is close to the critical power law described by the exponent 1+η1+\eta and C2​(L)C_{2}(L) is essentially the small size dependent magnetization squared, i.e., a function similar to Cs,d​(L/2)C_{s,d}(L/2) in Figs. 5, 6, and 7. The mixed term C3​(r,L)C_{3}(r,L) can of course not completely vanish, but if it is relatively small until rr approaches L/2L/2 then C′​(r,L)=∂C⁡(r,L)/∂rC^{\prime}(r,L)=\partial C(r,L)/\partial r will be close to d​C1​(r)/d​rdC_{1}(r)/dr, which, in turn, should be close to the critical form ∝r−2−η\propto r^{-2-\eta}. The results of Ref. [29] clearly showed this to be the case for the AFM and VBS correlation functions of the 3D loop model.

We here test the derivative method for the JJ-QQ models. We also fit the correlation function itself to a form including appropriate scaling corrections. Both methods produce compatible values of the scaling dimension, Δϕ≈0.61\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.61 from both spin and dimer correlations, slightly smaller than most previous estimates—in particular the SO(55) CFT input value Δϕ=0.63\Delta_{\phi}=0.63 in Table 1.

IV.3.1 Correlation functions and derivatives

We first examine the rr dependent spin and dimer correlation functions on relatively large systems, L=384L=384 for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model and L=320L=320 for the JJ-Q3Q_{3} and JJ-Q4Q_{4} models. Ground state results for Cs,d​(r)C_{s,d}(r) from PQMC simulations are shown in Fig. 8. For the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model the two couplings that we previously determined as brackets of the transition point (Fig. 5) are used in Fig. 8(a). The results are indistinguishable in the plot for short distances but slightly split off from each other for longer distances. The lines show the decay expected for a critical system with the scaling dimension Δϕ=0.63\Delta_{\phi}=0.63 assumed in the CFT bootstrap calculation [56], which is within the error bars of the values obtained with the loop model [29] and is also consistent with earlier results for the JJ-QQ model [28, 163]. The form indeed describes reasonably well both the AFM and VBS data up to r≈20r\approx 20, though corrections are also clearly present. It is not possible to determine a reliable exponent from these results from a fit to a single power law, primarily because of the crossover to a much slower decaying form reflecting the weak long-range order, but also because of the short-distance corrections. The results overall look very similar to those for the 3D loop model [33].

For the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model, in Fig. 8(b) we show results for the same near-critical coupling as in Fig. 5. Again the short-distance behaviors, beyond the regime where corrections are apparent, are reasonably well described by a common exponent Δϕ=0.63\Delta_{\phi}=0.63. This behavior applies up to somewhat shorter distances than for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model, which again indicates a slightly more ordered coexistence state. The same trend of diminishing range of the critical decay, due to more pronounced long-range order, is seen for the JJ-Q4Q_{4} model in Fig. 8(c), where we show results for the two couplings bracketing the transition point according to Fig. 7.

Next we study the derivatives. To minimize discretization errors, we use the fourth-order approximant of the first rr derivative and define C′​(r)C^{\prime}(r) with an overall minus sign in order to have a positive quantity;

C′​(r)\displaystyle C^{\prime}(r) =\displaystyle= 23​[C⁡(r−1)−C⁡(r+1)]\displaystyle\frac{2}{3}\left[C(r-1)-C(r+1)\right] (10)
−112​[C⁡(r−2)−C⁡(r+2)].\displaystyle~~-\frac{1}{12}\left[C(r-2)-C(r+2)\right].

Results for all three models and the same lattice sizes as above are shown in Fig. 9. The derivatives are not as sensitive as the correlation functions themselves to the exact value of the coupling in the neighborhood of the transition point. To reduce the statistical errors further, we have therefore taken the average over the two couplings used in Fig. 8(a) and Fig. 8(c) for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} and JJ-Q3Q_{3} model, respectively, which also corresponds to an interpolation with the two data sets to a value closer to the transition point than the two individual values.

For all three models, we find a very substantial range of distances over which the decay is closely described by ∝r−1−2​Δϕ\propto r^{-1-2\Delta_{\phi}}, with Δϕ≈0.63\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.63. The behavior is very similar to that in the 3D loop model [29]. It is remarkable that even the JJ-Q4Q_{4} model exhibits this critical behavior up to distances r≈100r\approx 100, though with larger corrections than the JJ-Q2Q_{2} and JJ-Q3Q_{3} models. This critical behavior is manifested even though the model has a clearly ordered coexistence state according to the size dependent correlation functions in Fig. 7—with the AFM correlations extrapolating to a value about 10 times larger than in the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model in Fig. 5. The good agreement between these results for all three JJ-QnQ_{n} models, as well as the previously studied 3D loop model [29], should leave no doubt that the behavior reflects universal scaling originating from a nearby critical point.

We use the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model, the transition of which is the closest to the critical point, to extract the most reliable value of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}. Based on just the results for L=384L=384 in Fig. 9(a), it appears that the data agree with the previous estimates of the scaling dimension, Δϕ≈0.63\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.63. However, the indicated scaling behavior is statistically good only over distance windows of a few tens of lattice spacings, and the best exponent also depends to some extent on how the window is chosen. We therefore proceed to study the evolution of the derivatives Cs,d′​(r)C^{\prime}_{s,d}(r) with increasing system size and also take corrections to the leading power law behavior into account in fits to Cs,d​(r)C_{s,d}(r).

As we have seen, the derivatives show much better scaling than the correlation functions themselves, for reasons that can be understood based on Eq. (9) when there is weak long-range order. We have observed a related favorable aspect of the PQMC simulation algorithm: the derivatives at large rr converge significantly faster with the projection power than the correlations themselves. The variant of the PQMC method used here (Sec. III.1) samples contributions to the normalization of the ground state projected out of a singlet state, ⟨Ψ|(−H)p​N|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|(-H)^{pN}|\Psi\rangle, where pp typically has to be larger than the system length LL for complete convergence to the ground state (we often use p=2​Lp=2L). In contrast, the derivatives of the spin correlations are well converged already for p≈L/2p\approx L/2, which allows us to reach larger system sizes when targeting the derivative C′​(r)C^{\prime}(r), even though C⁡(r)C(r) is not yet fully converged to the ground state. The derivative of the dimer correlation function appears to converge somewhat slower and is also noisier. We therefore only analyze the derivative of the spin correlation function here, using system sizes up to L=1024L=1024.

The faster convergence of C′​(r)C^{\prime}(r) can likely be traced to the role of the long-range ordered component of C⁡(r)C(r). The value of the ordered moment, which should most strongly affect the rr-independent term C2​(L)C_{2}(L) in Eq. (9), converges relatively slowly, while the power-law contribution dominating C1​(r)C_{1}(r) at the transition converges faster. In Fig. 10 we show results for system sizes L=256L=256, 512512, and 10241024, in each case with the projection parameter p=L/16p=L/16, L/8L/8, L/4L/4, and L/2L/2. In the case of L=1024L=1024, the largest pp is slightly smaller, p=500p=500 instead of 512512, because this is the largest value of pp for which our implementation of the PQMC method works with four-byte integers; with an address space of 2322^{32} elements of a linked list of vertices (see Refs. [166] and [111] for technical details on the sampling procedures). For L=256L=256 and L=512L=512 we also include results for p=2​Lp=2L, where also C⁡(r)C(r) is fully converged. In Fig. 10 we have multiplied the derivatives by r2.26r^{2.26}, which would give rr independent values (over some range of distances) if the scaling dimension takes the previously assumed value Δϕ=0.63\Delta_{\phi}=0.63.

For L=256L=256 and L=512L=512, already p=L/4p=L/4 gives well converged results for C′​(r)C^{\prime}(r). For 10241024, there are still some differences between the results for p=256p=256 and 500500. For L=512L=512, convergence is explicitly confirmed by the essentially perfect agreement between the results for p=L/2p=L/2 and p=2​Lp=2L. Given that reasonably good convergence is also seen for L=512L=512 already with p=L/4p=L/4 and the rather small differences between p=L/4p=L/4 and p≈L/2p\approx L/2 for L=1024L=1024, the latter calculation should also be well converged within error bars.

These results for three large system sizes allow us to refine the value of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}. We have fitted power laws to a range of distances where such behavior appears to hold. Though the range of distances with approximative power-law behavior is limited, it grows with increasing system size and an effective size dependent scaling dimension can be defined to within a rather small level of uncertainty.

In Fig. 10(a), we see that the effective scaling dimension is larger than 0.630.63 for L=256L=256, i.e., the power-law decay is faster than r−2.26r^{-2.26}. However, for both L=512L=512 and L=1024L=1024 the decay for large distances is slightly slower, corresponding to Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} smaller than 0.630.63. The decay exponent adjusted by the multiplier r2.26r^{2.26} is in the range [2.236,2.240][2.236,2.240] for L=512L=512 and [2.218,2.224][2.218,2.224] for L=1024L=1024, suggesting a rather rapid convergence for these larger systems and a scaling dimension Δϕ≈0.61\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.61. However, it should also be noted that the window of apparent power law behavior shifts to larger distances with increasing LL, which shows that the corrections to the leading power law continue to play some role and may still affect the effective exponent even for L=1024L=1024.

IV.3.2 Scaling corrections

To further investigate the stability of the value of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}, we also perform an analysis including scaling corrections, using fully converged C⁡(r)C(r) results for L=256L=256, 384384, and 512512. In order to properly account for the enhancement of the slowly decaying correlations close to (and even quite far away from) r=L/2r=L/2, because of the periodic boundary conditions, we should not just fit to a sum of power laws but use a form that respects the necessary condition C⁡(r)=C⁡(L−r)C(r)=C(L-r). For a quantum system in one spatial dimension, the proper CFT geometry is a periodic chain (a ring), where the conformal distance for a system of length LL is given by the chord length

x=(L/2)​sin⁡(r​π/L),x=(L/2)\sin{(r\pi/L)}, (11)

for lattice distances r=0,1,…,L−1r=0,1,\ldots,L-1. In two spatial dimensions, the proper conformal geometry is a sphere. On the torus, we still find it useful to define the distance xx as above with rr on the line (r,0)(r,0), which guarantees reflection symmetry about r=L/2r=L/2 of whatever function is fitted for x∈[0,L/2]x\in[0,L/2]. In the context of our 2D system, we will refer to xx as the proxy conformal distance.

The dominant corrections to the asymptotic critical form C⁡(x)∼x−2​ΔϕC(x)\sim x^{-2\Delta_{\phi}} would normally arise from conventional corrections, with the leading one often written as a factor x−ωx^{-\omega} with ω≡|yi|\omega\equiv|y_{i}| the smallest of all yi=3−Δiy_{i}=3-\Delta_{i} values with Δi>3\Delta_{i}>3 for irrelevant perturbations. There will also be contributions from descendants of the ϕ\phi operator. Because of lattice symmetry, only those with Lorentz spin ℓ=0\ell=0 mod 44 (with scaling dimensions Δϕ+2,Δϕ+4,…\Delta_{\phi}+2,\Delta_{\phi}+4,\ldots) are present and they produce power-law contributions by themselves and from cross-terms with the primary. Thus, contributions x−2​Δϕx^{-2\Delta_{\phi}}, x−(2​Δϕ+2)x^{-(2\Delta_{\phi}+2)}, x−(2​Δϕ+4)x^{-(2\Delta_{\phi}+4)} etc. are expected and the correction x−ωx^{-\omega} (and higher-order ones with larger ω\omega values) multiply all these collectively. Moreover, we have to account for the fact that there is also weak long-range order, which we do by adding a constant m2m^{2}.

Fitting the spin and dimer correlations, we find that the form m2+a​x−2​Δϕ+b​x−(2​Δϕ+2)m^{2}+ax^{-2\Delta_{\phi}}+bx^{-(2\Delta_{\phi}+2)} with Δϕ≈0.61\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.61 produces reasonable fits to the data except for the shortest distances, and by including also c​x−(2​Δϕ+4)cx^{-(2\Delta_{\phi}+4)} several shorter distances can also be included. The leading irrelevant correction (i.e., arising from an intrinsic perturbation in the lattice model) typically has ω≈1\omega\approx 1, e.g., in classical O(NN) models [189, 63] but such corrections appear to be missing here. It is possible that ω≈2\omega\approx 2 and therefore x−(2​Δϕ+ω)x^{-(2\Delta_{\phi}+\omega)} cannot be distinguished in fits from the expected term x−(2​Δϕ+2)x^{-(2\Delta_{\phi}+2)}. In the fuzzy sphere calculation [60] the only identified symmetry-allowed (in the square-lattice JJ-QQ models) perturbations with scaling dimension less than ≈5\approx 5 (i.e., corresponding to ω≲2\omega\lesssim 2) are those also studied here in Sec. VII; the SO(55) violating operators with scaling dimensions Δ4≈3.7\Delta_{4}\approx 3.7 and Δt′≈4.7\Delta_{t^{\prime}}\approx 4.7. The former corresponds to ω≈0.7\omega\approx 0.7, but the fact that we do not observe any such correction implies that this perturbation must have a very weak effect on the correlation functions. The larger dimension Δt′\Delta_{t^{\prime}} corresponds to ω≈1.7\omega\approx 1.7, which is likely close enough to 22 to not be detectable in the presence of other similar contributions. Overall, the fact that Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} extracted from both spin and dimer correlations are the same within small error bars (quantified below) suggests that intrinsic SO(55) violations are not important here (though clearly detectable in finite-size scaling of specific quantities in Sec. VII). The leading correction should then indeed arise from the x−(2​Δϕ+2)x^{-(2\Delta_{\phi}+2)} mixed primary and descendant contribution. Fitting to m2+a​x−2​Δϕ+b​x−(2​Δϕ+ω)m^{2}+ax^{-2\Delta_{\phi}}+bx^{-(2\Delta_{\phi}+\omega)}, the correction exponent ω\omega indeed comes out close to 22 and when fixing ω\omega to different values close to 22 there is no significant change in the resulting Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}.

While remaining agnostic as to the actual source of the corrections to the leading power law, given the above we here discuss results obtained with the fitting form

C⁡(x)=m2+ax2​Δϕ+bx2​Δϕ+2+cx2​Δϕ+4,C(x)=m^{2}+\frac{a}{x^{2\Delta_{\phi}}}+\frac{b}{x^{2\Delta_{\phi}+2}}+\frac{c}{x^{2\Delta_{\phi}+4}}, (12)

without any explicit further correction in the form of a factor (1+d​x−ω)(1+dx^{-\omega}). This form still cannot be completely correct, not just because of neglected higher-order terms but because additional terms beyond m2m^{2} should be expected in the ordered coexistence state. Given that the system at the transition point has emergent SO(55) symmetry, we should expect contributions to the correlation functions from the four associated Goldstone modes of the weakly ordered coexistence state (which is not symmetry-broken on the finite lattices we study), up to some large system size beyond which the SO(55) symmetry is violated due to perturbations that are irrelevant at the critical point but relevant in the ordered coexistence state (often referred to as dangerously irrelevant operators). Even after this crossover, the AFM component of the coexistence state has exact SO(33) symmetry and two associated Goldstone modes. The leading Goldstone contributions decay as r−1r^{-1}, i.e., slower than the critical correlations that we have assumed to be dominant above. The Goldstone contributions arise from the transverse fluctuations of the order parameter and its amplitude should be of the order of the stiffness constant (helicity modulus) of the SO(55) or SO(33) order parameter.

We analyze the spin stiffness ρs\rho_{s} at the transition point in Sec. IX.3 and find a very small value in the thermodynamic limit; as expected given the small ordered moment of the coexistence state. We therefore assume that the Goldstone contribution will not significantly impact the fitted value of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} as long as we restrict the fit to relatively short distances, thus largely avoiding the complications arising from the crossover into the expected complicated large-rr behavior. The constant m2m^{2} in Eq. (12) is necessary in order to obtain good fits even with only short-distance data included; it should be interpreted as a way to approximately include the effects of the long-range order at short to intermediate distances, as was also argued in Ref. [62]. We have nevertheless also explored fits with an additional x−1x^{-1} Goldstone term, which we will further comment on below.

We here use interpolated data at our best estimate of the transition point, (J/Q2)c=0.04502​(1)(J/Q_{2})_{c}=0.04502(1), which again falls between the ratios 0.045000.04500 and 0.045050.04505 that bracket the transition based on the correlation functions above in Sec. IV.3.1 but is obtained from extrapolating cumulant crossings in Sec. IX.1. We only consider even distances rr to avoid small even-odd effects seen in Fig. 8.

We first discuss fits including also the longest distances. With only the leading correction and constant included, i.e., c=0c=0 in Eq. (12), we can obtain visually good fits to Eq. (12) for all r≥10r\geq 10 (x≳15x\gtrsim 15), as shown in Fig. 11 for both spin and dimer correlations and system sizes L=256L=256, 384384, and 512512. The proxy conformal distance indeed works very well, suggesting that Eq. (11) should be close to an ideal CFT distance definition also in two spatial dimensions. All of these fits deliver values of the scaling dimension Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} close to 0.610.61. Deviations from Eq. (12) when this function is extended below the shortest distance included in the fitting procedure are obvious, but all the data points can be fitted well once the second correction, with exponent 2​Δϕ+42\Delta_{\phi}+4 in Eq. (12), is included (fits not shown here). The value of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} changes only marginally when the second correction is included.

While the fits in Fig. 11 look good for xx in the fitting range, they are actually of very poor statistical quality. Because data at different distances are highly correlated, it is necessary to compute the full covariance matrix and use it in the definition of the goodness of the fit χ2\chi^{2}. The dominant source of covariance—the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue—is a common, almost uniform fluctuation. The eigenvalue of this mode is typically (for large systems) more than an order of magnitude larger than the second largest eigenvalue. Therefore, even a statistically substandard fit can look visually good, with the fitted function falling very close to the center of the data points, as in Fig. 11, even though there are statistically significant deviations when covariance is properly taken into account.

Henceforth we include data covariance and assure statistical soundness by monitoring the reduced-χ2\chi^{2} value defined with the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix (in many cases using only the largest few eigenvalues, corresponding to clearly non-singular directions). In Fig. 12 we use smaller ranges of distances in order to eliminate distortions by potential shortcomings of the functional form Eq. (12) at both short and long distances. Here we also include the second correction, and in all cases we still obtain Δϕ≈0.61\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.61. However, in the case of the spin correlations, where we use the range of lattice distances r∈[10,40]r\in[10,40] in Fig. 12(a), the statistical quality of the fits is still not good, having reduced-χ2\chi^{2} values close to 5050 for L=256L=256 and 384384 and about 88 for L=512L=512, despite the fact that the relative deviation of the fitted function from the data points is typically less than 10−410^{-4}, as shown in the inset of Fig. 12(a). These remarkably small deviations are an order of magnitude below the naive statistical errors of the data points, defined using only the diagonal elements of the covariance matrix. The deviations versus xx show very similar patterns for all three system sizes, demonstrating that they are not purely statistical in nature but arise from additional corrections not taken into account by Eq. (12). Slightly changing the second correction from the form x−(2​Δϕ+2)x^{-(2\Delta_{\phi}+2)} to x−(2​Δϕ+ω)x^{-(2\Delta_{\phi}+\omega)} with ω≈2\omega\approx 2 does not alter the overall shape of the relative deviations versus rr. Including an overall multiplicative correction (1+d​x−ω)(1+dx^{-\omega}) improves the quality of the fit somewhat, but at the same time makes the target Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} value much more uncertain. In an absolute sense, the deviations from the fit without the further correction are very small and cannot appreciably distort the extracted value of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}, but they still cause formally poor χ2\chi^{2} values because of the very small eigenvalues of the covariance matrix (beyond the largest eigenvalue corresponding to the unison fluctuation). Below, we will still achieve full statistical soundness by further restricting the range of rr in the fit.

The dimer correlations, shown in Fig. 12(b) for distances r∈[10,60]r\in[10,60], have larger overall statistical errors and show less effects of neglected higher-order corrections. The χ2\chi^{2} values are good for all system sizes. While the deviations of the data from the fit have some similarities for small xx, and also for larger xx in the case of L=256L=256 and L=384L=384, they look quite different for L=512L=512 at larger xx, where the statistical errors are larger and the systematic deviations are therefore likely masked by the noise. For a given LL, the deviations are still not independent for different xx values, because of the covariance effects. Repeating the fitting procedure many times with Gaussian noise added to the data transformed to the eigenbasis of the covariance matrix (with the magnitude of the noise set by each eigenvalue), we can also obtain statistical errors (one standard deviation) on the scaling dimension. The final results from the dimer correlations with r∈[10,60]r\in[10,60] are Δϕ=0.592​(2)\Delta_{\phi}=0.592(2) for L=256L=256, 0.606​(3)0.606(3) for L=384L=384, and 0.606​(5)0.606(5) for L=512L=512.

In the case of the spin correlations, to achieve statistically good fits and compute meaningful error bars, we further reduce the range of distances to r∈[14,28]r\in[14,28], i.e., using only eight data points in the fit to the five-parameter form Eq. (12). While the number of degrees of freedom is now very small (3), the fits are statistically sound and deliver the following values of the scaling dimension: Δϕ=0.601​(2)\Delta_{\phi}=0.601(2) for L=256L=256, 0.605​(2)0.605(2) for L=384L=384, and 0.606​(5)0.606(5) for L=512L=512, all of which are consistent with the results obtained for the larger range r∈[10,40]r\in[10,40] in Fig. 11. Overall, the statistical errors of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} are very similar to those above from the dimer correlations. Though the raw dimer correlations have significantly larger statistical errors, these errors are compensated by the fact that a wider range of points can be included in fits with acceptable χ2\chi^{2} values. In fact, the range of the dimer correlations can be further extended and still allow good fits with only marginal changes in Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}, but to stay on the safe side in light of potential Goldstone effects we restrict the analysis to r∈[12,60]r\in[12,60] in Fig. 12(b).

The four scaling dimensions extracted from the spin and dimer correlations for L=384L=384 and 512512 are mutually consistent, while they are slightly smaller for L=256L=256. The size dependence is much weaker than what is observed in the derivative of the spin correlation function versus the original lattice distance rr in Fig. 10. The Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} value estimated from the L=1024L=1024 derivative in Fig. 10(c) is fully consistent with the results from the correlation functions at shorter distances for L=384L=384 and 512512.

If a Goldstone contribution e​x−1ex^{-1} is added to the fitted function, the amplitude ee becomes unrealistically large (given the small ordered moment and associated ρs\rho_{s} value) and the scaling dimension Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} becomes much larger, above 22, to compensate for the large x−1x^{-1} contribution. With our extracted value Δϕ≈0.61\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.61, the forms x−1x^{-1} and x−2​Δϕx^{-2\Delta_{\phi}} are very close to each other, and it is not surprising that they cannot be separated in an unconstrained fit. We can also add the e/xe/x term while keeping Δϕ≈0.61\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.61 and fitting only at long distances. Then the amplitude aa of x−2​Δϕx^{-2\Delta_{\phi}} becomes smaller to compensate for a rather large ee (with e/a≈0.5e/a\approx 0.5 in the case of the spin correlations). However, this kind of fit may not be meaningful, because the 1/x1/x term is only one aspect of the Goldstone effects. Higher powers of 1/x1/x are also expected [109, 111] and the crossover between the critical form and the asymptotic form in the presence of long-range order is likely complicated and beyond quantitative analysis with the present data and understanding. Fitting to a single power law plus a constant, C⁡(x)=a​x−1−η+m2C(x)=ax^{-1-\eta}+m^{2}, for large systems we find that η\eta approaches 00 from above when the fitting window is moved to larger xx values, as also found previously for the loop model [29]. We find similar behavior with x=L/2x=L/2, and for large LL such data can also be fitted to a polynomial with leading 1/L1/L behavior, as in Fig. 5.

The restriction of xx to rather short distances in our final analysis should ensure negligible impact of the Goldstone modes and crossover effects, and this conclusion is also supported by the derivatives in Figs. 10(a) and 10(b) for larger distances. In further support of not including the 1/x1/x term, in Fig. 7 there are no significant changes in the approximate power-law behaviors for the three different models up to r≈100r\approx 100, even though the JJ-Q4Q_{4} model has much larger ordered moments. Thus, we conclude that the expected Goldstone contributions must only play a significant role in the correlation functions of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model for distances beyond those used in Figs. 11 and 12.

To complete the analysis, we next study the correlation functions at distance r=L/2r=L/2 for a range of moderate system sizes LL, where the critical correlations dominate. In this case, we may also expect multiplicative corrections of the form L−|y|L^{-|y|} from the allowed irrelevant operators with scaling dimension Δ>3\Delta>3 and y=3−Δy=3-\Delta. Again, we do not find any significant effects of leaving these out, obtaining good fits to Eq. (12) with x=L/2x=L/2. The value of the scaling dimension Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} is also close to the results of the previous fits for r≪Lr\ll L, where the irrelevant scaling corrections should be absent for large LL (which is supported by the very small differences between results for L=256L=256, 384384, and 512512). In this case the data for different LL are of course statistically independent and χ2\chi^{2} is defined with only the individual standard deviations. In Fig. 13 we show results for spin and dimer correlations obtained with windows of r=L/2r=L/2 where good χ2\chi^{2} values can be obtained. The deviations from the fitted function in this case are naturally of the order of the error bars of the data points (on average about one standard deviation, corresponding to a statistically good χ2\chi^{2} value). The resulting scaling dimensions are Δϕ=0.606​(3)\Delta_{\phi}=0.606(3) and 0.613​(3)0.613(3) from spin and dimer correlations, respectively.

The suitability of the fitting form Eq. (12) is clearly supported by the stability of our results for Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} with respect to different system sizes and fitting windows, and also by the good agreement between results obtained with r=L/2r=L/2 and r≪Lr\ll L. The fact that the results obtained from spin and dimer correlations are statistically indistinguishable at the level below 1%1\% also lends further credibility to the SO(55) scenario, according to which Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} must be the common scaling dimension for the AFM and VBS order parameters. For the final common value reported in Table 1, we take the average of the spin and dimer results (for which the mutual correlation is rather weak; in fact the amplitudes of the raw correlation functions are somewhat anti-correlated) for L=512L=512; Δϕ=0.607​(4)\Delta_{\phi}=0.607(4). This value is also statistically consistent with the two values from the r=L/2r=L/2 fits and the derivatives for L=512L=512 and L=1024L=1024 in Fig. 10. The difference between our final value and the input value Δϕ=0.63\Delta_{\phi}=0.63 used in the CFT bootstrap calculation [56] could very plausibly account for the minor discrepancies between the other exponents seen in Table 1 [66]. It is also interesting to note that our Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} value is reasonably close to that obtained in the fuzzy sphere calculation, where this scaling dimension is rather stable as a function of the number of orbitals [60].

V Relevant perturbations

Here we present results for correlation functions of operators that deliver the scaling dimensions Δt\Delta_{t} and Δj\Delta_{j} in Table 1. In addition, we will present results for the “pseudo dimension” Δ∗\Delta_{*}, which we believe is not a true level in the CFT spectrum but presumably is a manifestation of the perturbed CFT slightly inside the first-order line. In principle, we should also be able to extract the singlet dimension Δs\Delta_{s} from the same correlation function that has the leading decay exponent 2​Δt2\Delta_{t} (i.e., assuming Δs>Δt\Delta_{s}>\Delta_{t}). However, it is difficult to separate its contribution from other potential corrections with similar exponents. The value of Δs\Delta_{s} in Table 1 will instead be extracted from the scaling of an SO(55) indicator giving the exponent ν∗\nu_{*} in Sec. VII together with its predicted pseudocritical relationship to Δs\Delta_{s} in Eq. (3) derived in Sec. VIII.1. The scaling behavior of the coexisting order parameters on the first-order line gives a consistent but less precise value (standard deviation of a few percent) in Sec. VI.

V.1 Operators and correlation functions

Given a critical Hamiltonian HcH_{c}, we are interested in the stability of the fixed point to perturbations. We here denote a generic extensive perturbing operator by

V=∑rϵr​Vr,V=\sum_{r}\epsilon_{r}V_{r}, (13)

where VrV_{r} are local operators on individual spins or groups of spins centered at lattice position rr, and ϵr\epsilon_{r} are phases that typically would be all unity or correspond to some regular pattern or “wave”. Upon adding VV to HcH_{c} at small strength λ\lambda, H→Hc+λ​VH\to H_{c}+\lambda V, the system can either remain critical or flow (here with increasing system size) to some other fixed point. Whether or not the perturbation is irrelevant or relevant in this sense depends on its scaling dimension ΔV\Delta_{V}, or, equivalently, the corresponding exponent (eigenvalue in an RG transformation)

yV=d+z−ΔV=3−ΔVy_{V}=d+z-\Delta_{V}=3-\Delta_{V} (14)

that controls the flow of the strength of the perturbation with the length scale.

In finite-size scaling, the length scale is the system size LL and the scaling function (of some quantity exhibiting critical scaling when λ=0\lambda=0) contains an argument λ​LyV\lambda L^{y_{V}}, which can be interpreted as the renormalized (coarse grained) strength of the perturbation at length scale LL [192, 193, 194]. Thus, the perturbation is relevant (the argument grows with LL) if yV>0y_{V}>0 and irrelevant (the argument approaches zero in the thermodynamic limit) if yV<0y_{V}<0. The length scale corresponding to a relevant perturbation diverges upon approaching the critical point as ξV∼λ−νV\xi_{V}\sim\lambda^{-\nu_{V}}, with νV=yV−1\nu_{V}=y_{V}^{-1}.

The most direct way to numerically extract a scaling dimension ΔV\Delta_{V} in the absence of the perturbation (λ=0\lambda=0) is to compute the two-point connected correlation function

CV​(r)=⟨V0​Vr⟩−⟨V0⟩2,C_{V}(r)=\langle V_{0}V_{r}\rangle-\langle V_{0}\rangle^{2}, (15)

of the local operator VrV_{r}. The asymptotic power-law decay C⁡(r)∼r−2​ΔVC(r)\sim r^{-2\Delta_{V}} is governed by the (leading) scaling dimension, as previously stated for the order parameters in Eq. (6). Here the correlation function should be considered in combination with the phase factors ϵr\epsilon_{r} in Eq. (13), and what matters in the relationship to yVy_{V} in Eq. (14) is C⁡(r)​ϵrC(r)\epsilon_{r} integrated over space (and imaginary time, which when z=1z=1 just gives one more factor of LL). When considering spatially uniform perturbations, i.e., ϵr=1​∀r\epsilon_{r}=1~\forall~r, we are targeting the uniform component of the corresponding correlation function. The previously studied critical order parameters are associated with phases taken into account in Eq. (4).

In this section we will study correlation functions of the operators illustrated in Fig. 14. The ZZ, XX, and WW operators were previously studied in Ref. [54] and the QQ operator was studied in Ref. [90] (with a slightly different definition in terms of singlet projectors instead of just 𝐒i⋅𝐒j{\bf S}_{i}\cdot{\bf S}_{j}). Here we provide more extensive analysis with improved PQMC data and discuss the results in light of the scaling dimensions recently obtained within the CFT bootstrap calculation [56] and the fuzzy sphere [60].

A given lattice operator will in general contain all the CFT operators consistent with its symmetries. For a system with a CFT description, the correlation function should therefore be an infinite sum of algebraic decays ai​j​r−(Δi+Δj)a_{ij}r^{-(\Delta_{i}+\Delta_{j})} (and possibly phases that we leave out here), with the amplitudes ai​ja_{ij} corresponding to the particular lattice operators chosen. The primary CFT operators are orthogonal, and two primaries aa and bb will therefore only produce contributions r−2​Δar^{-2\Delta_{a}} and r−2​Δbr^{-2\Delta_{b}}. There are also no cross terms from operators in different conformal towers. In general one would expect the decay corresponding to the smallest CFT scaling dimension to be clearly observable and in some cases it may be possible to also extract additional larger scaling dimensions from the corrections to the leading form. In this section we will focus on relevant operators, leaving the case of irrelevant perturbations of the SO(55) symmetry to Sec. VII, where we will use linear response techniques not relying on correlation functions.

The models we study cannot be brought exactly to the critical point, and we observed large effects of the long-range ordered coexistence state in Sec. IV.3. We were able to reduce these effects by taking derivatives. However, we will find here that connected correlation functions of operators not directly related to the order parameter are much less impacted by the ultimately first-order transition, which is natural since they do not approach nonzero constants at large distances. Because of the overall faster decays, there are also less distorting effects of periodic boundary conditions.

V.2 Fully symmetric operator

In the multicritical point scenario, the two tuning parameters required to reach the critical point of a lattice model must both control operators with the same microscopic symmetries as the Hamiltonian; no explicitly symmetry-breaking operators should be introduced. The previously studied correlation function of the ZZ cell operator in Fig. 14(a) exhibited a leading decay CZ∼r−2​ΔZC_{Z}\sim r^{-2\Delta_{Z}} with ΔZ≈1.40\Delta_{Z}\approx 1.40 [54] that we can now identify as the scaling dimension of the CFT tt operator; ΔZ≡Δt\Delta_{Z}\equiv\Delta_{t}.

All previous works had assumed that standard analysis of Binder cumulants or data collapse of the order parameters would deliver the exponent ν=νt\nu=\nu_{t} corresponding to the single correlation length expected within the original DQCP scenario. As already summarized in Sec. II.2, large finite-size drifts had been observed in this exponent in many different works, but the two most extensive studies, of the JJ-QQ model [90] and the 3D classical loop model [33], both achieved apparent convergence toward ν≈0.45\nu\approx 0.45, or Δ=3−1/ν≈0.80\Delta=3-1/\nu\approx 0.80. A power law decay consistent with this value of Δ\Delta was further obtained [90] from the correlation function of an interaction energy (similar to that of the QQ operator studied below in Sec. V.4). It was therefore natural to assume that ΔQ≈0.80\Delta_{Q}\approx 0.80 and ΔZ≈1.40\Delta_{Z}\approx 1.40 reflected a CFT with two relevant symmetric operators, and, under the assumption of emergent SO(55) symmetry, that ΔQ\Delta_{Q} and ΔZ\Delta_{Z} should be identified as Δt\Delta_{t} and Δs\Delta_{s}, respectively. However, in light of the CFT bootstrap calculation [56] (and in hindsight also Ref. [30]), it now seems more plausible that ΔZ≈1.40\Delta_{Z}\approx 1.40 is actually Δt\Delta_{t}, while the anomalous scaling dimension extracted from CQC_{Q} (which also contains the VBS order parameter) is the rather mysterious pseudoscaling dimension (a manifestation of the weak first-order transition) that we call Δ∗\Delta_{*} and for which we obtain an improved value in Sec. V.4.

Given the very large value Δs≈2.36\Delta_{s}\approx 2.36 of the relevant SO(55) singlet in the CFT [56] and our slightly smaller value in Table 1, it is not surprising that it could have been missed in previous lattice calculations. If indeed ZZ also contains this CFT operator, it should produce a r−2​Δsr^{-2\Delta_{s}} correction to the slower r−2​Δtr^{-2\Delta_{t}} decay of the Z-Z correlation function. However, we also expect a conventional correction from irrelevant fields present in the model, of the form r−(2​Δt+ω)r^{-(2\Delta_{t}+\omega)}, where ω≈2\omega\approx 2 was found in Sec. IV.3.2. If this correction is present also in the Z-Z correlations, the decay exponent 2​Δt+ω≈4.82\Delta_{t}+\omega\approx 4.8 is very close to the independent estimate of the exponent 2​Δs≈4.62\Delta_{s}\approx 4.6 from the relevant singlet obtained in Sec. VII.2. It will unfortunately then not be possible to separate these two corrections by fitting CZC_{Z}.

The value of the exponent that we call 2​Δt+ω2\Delta_{t}+\omega with ω≈2\omega\approx 2 could also be Δt+Δt′=2​Δt+2\Delta_{t}+\Delta^{\prime}_{t}=2\Delta_{t}+2, with Δt′\Delta^{\prime}_{t} being the lowest ℓ=0\ell=0 descendant of Δt\Delta_{t} (i.e., its second descendant), thus identical to the exponent with correction ω=2\omega=2. The second decay exponent that we extract here could in actuality be an effective exponent approximating contributions from three different sources (from the descendant Δt′\Delta^{\prime}_{t}, Δs\Delta_{s}, or ω≈2\omega\approx 2). The fact that this effective exponent is much larger than 2​Δt2\Delta_{t} nevertheless allows us to obtain a reliable value of Δt\Delta_{t}. Analyzing both JJ-Q2Q_{2} and JJ-Q3Q_{3} data, we reinforce the universal value Δt≈1.42\Delta_{t}\approx 1.42. Since the boundary enhancements of the ZZ correlation function are not significant, and also because we focus our quantitative analysis on r=L/2r=L/2, there is no need to use the proxy conformal distance Eq. (11) here.

The definition of ZZ on a 3×33\times 3 lattice cell with the sum of eight four-spin operators (two singlet projectors) in a staircase arrangement in Fig. 14(a) guarantees that the correlation function does not contain any potential contamination from scaling dimensions corresponding to symmetry-breaking singlet patterns [90]. The 90∘ rotation and reflection symmetries of the cell also imply that only CFT operators with Lorentz spin ℓ=0\ell=0 will contribute to their correlation functions (strictly ℓ=0\ell=0 mod 44, but the higher ones will be invisible because of their very large scaling dimensions). Fig. 15 shows results for both the JJ-Q2Q_{2} and JJ-Q3Q_{3} models versus the separation rr between the cells, in either case for r≪Lr\ll L (lattices much larger than the maximum separation beyond which the results become too noisy) and also at r=L/2r=L/2 up to LL exceeding 100100. In the case of r≪Lr\ll L, to improve the statistics we have averaged results for different lattice sizes L≥256L\geq 256 that do not show any differences beyond statistical errors. All these data sets indeed exhibit asymptotic decay with an exponent close to 2.82.8 and a secondary power law with exponent close to 4.84.8.

The data points for r=L/2r=L/2 in Fig. 15 represent independent stochastic outcomes, unlike the correlated rr points for the r≪Lr\ll L sets, and we therefore use the former to determine the best-fit exponents and statistical errors. For the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model, for which we have the best data, we fit to the function

CZ​(r)=ar2​Δt​(1+brω),C_{Z}(r)=\frac{a}{r^{2\Delta_{t}}}\left(1+\frac{b}{r^{\omega}}\right), (16)

and obtain a good χ2\chi^{2} value already starting from r=L/2=6r=L/2=6, with Δt=1.417​(7)\Delta_{t}=1.417(7) and ω=2.0​(2)\omega=2.0(2). If we interpret the term with exponent combination (2​Δt+ω)/2(2\Delta_{t}+\omega)/2 in Eq. (16) as the singlet scaling dimension instead, we would have the reasonable value Δs=2.40​(2)\Delta_{s}=2.40(2), though in reality the second term should also contain a very similar contribution from 2​Δt+22\Delta_{t}+2, as discussed previously. The leading contribution governed by Δt\Delta_{t} is very stable with respect to reducing the number of system sizes included in the fit (with the statistical error of course increasing) and we present the value given above as our final result for this important relevant scaling dimension in Table 1. This fitting result for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model at r=L/2r=L/2 is also fully consistent with the rr dependence for r≪Lr\ll L as well as with analogous results for the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model, all shown in Fig. 15, where we fixed the decay exponents to the same values as above to explicitly show the good consistency between all the data sets. Given the uncertainty in the interpretation of the subleading contributions to CZ​(r)C_{Z}(r), we do not report any value of Δs\Delta_{s} from this analysis.

Since the transitions in these models are eventually first-order, the algebraic decays seen in Fig. 15 cannot continue for ever but must eventually reflect phase coexistence. Given that the two phases should eventually, when the SO(55) symmetry has broken down, undergo separation in Hilbert space, the correlation function should asymptotically approach a constant, reflecting large fluctuations from the finite system tunneling between the two phases. In such a state, the generic connected energy correlation function CVC_{V} should approach a constant, due to the expectation value ⟨V0⟩\langle V_{0}\rangle of the local operator being different in the two phases (between which the system fluctuates) and, therefore, its square will not cancel the r→∞r\to\infty value of ⟨V0​Vr⟩\langle V_{0}V_{r}\rangle in the definition Eq. (15). There are no signs of deviations from the power-law behavior up to the largest distances studied here—not even for much larger distances than in Fig. 15, where the results are too noisy to be useful for extracting the exponents but do not indicate any obvious deviations from the fitted form.

V.3 Conserved current operator

The WW operator illustrated in Fig. 14(d) was studied in Ref. [54] in the context of a helically deformed VBS state. When the entire lattice is modulated in the staircase fashion as in the 5×55\times 5 cell depicted, the columnar VBS state acquires a twist that corresponds to helical order, most likely with arbitrary (incommensurate) periodicity in the thermodynamic limit. The staircase modulation of the Heisenberg couplings breaks the square-lattice symmetry, and it was shown that it induces nonzero winding number of the ground state wave function of the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model expressed in the valence-bonds basis [54], with the winding number directly related to the wavelength of the helical VBS order.

Many aspects of VBS states in S=1/2S=1/2 systems can be understood based on their close relationship to classical dimer models; in some cases they can be described by the same kind of height model, with a simple renormalized coupling constant [190, 195]. Winding numbers generally correspond to different topological sectors, which correspond to flux sectors when mapping to an effective electromagnetic theory [196]. The flux sectors are associated with a conserved Noether current, which in the present case should not only be associated with the emergent U(11) symmetry of the VBS but also with the larger emergent SO(55) symmetry. When applied as a macroscopic perturbation to a critical JJ-QQ model, the WW term induces the conserved current, as observed in the form of the helical VBS in Ref. [54].

We note here that the conserved winding number, and associated topological sectors (hence the conserved current), has been explicitly demonstrated in JJ-QQ models also at the AFM–VBS transition, not only in the ordered VBS phase [197]—where the conservation is essentially trivial, given that the valence bonds are short with zero winding and the system is gapped. Its conservation at criticality, where the gap closes and bond-length distribution decays as a power law of the length, is directly related to the emergent U(11) symmetry of the VBS.

The CFT current operator that is contained in the WW operator must have scaling dimension Δj=2\Delta_{j}=2, and a value close to 22 was indeed found in Ref. [54], ΔW=1.90​(2)\Delta_{W}=1.90(2), though the identification of WW as a current operator was not made. The conserved current has also been studied using a correlation function in imaginary time [198], but using real-space correlations of the WW operator seems an easier route. Though the operator may appear complicated, it is not difficult to study its correlation function in QMC simulations. It is also not necessary to use a cell as large as 5×55\times 5 spins, but any odd length can be used and results for 3×33\times 3 were also presented in Ref. [54]. The larger cell has the advantage of producing a correlation function with larger overall amplitude, making it easier to extract the power law.
