The correlations show an interesting structure in the full 2D space (rx,ry)(r_{x},r_{y}), as discussed in the Supplementary Material of Ref. [54]. The strongest signal for extracting the exponent is along the line (x,−x)(x,-x), which we focus on here.

The previous result [54] for ΔW\Delta_{W} was five error bars away from the expected result ΔW=Δj=2\Delta_{W}=\Delta_{j}=2, likely as a result of some remaining corrections in short-distance data. We now have improved PQMC data and show the results in Fig. 16. Looking at the xx dependence on lattices of size L=32L=32, 6464, 128128, and 256256, there is a systematic shift upward for rr approaching L/2L/2, reflecting boundary enhancement of these correlations. The trend for the distances where the finite-size effect becomes significant indicates that L=256L=256 is sufficiently large up to the largest rr for which we have results with reasonably small error bars. Fitting to the x≥12x\geq 12 data, we obtain ΔW=2.01​(3)\Delta_{W}=2.01(3), and this value is stable within error bars also when including L=10L=10, which gives ΔW=2.03​(2)\Delta_{W}=2.03(2). While the latter fit is also statistically sound, it may be marginally affected by remaining short-distance corrections, noting that ΔW\Delta_{W} further increases when additional small system sizes are included (which leads to fits of poor quality).

The data at x=L/2x=L/2 in Fig. 16 still delivers a scaling dimension close to 1.901.90 [54] when small system sizes are included, even when a scaling correction is included, while the data for larger distances are consistent with ΔW=Δj=2\Delta_{W}=\Delta_{j}=2. The data versus rr for L=256L=256 exhibit less scaling corrections and we have entered our result from fitting these data for r∈[12,32]r\in[12,32] as Δj\Delta_{j} in Table 1.

V.4 Pseudo-scaling correlator

The QnQ_{n} and JJ operators of the Hamiltonian must also contain both the tt and ss field operators, but the JJ-JJ and QQ-QQ correlation functions are complicated by the fact that they also contain the VBS order parameter. The dimer correlation function studied in Sec. IV is exactly a correlator of two JJ terms, though with phases corresponding to the modulation of singlet densities in a columnar state. The symmetric operators should be detectable in the uniform component of the same correlation functions but their contributions are harder to extract because of the faster power law decays (larger scaling dimensions)—we note that the value of 2​Δt≈2.82\Delta_{t}\approx 2.8 is not that far from 2​Δϕ+2≈3.22\Delta_{\phi}+2\approx 3.2, the leading correction exponent used in the fits in Fig. 11(b). The lattice arrangement of the spins of the ZZ operator in the previous section avoids this complication because it does not contain the VBS order parameter.

As first noted in Ref. [90], when the QQ-QQ plaquette correlations are averaged over the four columnar states in the ordered VBS phase the result vanishes on the line (r,0)(r,0) with rr odd. The same would be true also for a plaquette-ordered state, and then it will also hold for all fluctuations between the columnar and plaquette patterns that are realized when the critical VBS develops emergent U(11) symmetry. Thus, on the (r,0)(r,0) line it would appear that the uniform component of the QQ-QQ correlation function can be studied without trying to eliminate the dominant VBS contributions. Indeed, the power-law decay corresponding to scaling dimension Δ∗≈0.80\Delta_{*}\approx 0.80 found in Ref. [90] matched the expected value for a symmetric operator driving a phase transition with correlation-length exponent ν∗=(3−Δ∗)−1≈0.455\nu_{*}=(3-\Delta_{*})^{-1}\approx 0.455. However, we now have a more reliable estimate of ν∗\nu_{*} (Sec. VII.2), ν∗≈0.416\nu_{*}\approx 0.416, which ruins the above relationship to Δ∗\Delta_{*}, which still has a value close to that determined previously.

In Fig. 17(a) we show the QQ-QQ correlation function CQ​(r)C_{Q}(r) computed using PQMC simulations of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model on an L=384L=384 lattice with a slightly different definition of the QQ operator, with just 𝐒i⋅𝐒j{\bf S}_{i}\cdot{\bf S}_{j} as the individual bond operators instead of the singlet projector 𝐒i⋅𝐒j−1/4{\bf S}_{i}\cdot{\bf S}_{j}-1/4 used in Ref. [90], the latter being more practical in SSE simulations. The even and odd branches clearly show different power-law decays. On the even branch, as shown with the blue line, the decay is consistent with the scaling dimension Δϕ≈0.61\Delta_{\phi}\approx 0.61 before the effects of the nonzero ordered moment become significant, similar to Fig. 8. For the odd branch, the red line shows the decay with Δ∗=0.80\Delta_{*}=0.80, which is the value we determine below by analyzing the decay at r=L/2−1r=L/2-1 for a range of system sizes. This value obtained in the ground state with PQMC simulations is very close to the result of Ref. [54], which was obtained with the SSE method with the inverse temperature scaled in proportion to LL.

The XX operator illustrated in Fig. 14(c) consists of a single product of two-spin operators situated on the diagonals of a plaquette. Its correlation function CX​(r)C_{X}(r) shows a behavior similar to CQC_{Q}, with the same scaling dimensions used to draw the lines in Figs. 17(a) and 17(b), but the overall amplitude of CXC_{X} is more than two orders of magnitude smaller. It is interesting to note that the odd-rr branch does not show any significant enhancement of the correlations close to r=L/2r=L/2, neither in CQC_{Q} nor in CXC_{X}. Even though this branch, unlike even rr, does not sense the order parameter, one might still expect some boundary effect. The deviations from the power law are likely just small in this case.

Our finite-size analysis of both the QQ-QQ and XX-XX correlations is illustrated in Fig. 18, where we have multiplied the correlation functions at r=L/2−1r=L/2-1 by r2​Δ∗r^{2\Delta_{*}} in order to make the corrections better visible. In the case of CQC_{Q}, we see violations of the scaling behavior for r≳40r\gtrsim 40, which we interpret as a crossover to the constant value expected (beyond some distance) in a first-order coexistence state. The multiplier r2​Δ∗r^{2\Delta_{*}} then causes the upward trend that is small but statistically significant in Fig. 18(a). Such violations are not as apparent in CXC_{X}, though they may also be present for r≳50r\gtrsim 50, where the statistical errors are large. We fit the data only up to rr where the scaling violations do not seem significant. In light of these results, it is interesting, and somewhat puzzling, to again note that the large-rr deviations from the leading power law are not apparent in Fig. 17 for fixed L=384L=384, with the decay exponent fully consistent with those extracted from r=L/2−1r=L/2-1.

From CQ​(L/2−1)C_{Q}(L/2-1) we obtain Δ∗=0.800​(3)\Delta_{*}=0.800(3) by fitting data for r∈[9,39]r\in[9,39] to two power laws. The exponent of the correction is 4.7​(2)4.7(2), which matches 2​Δs2\Delta_{s} in Table 1 within the rather large error bar, but this exponent may again also be interpreted as 2​Δt+ω2\Delta_{t}+\omega with ω≈2\omega\approx 2. When a third power law is added with fixed exponent equal to 2​Δt2\Delta_{t}, the amplitude of this term becomes very small. Since QQ (summed without phases over the entire lattice) is the operator driving the AFM–VBS transition, the tt field must of course be present to some extent in its correlation function, but apparently very weakly so—on the line considered here and along other lines. It is possible that the contributions from the order parameter and Δ∗\Delta_{*} are overwhelmingly large, unlike in the ZZ operator where these contributions are excluded.

In the case of the XX-XX correlations, three power laws are required to describe the data. Unconstrained fits deliver exponents with large error bars and we instead fix the corrections to plausible values; the first one at 2​Δt2\Delta_{t} and the second one in the range [4.5,4.8][4.5,4.8], the latter again corresponding to either 2​Δt+ω2\Delta_{t}+\omega, 2​Δs2\Delta_{s}, or some average of these. The fits have good χ2\chi^{2} values for r∈[9,51]r\in[9,51] and produce Δ∗∈[0.799,0.800]\Delta_{*}\in[0.799,0.800], fully consistent with the value from CQC_{Q}. We therefore have a high confidence in the value of Δ∗\Delta_{*}.

It is noteworthy that the contribution from the imposed 2​Δt2\Delta_{t} decay appears to be a significant correction to the XX-XX correlations, unlike the case in the QQ-QQ correlations. This can be explained by the much smaller overall amplitude of CXC_{X}, by about two orders of magnitude in both Fig. 17 and Fig. 18, which could mean that, relatively speaking, the Δt\Delta_{t} contribution is now much larger.

The well defined common power law behavior controlled by Δ∗\Delta_{*} in both Fig. 17 and Fig. 18 indicates that we are not here dealing merely with some slow gradual crossover to the first-order behavior, but truly a specific pseudocritical behavior governed by an exponent that does not appear directly in the CFT spectrum. We believe that Δ∗\Delta_{*} and ν∗\nu_{*} must be related in some way, as two manifestations of the weakly perturbed CFT on the first-order line. The putative relationship 1/ν∗=3−Δ∗1/\nu_{*}=3-\Delta_{*} is clearly violated, with 1/ν∗≈2.401/\nu_{*}\approx 2.40 extracted in Sec. VII.3, and it is not clear what the exact relationship is. A perturbative study of the SO(55) CFT could hopefully give the answer.

In Fig. 19 we show results for the near-critical JJ-Q3Q_{3} model. The same critical decay as in the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model is manifested up to distances r≈50r\approx 50, but with different sign of the leading correction. In this case it is even more difficult to fit the corrections, and we only show a reference line to highlight a range of distances over which the decay controlled by Δ∗\Delta_{*} extracted from the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model holds rather well. At large distances there is an even clearer upturn of the correlations from the critical form than in the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model. This more prominent precursor to the first-order behavior in the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model should again be a consequence of the slightly stronger first-order nature of its transition. Note that the behavior is very different away from the transition point, as illustrated in Fig. 19(a) with data slightly inside the AFM and VBS phases. In general, energy-type correlators should be expected to decay rapidly inside ordered phases, as we find, though we do not know the exact expected form.

An important aspect of our interpretation of the pseudo dimension Δ∗\Delta_{*} is that it is not a member of the CFT spectrum and therefore cannot be present exactly at the critical point. The natural way in which “fading” of the effect characterized by Δ∗\Delta_{*} can take place upon approach to the critical point is that the overall amplitude of contributions to correlation functions from Δ∗\Delta_{*} diminish gradually when the transition takes place closer to the critical point. Comparing Figs. 18 and 19, it is apparent that the amplitude of both odd-branch correlations is more than three times larger in the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model, despite the fact that the values on the even-xx branch (in Fig. 17 for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model) differ by only about 10%. Thus, the amplitude of the Δ∗\Delta_{*} correlator of the more critical JJ-Q2Q_{2} model has faded off to about 0.30.3 of its value in the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model. Fading is also manifested in the correlation length crossover schematically illustrated in Fig. 4, which will be demonstrated with data in Sec. VIII.

VI Scaling on the AFM-VBS coexistence line

As we demonstrated in Sec. IV.2, the JJ-QnQ_{n} models exhibit increasingly strong first-order discontinuities with nn at their AFM–VBS transitions. We here add a third interaction to the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model in order to have two continuous tuning parameters and realize the line of first-order transitions shown schematically in Fig. 2. We study the evolution of the phase transition extending from that of the pure JJ-Q2Q_{2} model with increasing coupling Z2Z_{2}, Z3Z_{3}, or Q6Q_{6}. The Z2Z_{2} and Q6Q_{6} interactions are illustrated in Fig. 1(c) and Fig. 1(e), respectively, and Z3Z_{3} is a direct generalization of Z2Z_{2} with one more singlet projector in the product, forming a staircase with three treads.

All results in this section were obtained using the SSE method, with the inverse temperature taken equal to the system size LL. We define both order parameters, MzM_{z} (AFM) and D=(Dx,Dy)D=(D_{x},D_{y}) (VBS), using the diagonal SizS^{z}_{i} operators,

Mz\displaystyle M_{z} =2N​∑i=1NSiz​(−1)xi+yi,\displaystyle=\frac{2}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S^{z}_{i}(-1)^{x_{i}+y_{i}}, (17a)
De\displaystyle D_{e} =1N​∑i=1NSiz​Se⁡(i)z​(−1)ei,e∈{x,y},\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{e(i)}(-1)^{e_{i}},~~~e\in\{x,y\},~~ (17b)

where e⁡(i)e(i) in Eq. (17b) denotes the neighbor of site ii in the positive e∈{x,y}e\in\{x,y\} direction and ei∈{xi,yi}e_{i}\in\{x_{i},y_{i}\} are the corresponding lattice coordinates. A factor 22 is included in the definition of MzM_{z} in Eq. (17a) because the two order parameters are then of similar magnitude in their respective ordered phases. While this normalization is not crucial, when analyzing finite-size crossing points of the squared order parameters versus a tuning parameter, the LL dependence is expected to benefit from a roughly equal scale of the two order parameters. We here denote the expectation values of the squared order parameters by mz2=⟨Mz2⟩m^{2}_{z}=\langle M^{2}_{z}\rangle and md2=⟨D2⟩m^{2}_{d}=\langle D^{2}\rangle.

VI.1 Phase diagram of the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model

We have used both the criterion mz2=md2m^{2}_{z}=m^{2}_{d} and analogous Binder cumulant (defined below) crossing points to extract the phase diagrams shown in Fig. 20, with the two criteria producing compatible results. We use J/Q2J/Q_{2} as the control parameter on the horizontal axis for the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-ZnZ_{n} models, switching to Q2=1−JQ_{2}=1-J for the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model. In all three cases, we then have a phase boundary starting on the vertical axis and dropping down to zero versus the horizontal tuning parameter.

Like any generic lattice operator obeying all the symmetries of the Hamiltonian (when summed over all lattice translations), the added interactions can be expected to contain both the ss and tt fields of the CFT. Thus, we expect the introduction of Z2Z_{2}, Z3Z_{3}, or Q6Q_{6} into the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model to affect the way in which the phase transition is crossed, which corresponds to moving the dashed line in the schematic phase diagrams in Fig. 2. With the two generic tuning parameters gg and kk introduced in Fig. 4, as opposed to the orthogonal CFT scaling fields ss and tt, we can take g∈{J,Q2}g\in\{J,Q_{2}\} and k∈{Z2,Z3,Q6}k\in\{Z_{2},Z_{3},Q_{6}\} (shifted so that g=k=0g=k=0 is the critical point) in the models studied here. We will also use the notation δ\delta for a generic distance to the critical point in Hamiltonian parameter space, along with ss and tt used in expressions where both specific distances are required.

In the case of Q6Q_{6}, we know that the transition is first-order for Q2=0Q_{2}=0, continuing the trend of increasingly strong discontinuities found for JJ-QnQ_{n} models with nn up to 44 in Sec. IV.2. We therefore expect an increasing Q6Q_{6} value in the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model to move the system toward larger ss values at the AFM–VBS transition, i.e., shifting the dashed line upward in Fig. 2. In the case of the Z2Z_{2} and Z3Z_{3} interactions, when Q2=0Q_{2}=0 there is no phase transition versus Z2/JZ_{2}/J (for the positive values of JJ and Z2Z_{2} that can be accessed with QMC simulations), while increasing Z3/JZ_{3}/J eventually leads to a strongly first-order transition into a staggered VBS ground state [199]. When starting from the VBS phase of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model and turning on one of the ZnZ_{n} interactions, as on the left side of Figs. 20(a) and 20(b), both Z3Z_{3} and Z2Z_{2} rapidly destroy the VBS order, bringing the system into the AFM phase.

In the Q2Q_{2}-Z3Z_{3} model, further increasing the Z3Z_{3} coupling beyond the values shown in the phase diagram in Fig. 20(b) eventually leads to a subsequent transition from the AFM phase into the staggered VBS phase [199]. An extended phase diagram including both columnar and staggered VBS phases, and either a direct transition between the two or an intervening AFM phase, was studied in Ref. [200]. Here we will not consider the staggered VBS phase but observe that both Z2Z_{2} and Z3Z_{3} suppress the columnar VBS phase, in contrast to the clearly VBS enhancing Q6Q_{6} interaction.

To investigate how the AFM–VBS transition evolves on the first-order line, we first consider the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model. Here the changes with increasing Q6Q_{6} are very clearly observable because the coexisting order parameters in the JJ-Q6Q_{6} model are robust when Q6≳0.1Q_{6}\gtrsim 0.1, much larger than those in the plain JJ-Q2Q_{2} model. However, as we will see, mz2m_{z}^{2} and md2m_{d}^{2} on the coexistence line still only reach a small fraction of their maximum values deep inside the respective ordered phases, even up to the maximum value Q6≈0.5Q_{6}\approx 0.5 that we can reach.

VI.2 Scaling of the Binder cumulant

For testing scaling with an exponent νs=(3−Δs)−1\nu_{s}=(3-\Delta_{s})^{-1}, we first study the dimensionless Binder cumulants on the coexistence line. For a system of size LL at distance δ\delta from the critical point, a generic cumulant UU should asymptotically be governed by a scaling function u⁡(x)u(x), with the argument x=δ​L1/νx=\delta L^{1/\nu},

U⁡(δ,L)=u⁡(δ​L1/ν).U(\delta,L)=u(\delta L^{1/\nu}). (18)

For a system on the AFM–VBS coexistence line, i.e., (t=0,δ=s)(t=0,\delta=s), ν=νs\nu=\nu_{s} should be expected. Otherwise, on approach to the critical point along some other line where both ss and tt are nonzero and δ=δ⁡(s,t)\delta=\delta(s,t), there should be a second scaling argument in Eq. (18);

U=u⁡(s​L1/νs,t​L1/νt).U=u(sL^{1/\nu_{s}},tL^{1/\nu_{t}}). (19)

Since νt<νs\nu_{t}<\nu_{s}, the behavior for large systems will be governed by the second argument. Scaling of UU with ν=νs\nu=\nu_{s} can asymptotically be observed only on the coexistence line, which is what we will pursue here.

For scaling purposes, the distance of a system from the critical point on the first-order line can be taken as δ=Q6−Q6​c∝s\delta=Q_{6}-Q_{6c}\propto s (close enough to the critical point so that any nonlinear correction in the field ss can be neglected), with some yet to be determined critical value Q6​c<0Q_{6c}<0. A negative Q6​cQ_{6c} follows from our expectation that increasing Q6Q_{6} above 00 will bring the system further away from the critical point than the very nearly critical JJ-Q2Q_{2} model. We also implicitly assume that this multicritical point exists in the real model space (i.e., it corresponds to a unitary CFT), though it is located outside the region Q6≥0Q_{6}\geq 0 accessible with sign-free QMC simulations.

The most practical way to define a size dependent Binder cumulant at system size LL is to use the common value of the AFM and VBS cumulants when they cross each other versus JJ at fixed Q6Q_{6}. To define the crossing point in an optimal way, the symmetry of the order parameters should be properly taken into account. When defining the AFM and VBS cumulants, in the past the symmetries of the individual order parameters have been employed in the standard way in the definitions so that UAFM→1U_{\rm AFM}\to 1 and UVBS→0U_{\rm VBS}\to 0 with increasing LL in the AFM phase and UAFM→0U_{\rm AFM}\to 0 and UVBS→1U_{\rm VBS}\to 1 in the VBS phase. However, on the coexistence line close to the critical point (up to some large system size), we expect a combined order parameter with emergent SO(55) symmetry (which we will show further support for in Sec. VII.2). When studying the transition, it may therefore be better to define the two cumulants under the assumption that the AFM and VBS order parameters represent three and two components, respectively, of a five-component order parameter with SO(55) symmetry, which for our purposes again is no different from O(55).

The Binder ratio is defined as

R=⟨X4⟩⟨X2⟩2,R=\frac{\langle X^{4}\rangle}{\langle X^{2}\rangle^{2}}, (20)

where XX denotes an NN-component vector (x1,…,xN)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}). In the ordered phase X→1X\to 1 trivially, while in the disordered phase the value is easily obtained using Gaussian integrals. The cumulant with the desired values 00 and 11 in the two ordered phases is of the form U=a⁡(1−R/b)U=a(1-R/b) with aa and bb depending on NN. When it is in practice difficult to compute the full ratio RR including all NN components of XX as in Eq. (20), one can also use some subset of the components—typically those corresponding to diagonal observables in the basis used—which is exactly what we do here. The coefficients aa and bb then have to be adjusted accordingly.

First consider the standard definitions. We here include only the zz component of the 3-component AFM order parameter MM and define the ratio

RAFMz=⟨Mz4⟩⟨Mz2⟩2,R_{\rm AFMz}=\frac{\langle M_{z}^{4}\rangle}{\langle M_{z}^{2}\rangle^{2}}, (21a)
where MzM_{z} is defined in Eq. (17a) and is evaluated at a given “time slice” of an SSE configuration. The expectation values can be averaged in the usual way over many slices for better statistics. In the VBS case we use both components of the dimer order parameter defined in Eq. (17b);
RVBS=⟨(Dx2+Dy2)2⟩⟨Dx2+Dy2⟩2.R_{\rm VBS}=\frac{\langle(D_{x}^{2}+D_{y}^{2})^{2}\rangle}{\langle D_{x}^{2}+D^{2}_{y}\rangle^{2}}. (21b)

The properly normalized cumulants are given by

UAFMz=52​(1−RAFMz3),\displaystyle U_{\rm AFMz}=\frac{5}{2}\left(1-\frac{R_{\rm AFMz}}{3}\right), (22a)
UVBS=2​(1−RVBS2).\displaystyle U_{\rm VBS}=2\left(1-\frac{R_{\rm VBS}}{2}\right). (22b)

The adjustments necessary under the assumption of SO(55) symmetry again only require trivial Gaussian integrals. In terms of the Binder ratios defined in Eqs. (21a) and (21b), the SO(55) cumulants are

UAFM,SO⁡(5)=3510​(1−RAFMz3),\displaystyle U_{\rm AFM,SO(5)}=\frac{35}{10}\left(1-\frac{R_{\rm AFMz}}{3}\right), (23a)
UVBS,SO⁡(5)=3510​(1−RVBS2).\displaystyle U_{\rm VBS,SO(5)}=\frac{35}{10}\left(1-\frac{R_{\rm VBS}}{2}\right). (23b)

Asymptotically, for L→∞L\to\infty, the coexistence state does not host the higher symmetry, due to the dangerously irrelevant perturbations discussed in Sec. VII.2, which become relevant in the presence of long-range order. Nevertheless, the length scale above which the SO(55) symmetry breaks down will be large, at least for small values of Q6Q_{6}. Even after the symmetry has broken down, crossing points of UAFMU_{\rm AFM} and UVBSU_{\rm VBS} will still represent the phase boundary properly, though likely with some crossover affecting the form of the scaling function.

We here simply test data collapse of the crossing values of the two SO(55) cumulants with our value of Δs\Delta_{s} in Table 1, which corresponds to 1/νs=0.7271/\nu_{s}=0.727 in Eq. (18). For fixed Q6Q_{6}, we extract crossing values U⁡(Q6,L)U(Q_{6},L) with error bars from polynomial fits to several (of order 10) data points in the neighborhood of the transition versus Q2Q_{2}, i.e., scanning horizontally in Fig. 20. Results graphed versus the scaled distance to the critical point are shown in Fig. 21, where Q6​c=−0.07​(2)Q_{6c}=-0.07(2) is the only adjustable parameter for optimizing the data collapse. Though the collapse is not perfect, the deviations from an ideal common scaling function are largely what would be expected from scaling corrections, e.g., the way the data for the smallest sizes shown here, L=20L=20 and L=24L=24, deviate somewhat from the other points for the scaling variable in the range roughly from 1 to 4. There is also a systematic peeling-off of data from the emerging scaling function in the form of a slower growth with the scaling argument as Q6Q_{6} increases for given LL.

The scaling function to which the data should asymptotically collapse for sufficiently large LL is normally analytic in the scaling variable. In Fig. 21 we have therefore fitted a cubic polynomial to the set of points that do not appear to be affected significantly by finite-size corrections. The points for the three largest system sizes deviate somewhat from the fitted scaling function. This flaw is most likely related to the eventual breakdown of the emergent SO(55) symmetry, which will take place for any point on the first-order line above some system size that depends on the distance to the critical point (as we will demonstrate explicitly in Sec. VII.2). Since the violation of the SO(55) symmetry is shifted to larger system sizes upon moving closer to the critical point, a valid scaling function (one that has the correct asymptotic form on approach to the critical point) can be defined by using only system sizes that are below the scale of SO(55) breakdown, as we have done.

Considering the single adjustable parameter and no obvious flaws beyond likely scaling for the smallest and very largest (L>100L>100) systems, these results support the scenario of a critical end point of a first-order transition. It should also be noted again that the exponent νs\nu_{s} is unusually large, roughly twice the value at 3D O(NN) transitions with small NN [63]. The good data collapse without adjusting any exponent therefore confirms a very different and unconventional universality class.

VI.3 Scaling of coexisting order parameters

As a further test, we extrapolate the order parameters to infinite size, first defining a common value m2m^{2} as the crossing value mz2​(Q2,L)=md2​(Q2,L)m^{2}_{z}(Q_{2},L)=m^{2}_{d}(Q_{2},L) at fixed Q6Q_{6}. We have also tried to extrapolate the individual AFM and VBS order parameters to infinite size separately, but such a procedure is very challenging because of the uncertainties in the location of the coexistence line. We can again in principle use the cumulant crossing points, but doing so we find that the VBS order parameter sometimes is nonmonotonic in 1/L1/L, likely for similar reasons as discussed in Sec. IV.2 (Fig. 7). The crossing values m2​(L)=mz2​(L)=md2​(L)m^{2}(L)=m^{2}_{z}(L)=m^{2}_{d}(L) are ideal in this sense, guaranteeing that the coexistence line is followed in a completely systematic way, with the order parameters balanced at a consistent mix as a function of the system size.

It should be noted that the coexistence line is fundamentally broadened in a finite system, in the present case likely representing a window of asymptotic size ∝L−(d+z)\propto L^{-(d+z)} with d=2d=2 and z=2z=2, the latter expected when the transition involves continuous symmetry breaking [34]. Moving within this window will change the relative fraction of AFM and VBS order from values close to zero to order one and vice versa. For system sizes where the SO(55) symmetry remains at the transition, this change in order parameters corresponds directly to the deformation of the five-sphere when the field tt crosses 00. For larger systems, where the SO(55) symmetry should be violated, the coexistence state realized in QMC simulations will eventually (for very large system sizes that are not reached here) correspond to the fraction of configurations (strictly speaking the fractions of equal-time slices of the space-time configurations) with either type of order. In both cases, the change in relative fraction of the order parameters with the tuning parameter Q2Q_{2} will then be roughly linear around the value where mz2​(L)=md2​(L)m^{2}_{z}(L)=m^{2}_{d}(L).

Thus, the crossing method should provide a good definition of the center of the coexistence line, provided that the two order parameters have roughly the same scale. In practice, it is not possible to perfectly normalize the order parameters for an unambiguous center of the coexistence window, but, as shown in the inset of Fig. 22, our normalizations in Eq. (17) accomplish this balancing well. A good test for balance of the order parameters close to an idealized mid-point of the transition region is to confirm that the crossing point is located in the regime of the nearly linear dependence on the tuning parameter, which is the case in the inset of Fig. 22.

As illustrated in the main part of Fig. 22, we find that the common value m2​(L)m^{2}(L) exhibits monotonic smooth behavior for all Q6Q_{6} values studied. All these systems are still nearly critical, i.e., for large system sizes the order parameters tend to very small values relative to their maximum attainable values. To fit the data, we therefore use a constant (representing the infinite-size squared order parameter) plus a power law, representing the near-critical decay of correlations.

As already discussed in the case of Q6=0Q_{6}=0 in Sec. IV (in that case for the correlation functions at r=L/2r=L/2, which also extrapolate to the squared order parameter), this fitting form cannot be asymptotically completely correct. We there focused on distances where the long-range order can be taken into account by only adding a constant to the critical decay form of the correlation functions. Here we instead focus on the way the long range order approaches its asymptotic L→∞L\to\infty value, and the power-law form with optimized exponent (that is smaller than the critical exponent 1+η1+\eta but larger than 11) should be regarded as a way to approximately account for the crossover from the critical form to the asymptotic 1/L1/L form [109] for a system with Goldstone modes.

While polynomials including 1/L21/L^{2} and possibly higher-order terms may also seem appropriate, such fitting produces a high level of scattering (beyond the statistical errors) in the results versus Q6Q_{6}, which is not the case with the constant plus power law. The polynomial form should work well only when the systems are completely dominated by the Goldstone modes [109, 111], which is not yet true for the accessible system sizes here. Though the eventual crossover to polynomial form implies some errors in our extrapolated m2m^{2} values, if this crossover takes place only for much larger system sizes (which is the case here, judging from the results in Sec. IV.2), there is not much room remaining in 1/L1/L for any drastic changes in the intercepts, as long as the true m2m^{2} value is also not too small. To be clear, the balancing act here is rather delicate, and it is not a priori guaranteed that the procedure can deliver meaningful results.

The extrapolated order parameter in the entire range of QMC accessible Q6Q_{6} values is shown in Fig. 23. In the case of Q6=0Q_{6}=0 we have data for much larger system sizes than in the other cases, and the extrapolated value therefore has smaller error bars than the nearby Q6>0Q_{6}>0 points. For larger Q6Q_{6} the extrapolations are more stable, as the corrections to the L→∞L\to\infty constant (Fig. 22) are smaller. However, the simulations also become more demanding for larger Q6Q_{6}, and we are then limited to smaller systems and larger statistical errors on the raw data.

The squared order parameter in the thermodynamic limit should grow as δ2​β\delta^{2\beta}, here with δ=Q6−Q6​c\delta=Q_{6}-Q_{6c}. In Fig. 23 we show a fit with β\beta and Q6​cQ_{6c} as free parameters, leading to β=0.87​(5)\beta=0.87(5) and Q6​c=−0.07​(2)Q_{6c}=-0.07(2), the latter value (and error) coinciding with the critical point extracted from the optimized cumulant collapse in Fig. 21. Here we have excluded the two points with largest Q6Q_{6} values in Fig. 23. Including one or both of these points, the β\beta value increases somewhat (not beyond the error bars) but the goodness of the fit χ2\chi^{2} becomes larger than statistically acceptable. In general, the critical form governed by β\beta should only apply in the close neighborhood of the transition. In the case at hand, m2m^{2} is very small throughout the range of QMC accessible Q6Q_{6} values, and one may therefore expect the critical form to still apply at the largest Q6Q_{6} values (which it almost does). However, it is possible that the curve m2​(Q6)m^{2}(Q_{6}) for the largest Q6Q_{6} values begins to signal the gradual breakdown of the SO(55) symmetry with increasing Q6Q_{6}.

The exponent β\beta is related to scaling dimensions of the critical point according to

β=12​(1+η)​νs=Δϕ3−Δs=0.836​(8),\beta=\frac{1}{2}(1+\eta)\nu_{s}=\frac{\Delta_{\phi}}{3-\Delta_{s}}=0.836(8), (24)

where the numerical value is obtained with our values of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} and Δs\Delta_{s} in Table 1. Thus, the fitted form in Fig. 23 agrees within one error bar with what is expected under the multicritical scenario. Using the values of the scaling dimensions from the CFT bootstrap calculation gives β≈0.95\beta\approx 0.95. If we instead use our value β=0.87​(5)\beta=0.87(5) and solve for the singlet scaling dimension, we obtain Δs=2.30​(4)\Delta_{s}=2.30(4), which is consistent with our value in Table 1 that we will obtain in an alternative way later.

With Q6Q_{6} replaced by one of the ZnZ_{n} interactions, we also expect to see the same kind of evolution of m2m^{2} and the Binder cumulant on the first-order line. However, as shown in Fig. 24 for the Z3Z_{3} case, we observe almost no change in m2m^{2} when Z3Z_{3} increases, and this applies also with the Z2Z_{2} interaction. This insensitivity of the order parameters, even though the phase boundary shifts significantly, may suggest that there is very little overlap of the ss field of the CFT with the ZnZ_{n} operators (at least for n=2,3n=2,3). It should be noted, however, that the maximum transition values of Z2Z_{2} and Z3Z_{3} in Figs. 20(a) and 20(b), i.e., at J=0J=0, are small. Therefore, the impact of the ss field is also limited trivially by these small values of ZnZ_{n} on the first-order lines. In the case of Q6Q_{6}, its maximum transition value is above 0.50.5 in Fig. 20(c), more than an order of magnitude larger than the maximum Z2Z_{2} and Z3Z_{3} values. The singlet content of the Q6Q_{6} operator is presumably much larger as well, which we conjecture to be a consequence of the large spatial extent of this operator.

As a way to compare with the relatively large dependence on Q6Q_{6} in the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model, in Fig. 23 the value of m2m^{2} changes only marginally, in absolute terms, from Q6=0Q_{6}=0 to 0.020.02 (the maximum value of Z3Z_{3}), and the changes are most notable for large system sizes (larger than those we have used for the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model with small Q6Q_{6}). This comparison suggests that the combination of less singlet (likely much less) content in the ZnZ_{n} operators and the smaller range of the control parameter should be sufficient to explain the differences between the models. It would still be useful to study JJ-Q2Q_{2}-ZnZ_{n} models more extensively.

VII Emergent symmetries

The emergence of a symmetry higher than that of the Hamiltonian at a critical point requires that all perturbations VV of said symmetry are irrelevant, i.e., in the case at hand, have scaling dimensions ΔV\Delta_{V} larger than d+z=3d+z=3. Scaling dimensions of various perturbations can be computed using correlation functions of corresponding local operators, as in Sec. V. However, if a system already contains an irrelevant perturbation of a given symmetry, as is essentially guaranteed in the case of emergent symmetries (except at some accidentally fine-tuned point), there is a more direct and efficient method: investigating the size dependence of a global (system integrated) quantity VV that is zero if the symmetry is exact and nonzero in a finite system because of inherent perturbations. The coarse grained perturbation should decay with increasing size at the rate L−|yV|L^{-|y_{V}|}, where yV=3−ΔVy_{V}=3-\Delta_{V}, which is much more favorable for numerical purposes than analyzing a very fast decaying correlation function C⁡(r)∝r−2​ΔVC(r)\propto r^{-2\Delta_{V}} with 2​ΔV>62\Delta_{V}>6.

This method of exploiting intrinsic perturbations to extract irrelevant scaling dimensions was applied in Ref. [89] to 3D classical clock models i.e., the XY model with a nonzero ℤq\mathbb{Z}_{q} symmetric field added (for q≥4q\geq 4), or by restricting the spins to qq “clock” angles (for q≥5q\geq 5). In Sec. VII.1 we use the same method to study the emergent U(11) symmetry of the VBS order parameter, determining the scaling dimension Δ4≈3.72\Delta_{4}\approx 3.72 of the leading lattice-induced ℤ4\mathbb{Z}_{4} perturbation. In this case the perturbation is unavoidable, being truly intrinsic to the model system, in contrast to being added at arbitrary strength to the Hamiltonian as in the clock models.

We further examine the expected relationship between y4=3−Δ4y_{4}=3-\Delta_{4} of the deformation of the U(11) symmetry and the exponent μ4\mu_{4} governing its length scale, ξt′∼t−μ4\xi^{\prime}_{t}\sim t^{-\mu_{4}}, in the near-critical VBS phase. We write this relationship for general number of angles qq, with q=4q=4 for the square-lattice VBS:

μq=ν⁡(1+|yq|p).\mu_{q}=\nu\left(1+\frac{|y_{q}|}{p}\right). (25)

Here p=2p=2 in the classical qq-state clock models [5, 87, 89] while a crossover from p=2p=2 to p=3p=3 was found in a quantum clock model in Ref. [201]. Our results for the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model (which we use in order to reach sufficiently deep into the VBS phase) are also consistent with p=3p=3, though we cannot exclude p=2p=2.

In Sec. VII.2 we study the larger SO(55) symmetry of the combined five-component AFM and VBS order parameters. Here a key result is that the most obvious SO(55) perturbation inherent to the model, i.e., the ℤ4\mathbb{Z}_{4} lattice-induced perturbation with scaling dimension Δ4\Delta_{4}, is not causing the same degree of deformation of the mixed distribution P⁡(𝐃,𝐌)P({\bf D},{\bf M}) as in P⁡(Dx,Dy)P(D_{x},D_{y}). While the perturbation of the U(11) symmetry of the VBS is of the form Dx2​Dy2D_{x}^{2}D_{y}^{2}, which contains the rank-44 CFT operator with scaling dimension Δ4≈3.72\Delta_{4}\approx 3.72, the deformation involving both the AFM and VBS sectors is richer because of the lack of exact symmetry between them. The AFM components of course always retain their exact SO(33) symmetry and the symmetry between DxD_{x} and DyD_{y} is also exact. Therefore the dominant deformation involving both sectors is of the leading form D2​M2D^{2}M^{2}, which can still be probed in the probability distribution of individual components, specifically P⁡(Dx,Mz)P(D_{x},M_{z}). We find that the dominant source of deformation here has scaling dimension Δ2,3≈4.7\Delta_{2,3}\approx 4.7, which we then argue is actually Δt′\Delta_{t^{\prime}}, i.e., the main source of the deformation is the next primary in the same symmetry sector (ℓ=0\ell=0, rank-22, even parity) as the relevant tt operator driving the AFM–VBS transition. The expected contributions from the rank-44 operator are very small, possibly completely absent. In contrast, the rank-44 lattice-induced perturbation of the form Dx2​Dy2D_{x}^{2}D_{y}^{2} causes the leading deformation of the emergent VBS U(11) and has scaling dimension Δ4≈3.7\Delta_{4}\approx 3.7.

The finite-size scaling of the distribution P⁡(Da,Mb)P(D_{a},M_{b}) also offers a way to extract the exponent ν∗\nu_{*} in Eq. (3) to high precision, which is what allows us to obtain the best estimate of Δs\Delta_{s}, entered in Table 1. Further, in Sec. VII.4 we construct an effective O(55) model and compare its analogous D2​M2D^{2}M^{2}-deformed distribution with P⁡(Dx,Mz)P(D_{x},M_{z}), thus showing that the inherent effective interaction in the JJ-QQ models must be repulsive. This fact will be crucial when deriving the pseudocritical exponent ν∗\nu_{*} in Sec. VIII.

VII.1 ℤ4{\mathbb{Z}}_{4} perturbation and U(11) crossover

Following Ref. [89], we treat the components (Dx,Dy)(D_{x},D_{y}) of the VBS order parameter in analogy with the magnetization (mx,my)(m_{x},m_{y}) of the 3D qq-state clock models. For details of the method and tests of consistency with the conventional approach based on correlation functions, we refer to Ref. [89]. We use the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model in the analysis here, because it has a stronger ℤ4\mathbb{Z}_{4} deformation at criticality and can be pushed deeper into the VBS phase. The JJ-Q2Q_{2} model exhibits very similar behaviors but the statistical errors are larger.

Based on instances (Dx,Dy)(D_{x},D_{y}) of the VBS order parameter generated either in the converged ground state in PQMC simulations or in SSE simulations at T∝L−1T\propto L^{-1}, we define an angular order parameter as

ϕq=⟨cos⁡(q​θ)⟩,\phi_{q}=\langle\cos(q\theta)\rangle, (26)

where the angle (which we can always shift to the [0,π/2][0,\pi/2] quadrant because of lattice symmetries) is

θ=cos−1⁡(|Dx|/r),r=(Dx2+Dy2)1/2.\theta=\cos^{-1}(|D_{x}|/r),~~~r=(D^{2}_{x}+D^{2}_{y})^{1/2}. (27)

This angle is not defined if Dx=Dy=0D_{x}=D_{y}=0, but such QMC configurations become extremely rare with increasing system size, and when they do occur we simply do not include them in the averaging. In principle we could avoid this issue altogether by instead of Eq. (26) using, e.g., ⟨r​cos⁡(q​θ)⟩/⟨r⟩\langle r\cos(q\theta)\rangle/\langle r\rangle, or with some other power of rr. Here we follow Ref. [89] and obtain good results with Eq. (26).

In a system with perfectly U(11) symmetric order parameter, clearly ϕq=0\phi_{q}=0 for all qq. In the 3D classical qq-state clock models the clock perturbation is irrelevant for q≥4q\geq 4, and the scaling dimension Δq\Delta_{q} increases with increasing qq. In a quantum magnet on the square lattice, the lattice itself induces a perturbation of a presumed U(11) symmetric coarse-grained VBS order parameter corresponding to q=4q=4 by the fact that the local singlets form on the lattice links with coordination number 44. When the angle θ\theta is defined for the VBS order parameter on the entire lattice, the coarse-graining scale is the lattice length LL, and we therefore expect scaling of the q=4q=4 angular order parameter of the form ϕ4∼L−|y4|\phi_{4}\sim L^{-|y_{4}|}, with y4=3−Δ4<0y_{4}=3-\Delta_{4}<0. This is the scaling dimension that we target here.

In our PQMC simulations, we use the definition

De=∑i=1N(−1)ei​𝐒i⋅𝐒e⁡(i),e∈{x,y}D_{e}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}(-1)^{e_{i}}{\bf S}_{i}\cdot{\bf S}_{e(i)},~~e\in\{x,y\} (28)

of the components of the VBS order parameter, where e⁡(i)e(i) denotes the nearest neighbor of site ii in the xx or yy lattice direction, and eie_{i} is either the xx or yy coordinate of ii. The off-diagonal quantity 𝐒i⋅𝐒j{\bf S}_{i}\cdot{\bf S}_{j} for any i,ji,j has a simple expression in the valence-bond basis used, being simply −3/4-3/4 or 00, for sites ii and jj being, respectively, in the same loop or different loops in the transition graph representing overlap of the bra and ket states propagated by a sampled string of operators drawn from the Hamiltonian (Sec. III.1) [111]. In SSE simulations, we instead use the diagonal definition, Eq. (17b), in the basis of SzS^{z} spins, taken at any “slice” in the periodic propagation dimension (which is directly related to imaginary time [202]). The corresponding angle θ\theta is then extracted in each case and the average ϕ4\phi_{4} is taken over slices.

We can also average all SizS^{z}_{i} over imaginary time first and define (Dx,Dy)(D_{x},D_{y}) using such averages S¯iz\bar{S}^{z}_{i}, which in SSE correspond exactly to imaginary time integrals;

S¯iz=1β​∫0βd​τ​Siz​(τ).\bar{S}^{z}_{i}=\frac{1}{\beta}\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau S^{z}_{i}(\tau). (29)

We then use S¯iz\bar{S}^{z}_{i} in Eq. (17b) to define the instance of the order parameter (Dx,Dy)(D_{x},D_{y}) from which θ\theta is extracted according to Eq. (27), which corresponds to a full space-time definition of the global angle. The scaling dimension extracted from Eq. (26) should be the same as with the space-only definition.

Yet another way to define θ\theta in the angular order parameter is to use QnQ_{n} operators to define (Dx,Dy)(D_{x},D_{y}). The QnQ_{n} operator summed over space with the appropriate (π,0)(\pi,0) or (0,π)(0,\pi) phase detects the VBS order parameter as discussed in the context of the QQ-QQ correlation function in Sec. VIII. For the present purpose we use a space-time definition, because of the simplicity within the SSE approach of time integrals of operators in the Hamiltonian—they are obtained by counting operators in the sampled operator strings [202, 203]. Thus, for a given SSE configuration, we can compute

O¯i=1β​∫0βd​τ​Oi​(τ),\bar{O}_{i}=\frac{1}{\beta}\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau O_{i}(\tau), (30)

where the operators OiO_{i} of interest here are the local QQ interactions (Q2Q_{2}, Q3Q_{3}, etc., depending on the model considered). Since we here use the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model, we should also take into account the lattice orientation of a given operator. Therefore, to evaluate this definition of DeD_{e}, e∈{x,y}e\in\{x,y\}, we count only the set qeq_{e} of Q3Q_{3} operators with ee-oriented singlet projectors;

De=∑i∈qe(−1)ei​Q¯3,i,e∈{x,y}.D_{e}=\sum_{i\in q_{e}}(-1)^{e_{i}}\bar{Q}_{3,i},~~e\in\{x,y\}. (31)

Then again we extract the angle θ\theta corresponding to (Dx,Dy)(D_{x},D_{y}) and use it in Eq. (26).

VII.1.1 Scaling dimension Δ4\Delta_{4}

Results for the size dependence of ϕ4\phi_{4} with all four definitions of θ\theta are shown in Fig. 25. We include PQMC data for three different couplings close to the transition point of the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model, in order to demonstrate the insensitivity of the results to small variations of JJ close to JcJ_{c}; among these, JcJ_{c} is closest to J=0.4015J=0.4015, which is also the coupling used in the SSE simulations. The PQMC results show very good power law scaling already from L=14L=14, and taking L=16L=16 as the smallest size in a fit we obtain y4=−0.723​(11)y_{4}=-0.723(11), corresponding to the value Δ4=3.723​(11)\Delta_{4}=3.723(11) entered in Table 1. The SSE results with the three different θ\theta definitions are fully consistent with the above value of y4y_{4}, but the finite-size corrections are much larger for the smaller systems. In this case we therefore do not carry out independent fitting but just show consistency with the same asymptotic power-law form for the larger system sizes. The presumed leading VBS deforming lattice operator Dx2​Dy2D_{x}^{2}D_{y}^{2} also contains rank-22 contributions in addition to the leading rank-44 operator; its U(11) charge-22 nematic component Dx2−Dy2D_{x}^{2}-D_{y}^{2} is forbidden because of the exact Dx↔DyD_{x}\leftrightarrow D_{y} (i.e., lattice C4C_{4}) symmetry. Moreover, the charge-00 contributions are not detected by ϕ4\phi_{4}. The visible corrections in Fig. 25, which we do not analyze further here, must therefore have some other origin.

Our value of Δ4\Delta_{4} is somewhat smaller than the CFT and fuzzy sphere results in Table 1, though here again we point out that the bootstrap results depend to some extent on the exact value of the input parameter Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}. In the case of the fuzzy sphere, the results are likely not yet fully converged in the number of orbitals included (or possibly the coupling used may not be located exactly at its critical value).

VII.1.2 Emergent U(11) scale in the VBS phase

While the ℤ4{\mathbb{Z}}_{4} perturbation is irrelevant at the critical point, it becomes relevant inside the VBS phase; the ground state is a four-fold degenerate columnar pattern with tunneling paths corresponding to ℤ4{\mathbb{Z}}_{4} symmetry for finite systems (see Ref. [36] for a discussion of the role of tunneling paths between the degenerate states) [25]. Such a perturbation is often referred to as dangerously irrelevant [84].

The length scale on which the emergent U(11) symmetry is manifested inside the VBS phase should diverge faster than the conventional correlation length on approach to the critical point [23, 24, 25]. The exponent μq\mu_{q} governing this U(11) scale has been the subject of much work, and some controversy, in the context of the 3D clock models [85, 86, 87, 88]. There is now overwhelming numerical evidence [87, 89] for Eq. (25) with p=2p=2, a relationship first (to our knowledge) derived in Appendix B of Ref. [5]. The derivation of this relationship involves the linearly dispersing gapless Goldstone mode of the U(11) phase that the system flows toward (in a RG sense) before the clock perturbation becomes effectively large and brings the system to the ultimately ℤq\mathbb{Z}_{q} breaking fixed point. While p=2p=2 works well for the classical 3D clock models, results for a 2D quantum clock model suggested a crossover from p=2p=2 to p=3p=3 with increasing systems size [201]. The value p=3p=3 had also previously been argued for in the case of the clock models [86]. In Ref. [201] the crossover to p=3p=3 was also demonstrated in 3D classical clock models on lattices with L×L×LzL\times L\times L_{z} spins when Lz≫LL_{z}\gg L, which in the quantum to classical mapping corresponds to the ground state of the 2D quantum clock model.

Like in the clock models, we expect Eq. (25) with ν→νt\nu\to\nu_{t} to hold also in the VBS phase of the JJ-QnQ_{n} models close to the critical point (i.e., for values of nn for which the VBS–AFM transition is near critical). Thus, there should be an exponent μ4\mu_{4} related to νt\nu_{t} (the relevant correlation length exponent when tuning the system into the VBS phase) and y4=3−Δ4y_{4}=3-\Delta_{4} according to Eq. (25). We next test this relationship with both p=2p=2 and p=3p=3.

SSE and PQMC calculations again deliver consistent results; here we show SSE results for the definition of the VBS order parameter used to extract θ\theta based on the τ\tau-integrated QQ operators, Eq. (30). Fig. 26(a) shows ϕ4\phi_{4} versus the system size for several values of the coupling JJ of the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model in the regime where ϕ4\phi_{4} is already approaching 11. Its scaling dimension is therefore 00, which is where Eq. (25) should apply [87, 89]. From these data, we can extract a length scale versus JJ by finding the intersection point with a line at fixed ϕ4\phi_{4}, with three such lines drawn in Fig. 26(a). The resulting length scales LcL_{c} corresponding to the three lines are graphed versus J−JcJ-J_{c} in Fig. 26(b). Here the behavior is not yet the ultimately expected pure power law, Lc∼L−μ4L_{c}\sim L^{-\mu_{4}}. To study the evolution of μ4\mu_{4} systematically, we therefore define a size-dependent exponent by assuming the power-law form to apply between adjacent-JJ points (which are equally spaced in JJ) in Fig. 26(b). The result for this floating exponent, where we have averaged results corresponding to all three fixed-ϕ4\phi_{4} lines, is graphed versus J−JcJ-J_{c} in Fig. 26(c).

According to Eq. (25) with ν→νt≈0.63\nu\to\nu_{t}\approx 0.63 from Table 1 and |y4|≈0.72|y_{4}|\approx 0.72 extracted above, we should have μ4≈0.85\mu_{4}\approx 0.85 if p=2p=2 and μ4≈0.77\mu_{4}\approx 0.77 if p=3p=3. To check the consistency with these values we simply assume it to be asymptotically correct and fit the data with a single adjustable power law correction in Fig. 26(c). Even without such fits, the results are clearly statistically consistent with Eq. (25) with either p=2p=2 or p=3p=3, given the large error bars. An independent reliable fit to the data with a constant plus power-law correction is not meaningful. The fit is marginally better with p=3p=3 but not enough so to rule out p=2p=2.

The way the data approach μ4\mu_{4} in the expected range is reassuring, and there is no reason to doubt that emergent U(11) symmetry crossover in the near-critical VBS phase is governed by the same mechanisms as the emergent symmetry in the classical 3D clock models, only with different values of the exponents involved. It would be interesting to improve the results further by going to larger system sizes and reducing the error bars. These calculations are very time consuming, however.

Note that y4≈−0.11y_{4}\approx-0.11 in the q=4q=4 clock model [89], i.e., this clock perturbation is much closer to being relevant than the lattice deformation of the U(11) symmetry at the AFM–VBS transition. Most of the works on the clock models were done for q=6q=6 [89, 201], where |y4||y_{4}| is larger and all the crossovers can be studied in greater detail.

Here we also point out that studies of JJ-QQ models on the honeycomb lattice, with coordination number and VBS degeneracy q=3q=3, have indicated that there are stronger violations of the U(11) symmetry on this lattice [204, 205]. The quantity ϕ3\phi_{3} does not decay to zero but appears to approach a constant, which would imply that the perturbation is marginal. It is also possible that the ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} perturbation is weakly relevant, so that larger lattices would be required to observe a clearly growing ϕ3\phi_{3}. In the presumed SO(55) CFT, the q=3q=3 perturbation is indeed clearly relevant [64, 56, 60], but recent QMC calculations of the entanglement entropy have nevertheless demonstrated consistency with the SO(55) CFT expectations [174].

VII.2 SO(5)(5) →\to SO(3)(3) ×\times U(1)(1) perturbation

The U(11) symmetry of the VBS order parameter is just one aspect of the emergence of the higher SO(55) symmetry. We next study another inherent deformation of the SO(55) sphere, using quantities involving one component each of the AFM and VBS order parameters in order to characterize the asymmetry between them. We choose the zz spin component MzM_{z} of the staggered magnetization and one of the components, DxD_{x} or DyD_{y}, of the VBS order parameter and use these to test for SO(55) symmetry in the full five-component vector (Mx,My,Mz,Dx,Dy)(M_{x},M_{y},M_{z},D_{x},D_{y}). The diagonal MzM_{z} AFM order parameter was defined in Eq. (17a). For the VBS order parameter, we again use the definition in Eq. (17b) and Eq. (28) with the PQMC and SSE methods, respectively. We can then extract an angle θ\theta as in Eq. (27) based on the components (Mz,Dx)(M_{z},D_{x}) or (Mz,Dy)(M_{z},D_{y}) and study the angular order parameters ϕq\phi_{q} in Eq. (26) for different values of qq. However, to stay closer to previous works studying emergent SO(55) symmetry, we will here proceed with other related quantities.

Nahum et al. [33] considered generalizations of ϕq\phi_{q}:

ϕq,a=⟨ra​cos⁡(q​θ)⟩,\phi_{q,a}=\langle r^{a}\cos(q\theta)\rangle, (32)

where θ\theta is the angle between an AFM and a VBS component and rr is a normalized length of the vector that in our notation has the components Mz/⟨Mz2⟩1/2M_{z}/\langle M_{z}^{2}\rangle^{1/2} and Dx/⟨Dx2⟩1/2D_{x}/\langle D_{x}^{2}\rangle^{1/2}. They noted that, for a=4a=4, these expressions can be converted into simple forms only involving expectation values of powers of the order parameters; specifically, for q=2q=2 and q=4q=4 they used

F2\displaystyle F_{2} =\displaystyle= ⟨Mz4⟩⟨Mz2⟩2−⟨Dx4⟩⟨Dx2⟩2,\displaystyle\frac{\langle M_{z}^{4}\rangle}{\langle M_{z}^{2}\rangle^{2}}-\frac{\langle D_{x}^{4}\rangle}{\langle D_{x}^{2}\rangle^{2}}, (33a)
F4\displaystyle F_{4} =\displaystyle= ⟨Mz4⟩⟨Mz2⟩2+⟨Dx4⟩⟨Dx2⟩2−6​⟨Mz2​Dx2⟩⟨Mz2⟩​⟨Dx2⟩,\displaystyle\frac{\langle M_{z}^{4}\rangle}{\langle M_{z}^{2}\rangle^{2}}+\frac{\langle D_{x}^{4}\rangle}{\langle D_{x}^{2}\rangle^{2}}-6\frac{\langle M_{z}^{2}D_{x}^{2}\rangle}{\langle M_{z}^{2}\rangle\langle D_{x}^{2}\rangle}, (33b)

which are equivalent to ϕ4,2\phi_{4,2} and ϕ4,4\phi_{4,4}, respectively, in Eq. (32). Both these quantities must vanish if the system has exact SO(55) [or O(55)] symmetry, and the nonzero values inside the SO(33) symmetric AFM phase and the ℤ4{\mathbb{Z}}_{4} or U(11) symmetric (depending on the length scale) VBS phase can also be easily computed.

We here consider the JJ-Q2Q_{2}, JJ-Q3Q_{3}, and JJ-Q4Q_{4} models only at and very close to their transition points but have also confirmed the correct asymptotic values of F2F_{2} and F4F_{4} inside the phases. In the expressions above we can substitute DxD_{x} for DyD_{y}, but when considering a single component of the staggered magnetization we only have diagonal access to MzM_{z} in both SSE and PQMC simulations (though we also have access to M2M^{2} and M4M^{4} through loop estimators, which we will not make use of here).

Nahum et al. showed that the 3D loop model has very small F2F_{2} and F4F_{4} values at the transition point, vanishing within statistical errors that were relatively large for large systems [29]. However, size dependences were not studied in detail. Here we use the size and coupling dependence to gain further insights into the emergence and eventual violation of SO(55) symmetry.

Figure 27 shows results for both F2F_{2} and F4F_{4} in the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model for three different lattice sizes. In the AFM phase, for L→∞L\to\infty we must have F2→−6/5F_{2}\to-6/5, while in the VBS phase F2→2F_{2}\to 2 because of the ℤ4{\mathbb{Z}}_{4} symmetry of (Dx,Dy)(D_{x},D_{y}) and there is an intermediate scale at which F2→3/2F_{2}\to 3/2 because of the emergent U(11) symmetry [33]. Thus, we expect F2F_{2} to change signs close to the transition point, eventually approaching 00 at the transition if there is emergent SO(55) symmetry. The point at which 00 is crossed indeed moves toward the transition point in Fig. 27(a), which is shown in detail in Fig. 28(a) with results for LL up to 256256. The quantity F4F_{4} is negative inside both phases and, as seen in Fig. 27(b), is positive within a window of couplings that shrinks as LL increases, as also demonstrated explicitly in Fig. 28(a). Note that the F4=0F_{4}=0 points always bracket the F2=0F_{2}=0 point. Fig. 28(b) shows how the bracket shrinks as a power law with increasing system size; we will discuss the meaning of the corresponding exponent further below.

In analogy with the quantity ϕ4\phi_{4} studied in Sec. VII.1, F4F_{4} at the transition point is a quantitative measure of the violation of the SO(55) symmetry (provided that this symmetry really is emergent) at a scale given by the system size LL. Thus, F4F_{4} should scale as L−|y|L^{-|y|}, where y=3−Δy=3-\Delta, with Δ\Delta the smallest of scaling dimensions of the inherent irrelevant SO(55) perturbations visible to the F4F_{4} definition. At first sight, one might expect Δ=Δ4\Delta=\Delta_{4}, but, as shown in Fig. 29, the exponent governing F4F_{4} of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model is much larger in magnitude; y2,3≈−1.71≈y4−1y_{2,3}\approx-1.71\approx y_{4}-1 (where the subscripts 2,32,3 refer to the number of components of the two order parameters) for system sizes from L=6L=6 to L≈60L\approx 60. The rather small deviations from the fitted line occur for slightly smaller system sizes for the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model, and for the JJ-Q4Q_{4} model there is no range of LL with power-law decay at all, only a gradual flattening out. Knowing that the first-order discontinuities of the AFM–VBS transition become stronger for JJ-QnQ_{n} models as nn increases, the large-LL behaviors of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} and JJ-Q3Q_{3} data in Fig. 29 are plausibly explained as the initial, barely detectable stage of the breakdown of the SO(55) symmetry to SO⁡(3)×U⁡(1){\rm SO}(3)\times{\rm U}(1) and finally to SO⁡(3)×ℤ4{\rm SO}(3)\times\mathbb{Z}_{4}, as expected in the coexistence state. There could also in principle be some effects of crossover from behavior y2,3y_{2,3} to y4y_{4} dominance, but it is clearly not possible to determine the exact source of the small (especially for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model) deviations from y2,3y_{2,3} scaling in Fig. 29 just based on the data.

To understand the at first sight unexpected behavior of F4F_{4}, note that the SO(33) symmetry of the AFM order parameter is exact and likewise the symmetry between DxD_{x} and DyD_{y} is exact, whether in the regime of emergent U(11) symmetry or just ℤ4\mathbb{Z}_{4}. Therefore all perturbations of the form λa​b​Ma2​Db2\lambda_{ab}M^{2}_{a}D^{2}_{b} with a∈{x,y,z}a\in\{x,y,z\} and b∈{x,y}b\in\{x,y\} must share the same value of the coupling λa​b\lambda_{ab}. Thus, the dominant intrinsic SO(55) perturbing interaction involving both order parameters is really of the form M2​D2M^{2}D^{2}, which is different from the Dx2​Dy2D^{2}_{x}D^{2}_{y} perturbation that is detected by the VBS distortion measure ϕ4\phi_{4}. We therefore have to consider the possible CFT operator content of M2​D2M^{2}D^{2} more carefully and compare with that of Dx2​Dy2D^{2}_{x}D^{2}_{y}.

Both interactions are quartic in the number of order parameters and, therefore, contain ℓ=0\ell=0, parity-even CFT operators of rank-00 (singlet), rank-22, and rank-44. The singlet corresponds to the ss field with scaling dimension Δs\Delta_{s} and, by definition, does not deform the SO(55) sphere. The VBS symmetry indicator ϕ4\phi_{4} explicitly detects the effects of a U(11) charge-44, rank-44 operator, which should also in principle be present in M2​D2M^{2}D^{2}. However, its overlap with the intrinsic deformations in the model must be very small, to explain the much faster decay with exponent y=y2,3y=y_{2,3}. This dominant perturbation must then originate from a rank-22 contribution, at least for system sizes up to L≈60L\approx 60 (and likely beyond, as we will argue below). One operator in the symmetry sector in question is the tt field tuned by J/QnJ/Q_{n} (with scaling dimension Δt≈1.42\Delta_{t}\approx 1.42), which vanishes at the critical point. We then conclude that the F4F_{4} decay is dominated by the second primary operator t′t^{\prime} in the same rank-22 sector as tt, with the observed scaling dimension Δt′≡Δ2,3≈4.71\Delta_{t^{\prime}}\equiv\Delta_{2,3}\approx 4.71. In the fuzzy-sphere approach, Zhou et al. indeed identified a primary CFT operator with matching quantum numbers and scaling dimension Δt′≈4.35\Delta_{t^{\prime}}\approx 4.35 [60]. Although the values do not agree perfectly, considering the significant drifts of some of the scaling dimensions with the number nfn_{f} of orbitals in the fuzzy sphere, our symmetry arguments strongly support this matching of the two calculations and our improved value of the scaling dimension Δt′\Delta_{t^{\prime}}.

The results in Fig. 29 were all obtained with PQMC simulations very close to the transition point, but SSE results for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model, like those in Fig. 27 interpolated to the transition point, fall almost exactly on top of the PQMC results (with larger error bars). Because of the finite-size drifts, one might question the reliability of the value of yt′y_{t^{\prime}}. The statistical errors are, however, very small for system sizes up to L≈50L\approx 50, and the extracted exponent from statistically good fits in the range from L=16L=16 to 3232 (to minimize corrections both for small and large LL) is stable with respect to exactly which system sizes are included. Our final estimate from this analysis is yt′=−1.711​(4)y_{t^{\prime}}=-1.711(4).

The corresponding dangerously irrelevant length-scale of SO(55) symmetry in the coexistence state should be given by Eq. (25), now with ν→νs\nu\to\nu_{s} and |yq|→|yt′||y_{q}|\to|y_{t^{\prime}}|. Using the scaling dimensions in Table 1, we obtain a very large exponent, μs≈2.8\mu_{s}\approx 2.8, for the exponent governing the divergence of the SO(55) length scale upon approaching the critical point. In principle we could test this value in the same way as we tested the expected value of μ4\mu_{4} in Sec. VII.1, by monitoring F4F_{4} versus the system size for points on the coexistence line that we determined in the phase diagram of the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model in Sec. VI. However, such a program is currently computationally too expensive and we have not pursued it.

Though eventually F4F_{4} may be governed by y4y_{4}, we assume that yt′y_{t^{\prime}} is to be used in Eq. (25), and also in the ν∗\nu_{*} relationship Eq. (3), either because the corresponding intrinsic perturbation is very small and does not come into play before the ultimate onset of the first-order behavior with convergent length scales, or possibly its amplitude completely vanishes. One would indeed expect operators of higher rank to have smaller overlap with “smooth” intrinsic perturbations, which would be a generic explanation for F4F_{4} to be dominated by the rank-22 operator up to some length scale. We will see in the next section that the length scale on which the rank-44 operator possibly takes over must be much larger than the size L≈60L\approx 60, where small deviations from the fit to the JJ-Q2Q_{2} data first become apparent in Fig. 29.

VII.3 Length scale of SO(55) perturbation

Returning to the JJ-Q2Q_{2} data in Fig. 27, we next investigate the zeros of the F2F_{2} and F4F_{4} functions in Fig. 28(a) more carefully. Here we observe that the JJ point where F2​(J,L)=0F_{2}(J,L)=0 moves toward the previously extracted transition point with increasing LL, and this point is always (for any LL studied) between the two points where F4​(J,L)=0F_{4}(J,L)=0. We have already seen above that F4→0F_{4}\to 0 at the infinite-size critical point (though in the models, which are not exactly at the critical point, F4F_{4} will eventually flow away from 00 for large system sizes), and we have also confirmed that F4F_{4} at its LL dependent peak exhibits the same scaling governed by the exponent yt′≈−1.71y_{t^{\prime}}\approx-1.71. Thus F4→0F_{4}\to 0 as LL grows in the entire region between the couplings where the function vanishes. This behavior is of course qualitatively necessary for there to be emergent SO(55) symmetry at the critical point, and the above results reinforce the notion that such a critical point is almost realized in the JJ-QQ models in the QMC accessible part of their phase diagrams.

The region between the zeros of F4​(J,L)F_{4}(J,L) can be taken as a practical definition of the finite-size region where the system hosts an emergent SO(55) symmetry that is gradually violated when moving out from the transition point, which can be taken as the point where F2=0F_{2}=0 or the peak location of F4F_{4}. An important quantitative question is then how this region shrinks with increasing LL. The width w4w_{4} of the SO(55) region defined by the zeros of F4F_{4} is graphed versus the inverse system size in a log-log plot in Fig. 28(b) for both the JJ-Q2Q_{2} and JJ-Q3Q_{3} models. In both models we observe the same kind of decay by a single power law, w4∼L−aw_{4}\sim L^{-a}, with apparently very small corrections. From the JJ-Q2Q_{2} results we can extract the exponent a=2.402​(6)a=2.402(6), which is a stable value with respect to the number of points included in the fit. Here we point out that the smallest system size included in Fig. 28(b) is the first size for which the two zeros of F4F_{4} are both within the QMC accessible region J≥0J\geq 0 (as is in Fig. 27). The fit to the single power law is of good statistical quality already starting from this LL.

The power-law forms of F4​(Jc,L)F_{4}(J_{c},L) and w4w_{4} suggest that F4​(J,L)F_{4}(J,L) obeys the scaling form

F4=L−|yt′|​f​(δ​La),F_{4}=L^{-|y_{t^{\prime}}|}f(\delta L^{a}), (34)

in the close neighborhood δ=J−Jc\delta=J-J_{c} of the transition at δ=0\delta=0. In Fig. 30(a) we show PQMC data for the JJ-Q3Q_{3} model over a wide range of the tuning parameter and system sizes, which we replot in Fig. 30(b) in the manner that should lead to data collapse if Eq. (34) holds. Systematic collapse indeed builds up as the system size increases, with f⁡(x)f(x), x=δ​Lax=\delta L^{a} forming a close to parabolic shape and with data peeling off from this form at values of |x||x| that increase with LL. As shown in Fig. 30(c), the peeled off data instead exhibit data collapse when the rescaled variable is x=δ​L1/νtx=\delta L^{1/{\nu_{t}}}, then with no rescaling of the value of F4F_{4}.

The asymptotic value of F4F_{4} inside both ordered phases is negative of order one. Thus, its scaling dimension in the ordered phases should be taken as zero, as we do in Fig. 30(c). It is also natural that the scaling here is controlled by the exponent νt\nu_{t} corresponding to the tuning parameter, with JJ largely driving the tt field. The different scaling seen very close to the transition in Fig. 30(b) reflects the emergence of the SO(55) symmetry in the overall decay of F4F_{4} to zero, F4∝L−|yt′|F_{4}\propto L^{-|y_{t^{\prime}}|}, but the scaling variable x=δ​Lax=\delta L^{a} with a=2.40a=2.40 does not have any apparent explanation from the CFT, matching neither 1/νt1/\nu_{t} nor 1/νs1/\nu_{s}. The value is very close to 1/νϕ=3−Δϕ1/\nu_{\phi}=3-\Delta_{\phi}, with the order parameter scaling dimension Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} from Table 1. However, 1/νϕ1/\nu_{\phi} controls the behavior when an order parameter field is added to the Hamiltonian, i.e., breaking its symmetries explicitly. There are no such symmetry breaking terms in the Hamiltonian, and therefore the exponent aa cannot be 1/νϕ1/\nu_{\phi}.

The only plausible explanation we can find for the value of aa is to identify it with the pseudocritical length scale illustrated in Fig. 4. It was previously believed that 1/ν≈2.201/\nu\approx 2.20 [41, 90] with ν\nu the misidentified conventional correlation length exponent ν≈0.45\nu\approx 0.45 in both the JJ-Q2Q_{2} [41, 90] and the classical loop model [29]. However, the extrapolations of the quantities used to obtain this value of ν\nu are challenging, as large system sizes are required for convergence of, e.g., Binder cumulant slopes, and the statistical errors grow with LL. As we will see in Sec. VIII, 1/ν=2.401/\nu=2.40 also fits high quality data very well but this exponent should actually be identified as 1/ν∗1/\nu_{*}. Thus, we identify the exponent aa in Eq. (34) as 1/ν∗1/\nu_{*}. It is then very interesting to note that this exponent describes the w4w_{4} window [and the scaling function f⁡(δ​L1/ν∗)f(\delta L^{1/\nu_{*}}) in Eq. (34)] up to the largest system sizes studied, L=256L=256, even though some signs (though rather weak) of an impending breakdown of the overall decay governed by yt′y_{t^{\prime}} begin to appear already at L≈60L\approx 60 for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model in Fig. 29. This seems to imply that the latter crossover to some slower decay is indeed the result of the coexistence state, that the w4w_{4} window is much less sensitive to the first-order transition, and that the rank-22 operator is governing 1/ν∗1/\nu_{*} in Eq. (3) up to the largest length scale reached here without contamination by a possible slower y4y_{4} decay originating from the rank-44 operator.

In Sec. VIII.1 we will derive an expression for 1/ν∗1/\nu_{*}, already given in two different forms in Eqs. (1) and (3), by explicitly evoking the dangerously irrelevant interaction that is primarily responsible for violations of the SO(55) relation between the AFM and VBS amplitude on the first-order line, which we take as the rank-22 operator with Δt′≈4.71\Delta_{t^{\prime}}\approx 4.71. The relationship is then fully consistent with the value of Δs\Delta_{s} that we found in Sec. VI using scaling on the first-order line and also with the bootstrap value of the exponent in Table 1. However, if we use y4y_{4} in place of yt′y_{t^{\prime}} in Eq. (1), the predicted value of ν∗\nu_{*} comes out much smaller, far from consistent with the behavior of F4F_{4}. This fact as well supports the identification of the rank-22 part of the mixed AFM and VBS SO(55) deformation as being solely responsible for the pseudocritical length scale ξ∗\xi_{*}.

Beyond Eq. (34), a more complete scaling form of F4F_{4} involves also νt\nu_{t} and νs\nu_{s}

F4=L−|yt′|​f​(δ​L1/ν∗,δ​L1/νt,δ​L1/νs),F_{4}=L^{-|y_{t^{\prime}}|}f(\delta L^{1/\nu_{*}},\delta L^{1/\nu_{t}},\delta L^{1/\nu_{s}}), (35)

which we will discuss and motivate in a more general context of finite-size scaling in Sec. VIII.2. Since 1/ν∗>1/νt>1/νs1/\nu_{*}>1/\nu_{t}>1/\nu_{s}, there is a regime where δ​L1/ν∗\delta L^{1/\nu_{*}} is much larger than the other two arguments but still relatively small so that the function ff can be Taylor expanded in this argument—this regime corresponds to the near parabolic shape formed by the collapsed data in Fig. 30(b). When also the argument δ​L1/νt\delta L^{1/\nu_{t}} becomes large δ​L1/ν∗\delta L^{1/\nu_{*}} can be considered as approaching infinity and the function therefore crosses over to a form f⁡(δ​L1/νt)f(\delta L^{1/\nu_{t}}), as seen in the data collapse plot Fig. 30(c). The third argument δ​L1/νs\delta L^{1/\nu_{s}} will also to some extent influence the behavior further away from δ=0\delta=0. In Sec. VIII we will present several examples of physical observables that can be described by similar functions of three arguments, and where all of them are needed to fully describe numerical data.

To conclude the discussion of the emergent SO(55) symmetry, in Fig. 31 we show a data collapse analysis for the function F2F_{2} obtained with both PQMC and SSE calculations (using different windows on the xx axis). This analysis confirms that F2F_{2} should be regarded as dimensionless, i.e., no scaling of the function values are required to achieve data collapse. This may not be surprising, considering that F2F_{2} in Eq. (33a) is the difference between two Binder ratios, both of which are dimensionless.

In Fig. 31(b) and the main part of Fig. 31(a) the distance from the transition point is scaled with the conventional correlation length exponent νt\nu_{t}, which follows from the fact that F2F_{2} measures the violations of the SO(55) symmetry that are “manually” tuned by the parameter JJ, taking the system between the AFM phase with SO(33) order parameter and the VBS phase with emergent U(11)==O(22) symmetry by effectively deforming the five-sphere defining the order parameter. To effectively cancel a possible scaling correction, we have here used the size dependent distance J−Jc​(L)J-J_{c}(L) from the critical point, with Jc​(L)J_{c}(L) defined as the point where F2​(J,L)=0F_{2}(J,L)=0, graphed for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model in Fig. 28(a). The essentially perfect data collapse for system sizes up to L≈100L\approx 100 of a function manifestly probing the imposed deformation of the SO(55) order away from the transition lends further support to the interpretation of the exponent νt≈0.63\nu_{t}\approx 0.63 as that of the traceless symmetric tensor.

In Fig. 31(a) we also observe clearly that the data for system sizes L=128L=128 and above do not collapse to the common function. As shown in the inset plot, for the large system sizes we instead see good data collapse when J−JcJ-J_{c} is scaled with L1/ν∗L^{1/\nu_{*}}. This crossover between behaviors controlled by νt\nu_{t} and ν∗\nu_{*} is a manifestation of the pseudocriticality illustrated in Fig. 4. In the case of Fig. 31(a), the larger sizes in finite-size scaling translate to systems closer to the transition, i.e., moving to the right on the logarithmic scale in Fig. 4. It is important to note that F4F_{4}, in contrast to F2F_{2}, exhibits scaling with ν∗\nu_{*} already from much smaller system sizes in Fig. 30, which shows that the length scale ξ∗\xi_{*} exists already further away from the transition but is manifested in many physical observables only closer to the transition, at larger scales.

VII.4 O(5) deformation model

Bruce and Aharony considered an O(NN), N=NA+NBN=N_{A}+N_{B}, classical multicritical point separating O(NAN_{A}) and O(NBN_{B}) critical lines, where an attractive interaction between the O(NAN_{A}) and O(NBN_{B}) order parameters AA and BB is presumed irrelevant [67]. While it is now known that such a multicritical point is stable only for NA=NB=1N_{A}=N_{B}=1 (i.e., the interaction is actually relevant for NA+NB>2N_{A}+N_{B}>2) [80, 81], the arguments of a coexistence phase versus a first-order line and, in the former case, the shape of the boundaries of the coexistence phase between the pure A and B phases, are still formally correct and useful. Moreover, while the scenario in practice is invalid for classical O(NN) models, a central aspect of our findings is that the multicritical DQCP exists and corresponds to phase A being VBS ordered with NA=2N_{A}=2 and B is AFM ordered with NB=3N_{B}=3. However, unlike the case of attractive interactions that cause the coexistence phase studied by Bruce and Aharony, we will show here that the interactions are repulsive, thus leading instead to the first-order line extending from the multicritical point, as illustrated in Figs. 2(a), 2(b), and 3.

It is normally very difficult, even impossible, to distinguish a first-order line from the extremely narrow coexistence phase, as qualitatively drawn in Fig. 2(c), in the neighborhood of the critical point. The shape of the coexistence boundaries were derived by Bruce and Aharony, and in Sec. VIII we will generalize their arguments to define a crossover region in which the repulsive order-parameter interactions are important and give rise to the emergent bubble length scale ξ∗\xi_{*}. Here we will first present our arguments for detecting repulsive interactions through the form of the SO(55) deformation.

Inspecting the definition of F4F_{4} in Eq. (33b) and considering the fact that the denominators do not decay to zero with increasing system size in a coexistence state (since both order parameters are nonzero by definition), it seems plausible that F4>0F_{4}>0 in the neighborhood of the transition, as seen in Figs. 27(b) and 29, corresponds to anti-correlation between AFM and VBS order parameters, relative to how they must relate to each other for perfect SO(55) symmetry with F4=0F_{4}=0. Anti-correlation clearly would correspond to effectively repulsive interactions that eventually must vanish in the RG sense (as the interaction is irrelevant) at the critical point on large length scales [and note that F4F_{4} stays positive also when the SO(55) symmetry breaks down for all the models in Fig. 29]. For attractive SO(55) breaking interactions, we should instead have positively correlated order parameters, thus F4→0F_{4}\to 0 from below with increasing system size in the critical regime.

In order to confirm the ways attractive and repulsive interactions manifest themselves differently in F4F_{4}, and for additional insights into possible causes of the symmetry violations, we here study a classical O(55) deformation model of a five-component order parameter 𝐯=(v1,…,v5){\bf v}=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{5}), where 𝐃=(v1,v2){\bf D}=(v_{1},v_{2}) and 𝐌=(v3,v4,v5){\bf M}=(v_{3},v_{4},v_{5}) correspond, respectively, to the VBS and AFM order parameters. Our unperturbed model is simply a 5-sphere of radius 11 with perfect O(55) symmetry of 𝐯{\bf v}. We then introduce perturbations by considering the following “action”:

S⁡(𝐯)=λ⁡(D2−M2)+κ​M2​D2+μ​D12​D22.S({\bf v})=\lambda(D^{2}-M^{2})+\kappa M^{2}D^{2}+\mu D_{1}^{2}D_{2}^{2}. (36)

Here λ\lambda tunes the system from VBS order for λ<λc\lambda<\lambda_{c} to λ>λc\lambda>\lambda_{c}, with λc=0\lambda_{c}=0 if κ=μ=0\kappa=\mu=0. This tuning parameter plays the role of the tt field (the horizontal axis in Fig. 2) in the CFT or J/QJ/Q in a JJ-QQ model. In general, we can define λc\lambda_{c} as the point where F2F_{2} in Eq. (33a) changes sign. The second term in Eq. (36) is the simplest form of an interaction between the order parameters and we already analyzed it in the context of the SO(55) CFT in Sec. VII.2. The last term breaks the symmetry between the two components of the VBS order parameter, similar to the lattice in the JJ-QQ model.

In order to mimic a non-uniform critical radial distribution we define the probability of 𝐯{\bf v} with a factor r2=∑ivi2r^{2}=\sum_{i}v_{i}^{2} in front of the exponential;

P⁡(𝐯)=1Z​r2​e−S⁡(𝐯),P({\bf v})=\frac{1}{Z}r^{2}{\rm e}^{-S({\bf v})}, (37)
