though the results presented below are qualitatively insensitive to the presence of this factor or the exponent 22 used. We can now define physical observables GG in the model by computing

⟨G⟩=∫d​v5​G​(𝐯)​P​(𝐯),Z=∫d​v5​P​(𝐯).\langle G\rangle=\int dv^{5}G({\bf v})P({\bf v}),~~~~Z=\int dv^{5}P({\bf v}). (38)

It should be possible to solve this model analytically, at least perturbatively for small values of the interaction parameters, but here we simply sample the vector.

We first keep μ=0\mu=0 for the purpose of testing the effects on the O(55) symmetry on the interaction strength κ\kappa. Results for κ=0\kappa=0 and κ=±1\kappa=\pm 1 are shown in Fig. 32 and can be compared with those for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model in Fig. 27, which includes results only very close to the transition point. In Fig. 32 we show results for a larger range of the tuning parameter λ\lambda in the O(55) model in order to confirm the known asymptotics. As expected, a repulsive interaction, κ>0\kappa>0 is required for the F4F_{4} peak to move above 00 in the transition region. Since here it is definitely true that it is the repulsion that causes F4>0F_{4}>0, we can also define the distance between the points at which F4=0F_{4}=0 as the window in which the repulsion has a significant effect. In this simple model we of course only get trivial values of the exponents that we investigated in the JJ-QQ models in Figs. 28 and 29. The F4F_{4} peak value (or the value at λ=0\lambda=0) decays linearly with κ\kappa and the window of F4>0F_{4}>0 is of size ∝κ1/2\propto\kappa^{1/2}. The decay versus system size in the spin models of course reflects a non-trivial renormalized (coarse grained on scale LL) effective interaction, and the scaling of the order parameters themselves, versus the length scale LL.

We next turn on the μ​D12​D22\mu D_{1}^{2}D_{2}^{2} interaction in Eq. (36) and investigate the ϕ4\phi_{4} order parameter defined in Eq. (26). Note that Dx2​Dy2=[1−cos⁡(4​θ)]/8D_{x}^{2}D_{y}^{2}=[1-\cos(4\theta)]/8, i.e., the quantity ϕ4\phi_{4} measures the expectation value of this same interaction operator. Though of course this interaction leads to a nonzero ϕ4\phi_{4} (and ϕ4∝μ\phi_{4}\propto\mu), as shown in Fig. 33 for a rather large value of μ\mu to compensate for the 1/81/8 factor above, another interesting point is that a positive F4F_{4} is also generated. This behavior should not necessarily be strictly interpreted as D12​D22D_{1}^{2}D_{2}^{2} corresponding to a repulsive interaction between the VBS and AFM components, though F4>0F_{4}>0 does signal a similar effect of anti-correlated order parameters.

In the many-body system as well we would expect the lattice by itself to not just cause the eventual crossover of the VBS order parameter symmetry from O(22) to Z4Z_{4}, but in the process also induce other violations of the SO(55) symmetry. However, and importantly, in the JJ-QQ models the length scale of the O(22) symmetry is very large, as we quantitatively demonstrated in Sec. VII.1, with the exponent μ4≈0.80\mu_{4}\approx 0.80 governing the U(11) length scale ξU⁡(1)∼t−ν\xi_{{\rm U}(1)}\sim t^{-\nu} in the VBS phase being larger than the conventional correlation-length exponent νt≈0.63\nu_{t}\approx 0.63 and the bubble-size exponent ν∗≈0.42\nu_{*}\approx 0.42. Moreover, the amplitude of the size dependent ϕ4\phi_{4} in Fig. 25 is also very small in the PQMC case (where ϕ4\phi_{4} is on equal footing with the PQMC results for F2F_{2} and F4F_{4} in Figs. 28 and 29). Since the deviations from the U(11) VBS symmetry are required before this distortion can have a secondary effect on the SO(55) symmetry (e.g., as manifested in F4F_{4}), the SO(55) distortion with its faster decay (but rather large amplitude) in Fig. 29 cannot be a direct byproduct of the rank-44 lattice-induced perturbation, or any other member of the multiplet with scaling dimension Δ4\Delta_{4}, but of a different perturbation that we have argued above is the second rank-22 primary operator.

VIII Pseudocritical scaling

We have argued that the exponent ν∗\nu_{*} describes a novel phenomenology of the weakly first-order AFM–VBS transition, in the form of the crossover of the correlation length illustrated in Figs. 3 and 4, and also in finite-size scaling of an important indicator of emergent SO(55) symmetry above in Sec. VII.2. No scaling dimension matching ν∗\nu_{*} appears in the (approximate) CFT spectrum now available from the CFT bootstrap calculations [65, 56] and the fuzzy sphere model [60]. In light of the CFT results, the initial observation of ξ∗\xi_{*} in the form of a correlation length with anomalously small growth appears puzzling—reminding us of Rabi’s famous question “Who ordered that?” when pondering Anderson’s 1936 discovery of (as it turned out to be) the muon [206].

The emergent pseudocriticality actually does fit perfectly into the SO(55) multicritical scenario, though it is not directly observable exactly at the critical point, only in its neighborhood of small s≠0s\not=0. The main manifestations of the pseudocriticality are in the evolution of observables on approach to the critical point, as illustrated with the emergence of the bubble scale ξ∗\xi_{*} in Fig. 3. This scale corresponds directly to the exponential decay rate of VBS correlations in the AFM phase and vice versa, and, therefore, is easy to extract. Here in Sec. VIII.1 we will derive the expression Eq. (1) relating ν∗\nu_{*} to conventional scaling dimensions of the underlying CFT and then in Sec. VIII.2 we deduce the crossover points g1∗​(k)g_{1}^{*}(k) and g2∗​(k)g_{2}^{*}(k) (with g2∗<g1∗g_{2}^{*}<g_{1}^{*}) between which bubble size grows as g−ν∗g^{-\nu_{*}}. In Sec. VIII.3 we demonstrate the finite-size crossover from ξt\xi_{t} to ξ∗\xi_{*} in the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model and also analyze the correlation length computed on large lattices with the 3D classical loop model in Ref. [33]. The crossover there had been noted by Nahum et al., but not explained, and here we go further and show that the largest values of the correlation length versus the distance gg to the critical point agree with our ξ∗∼g−ν∗\xi_{*}\sim g^{-\nu_{*}} with ν∗\nu_{*} obtained from the F4F_{4} analysis in Fig. 27(b).

VIII.1 Emergent length scale

Bruce and Aharony [67] considered a system with two order parameters, ϕA{\bf\phi}_{A} and ϕB{\bf\phi}_{B}, in Landau theory including an interaction term v​ϕA2​ϕB2v\phi_{A}^{2}\phi_{B}^{2}. They further assumed that the joint order parameter with a total of NN components develops an emergent O(NN) symmetry at an isolated critical point in the space of a parameter preserving this symmetry and one that violates it; like the ss and tt field strengths in our phase diagrams in Fig. 2. Within this scenario, a first-order line forms, as in Fig. 2(b), if the two order parameters are mutually repulsive, i.e., v>0v>0. For attractive order parameters, v<0v<0, the coexistence phase forms instead, as in Fig. 2(c).

Though we do not have a coexistence phase in our case, as demonstrated in Sec. VII.4, for the moment our discussion will be framed around such an imagined phase, in order to derive useful results that also will apply once we have abandoned the extended coexistence phase in favor of a coexistence line. The key result of Ref. [67] for our purpose here is that the shape of the phase boundaries of either side (t<0t<0 and t>0t>0) of the coexistence phase (in our case an imagined coexistence phase) is given by

sc​(t)∼|t|1/ψ,s_{c}(t)\sim|t|^{1/\psi}, (39)

where the exponent ψ\psi depends on the crossover exponent as well as the scaling dimension of the leading irrelevant perturbation of the O(NN) symmetry. According to Eq. (5.11) of Ref. [67], ψ=ϕg−ϕv\psi=\phi_{g}-\phi_{v}, which is translated to the situation at hand here as ϕg→yt=1/νt=3−Δt\phi_{g}\to y_{t}=1/\nu_{t}=3-\Delta_{t} and ϕv→yt′=3−Δt′\phi_{v}\to y_{t^{\prime}}=3-\Delta_{t^{\prime}}. Thus, the exponent controlling the observed behavior of the phase boundaries (if they were actually to exist) would be

ψ=yt−yt′=Δt′−Δt.\psi=y_{t}-y_{t^{\prime}}=\Delta_{t^{\prime}}-\Delta_{t}. (40)

As discussed in Secs. VII.3 and VII.4, we cannot prove that yt′y_{t^{\prime}} should be used here (after we generalize to repulsive interactions) instead of Δ4\Delta_{4}, and in principle Δ4\Delta_{4} might control the behavior on even larger length scales, i.e., there would be yet another crossover before the growth of the bubble scale halts when the ξt\xi_{t} converges to the finite ξs\xi_{s} as illustrated in Fig. 4. However, the crossover may also formally take place after the final convergence of all the length scales, in which case it would play no role at all. We see no signs of such crossover, and, given that we obtain remarkable agreement with all numerical results when using Δt′\Delta_{t^{\prime}}, we conjecture that the operator responsible for the irrelevant violation of SO(55) symmetry here is the first irrelevant rank-22 CFT primary operator discussed in Sec. VII.2.

Using Eq. (39), we can also obtain the width wcow_{\rm co} of the coexistence phase in the tt field direction as a function of the ss field:

wco​(s)∼sψ.w_{\rm co}(s)\sim s^{\psi}. (41)

From this expression we can obtain an effective finite-size width of the coexistence phase at the critical point, s→0s\to 0, in the standard way by expressing ss using the correlation length ξs∼s−νs\xi_{s}\sim s^{-\nu_{s}} and replacing ξs\xi_{s} by LL:

wco(L)=L−ψ/νs,w_{\rm co}(L)=L^{-\psi/\nu_{s}}, (42)

which of course vanishes for L→∞L\to\infty. If a length scale diverges as t−νt^{-\nu} with some ν>0\nu>0, then the value of tt for which this length reaches the system length LL scales as L−1/νL^{-1/{\nu}}. Applying these arguments in the reverse, from Eq. (42) we can identify an exponent

ν∗=νsψ\nu_{*}=\frac{\nu_{s}}{\psi} (43)

governing a divergent length scale ξ∗∼t−ν∗\xi_{*}\sim t^{-\nu_{*}}, which, when using the form of ψ\psi in Eq. (40), leads to Eq. (1) or, equivalently, Eq. (3).

Another way to arrive at the same result is to consider the ss correlation length ξs∼s−νs\xi_{s}\sim s^{-\nu_{s}} in combination with a proposed new length scale ξ∗∼|t|−ν∗\xi_{*}\sim|t|^{-\nu_{*}}. If there is a singular boundary in the (s,t)(s,t) plane given by Eq. (39), then its functional form should correspond to ξ∗∼ξs\xi_{*}\sim\xi_{s}, i.e., sc​(t)=|t|ν∗/νs=|t|1/ψs_{c}(t)=|t|^{\nu_{*}/\nu_{s}}=|t|^{1/\psi}, so that ψ=νs/ν∗\psi=\nu_{s}/\nu_{*}. Such an argument applies generally to the shape of a transition line emerging from a critical point when a relevant perturbation is turned on, which would correspond to νs\nu_{s} and νt\nu_{t} being known and the exponent ψ\psi is the one sought. Here instead the general form of ψ\psi in Eq. (40) is known, and we propose a related length scale controlled by ν∗\nu_{*}, which according to the above steps is given by Eq. (43). The unusual aspect here is that ψ\psi in Eq. (40) involves not only Δt\Delta_{t} but also Δt′\Delta_{t^{\prime}}, because of the emergent symmetry with its dangerously irrelevant perturbation.

Note that, with the form of ψ\psi in Eq. (40), the coexistence phase shrinks when Δt′\Delta_{t^{\prime}} increases, i.e., when the SO(55) perturbation becomes more irrelevant. Thus, if the symmetry is exact there will be no coexistence phase, only a line with SO(55) symmetry (and spontaneous symmetry breaking). For reasonable values of the scaling dimensions, the coexistence phase is extremely narrow in the tt direction for small s>0s>0, and, as pointed out already in Ref. [67], it can easily be mistaken for a direct first-order transition.

In our present case we do not have a coexistence phase. Why then are the above results relevant to our case? The reason is that the scaling forms do not rely on the sign of the interactions between the order parameters; only the physical interpretation does. For repulsive interactions, the form of scs_{c} versus tt in Eq. (39) should not be interpreted as a phase boundary, but as a crossover value of ss for given tt above which the repulsive interaction becomes strong enough (relative to the tt and ss scales) to be the main source of gapping the pseudo-Goldstone modes corresponding to the components of the AFM order parameter inside the VBS phase or vice versa. Similarly, the key result in Eq. (42) should be interpreted as the window of tt values around t=0t=0 in which the order parameter repulsion has detectable consequences in a finite system. Thus, all the above arguments that lead to Eq. (42), and then to Eq. (1), still formally apply though the physical situation is quite different. In the repulsive case, the pseudo-Goldstone modes develop anomalously large gaps corresponding to smaller bubble size, as discussed qualitatively in Sec. I.2 and illustrated in Fig. 3. The exponent ν∗\nu_{*} describes the impeded growth of the bubble size ξ∗\xi_{*}.

A practically useful aspect of the exponent ν∗\nu_{*} is that its numerical estimate from the finite-size scaling of the SO(55) window extracted from F4F_{4} in Fig. 28 has rather small statistical errors. If correct, the form Eq. (3) can therefore be used to obtain a good estimate of Δs=3−1/νs\Delta_{s}=3-1/\nu_{s}, which we were not able to extract from the correlation function that gave us Δt\Delta_{t} in Sec. V.2. The resulting value Δs=2.271​(3)\Delta_{s}=2.271(3) has been entered in Table 1 and it also is consistent with the value of the critical exponent β\beta governing the growth of the coexisting order parameters on the first-order line, Fig. 23, which corresponds to Δs=2.30​(4)\Delta_{s}=2.30(4).

VIII.2 Scaling crossover

We now consider tuning a system on a line where the ss and tt fields are parametrized by gg as in Fig. 4; s=s⁡(g)s=s(g), t=t⁡(g)t=t(g). A scaling function governing a dimensionless observable when the line crosses the multicritical point should be of the form f⁡(g​Lys,g​Lyt)f(gL^{y_{s}},gL^{y_{t}}), while for a dimensionful quantity a power of LL also multiplies ff. Eventually for g→0g\to 0, the larger of the two arguments will dominate the scaling behavior, which in our case means f⁡(g​Lys,g​Lyt)→f⁡(g​Lyt)f(gL^{y_{s}},gL^{y_{t}})\to f(gL^{y_{t}}), except on the coexistence line (t=0t=0) where f⁡(s​Lys)f(sL^{y_{s}}) applies. If instead the first-order line is crossed at a small value of s=s0s=s_{0} (k>0k>0 in Fig. 4), the scaling function also will depend on y∗y_{*};

f=f⁡(s​Lys,t​Lyt,t​s0b​Ly∗),f=f(sL^{y_{s}},tL^{y_{t}},ts_{0}^{b}L^{y_{*}}), (44)

where we could replace s0s_{0} by ss but we here keep s0s_{0} as an indication that we have in mind traversing the transition versus tt with ss almost constant and crossing t=0t=0 at s=s0s=s_{0}. The factor s0bs_{0}^{b} with b>0b>0 has been introduced to account for the diminished effects of the pseudocritical scaling when s0→0s_{0}\to 0. While we do not know the value of the exponent bb, we can obtain a bound from the fact that pseudocriticality has been observed on rather large length scales [29, 41, 90], as we will also show with improved numerical results below in Sec. VIII.3.

We would like to know the range of length scales over which the bubble size dominates, i.e., in the thermodynamic limit the range [ξ∗​(g1∗),ξ∗​(g2∗)][\xi_{*}(g_{1}^{*}),\xi_{*}(g_{2}^{*})] in Fig. 4. We consider a corresponding finite-size version first and cross the transition versus tt at some small s>0s>0. For the three inverse correlation length exponents we have ys<yt<y∗y_{s}<y_{t}<y_{*}, and there will therefore be an (s,t)(s,t) region where the correlation length is controlled by tt and the first argument of the scaling function in Eq. (44) is unimportant (effectively ss can be taken as 00 but we have to keep s0>0s_{0}>0). Further, since y∗≈2.4y_{*}\approx 2.4 is significantly larger than yt≈1.6y_{t}\approx 1.6, above some large LL the function crosses over to effectively one of a single argument, f→f⁡(t​s0b​Ly∗)f\to f(ts_{0}^{b}L^{y_{*}}), disregarding for now the fact that this scaling form must break down when LL becomes sufficiently large for the final crossover to finite length scales at the first-order transition (inside the dashed fan in Fig. 3). However, when s0bs_{0}^{b} is small, there will also be some range of smaller system sizes for which t​LyttL^{y_{t}} dominates in Eq. (44). Balancing the two arguments, in a scaling sense, produces the crossover length scale. From Lyt∼s0b​Ly∗L^{y_{t}}\sim s_{0}^{b}L^{y_{*}} we obtain the finite-size crossover length, and by replacing LL by the generic correlation length ξ\xi in the thermodynamic limit we can write the first crossover length in Fig. 4 as

ξ(g1∗)∼s0−b/(y∗−yt).\xi(g_{1}^{*})\sim{s_{0}}^{-b/(y_{*}-y_{t})}. (45)

The upper crossover length ξ⁡(g2∗)\xi(g_{2}^{*}) in Fig. 4 will roughly correspond to the saturation length—the final converged bubble size at the first-order transition. With the bubble growth ceasing when ξt→ξs∼s−νs\xi_{t}\to\xi_{s}\sim s^{-{\nu_{s}}} and ξ∗=ξtν∗/νt\xi_{*}=\xi_{t}^{\nu_{*}/\nu_{t}}, the second crossover length is given by

ξ(g2∗)∼s0−νsν∗/νt,\xi(g_{2}^{*})\sim{s_{0}}^{-{\nu_{s}\nu_{*}/\nu_{t}}}, (46)

and the entire window in which the pseudoscaling holds

ξ∗∈[s0−b/(y∗−yt),s0−νsν∗/νt].\xi_{*}\in[{s_{0}}^{-b/(y_{*}-y_{t})},{s_{0}}^{-{\nu_{s}\nu_{*}/\nu_{t}}}]. (47)

Provided that νs​ν∗/νt>b/(y∗−yt)\nu_{s}\nu_{*}/\nu_{t}>b/(y_{*}-y_{t}), the range diverges when s→0s\to 0, and it is in this sense that ξ∗\xi_{*} can be a truly divergent length scale even if it is completely invisible exactly at the multicritical point, where the first crossover never takes place. The fact that we can observe the crossover suggests that the above condition holds, i.e., that the unknown “fading exponent” bb in Eq. (44) satisfies 0<b<(y∗−yt)​νs​ν∗/νt0<b<(y_{*}-y_{t})\nu_{s}\nu_{*}/\nu_{t}, or, using the numerical values of the scaling dimensions, 0<b≲1.700<b\lesssim 1.70, which is quite a substantial range of values.

VIII.3 Tests of the correlation length

A common way to extract a generic correlation length exponent ν\nu is to consider the finite-size scaling form of a dimensionless singular quantity. The dependence of such a quantity on the distance δ\delta to the critical point is exemplified in the case of the Binder cumulant in Eq. (18). This form is often used to collapse data for a range of δ\delta values and system sizes, as we did with the Binder cumulant in the coexistence state with ν=νs\nu=\nu_{s} in Fig. 21. If the exponent is not known, it can be determined by adjusting the value of ν\nu for optimal collapse onto a scaling function when LL is sufficiently large for scaling corrections to be negligible. We have already seen above that a scaling function with three arguments is in principle needed in the present case when crossing the first-order transition, Eq. (44). This function crosses over into a function f∗​(t​Ly∗)f_{*}(tL^{y_{*}}) with a single argument y∗≈2.4y_{*}\approx 2.4 for large LL, while for smaller LL the argument t​s0bts_{0}^{b} can be small relative to just tt and then f≈ft​(t​Lyt)f\approx f_{t}(tL^{y_{t}}) with yt≈1.58y_{t}\approx 1.58.

Instead of performing a full data collapse analysis, the presence of two scaling regimes, separated by a smooth crossover, can be tested more systematically (without having to make choices on what data points should be included) by analyzing the derivative of the cumulant with respect to the tuning parameter. Using JJ as the tuning parameter in the JJ-QQ models, δ=J−Jc\delta=J-J_{c}, the scaling form Eq. (18) of the cumulant implies that its derivative with respect to JJ scales as

d​U​(J)d​J|δ=0∝L1/ν,\frac{dU(J)}{dJ}|_{\delta=0}~\propto L^{1/\nu}, (48)

at the critical point. This way of extracting ν\nu from the derivative was used in Refs. [29], [41], and [90].

We now generalize the above conventional form of the cumulant slope U′U^{\prime} to multiple length scales. Using the scaling form of a generic dimensionless quantity in Eq. (44), where the fields ss and tt depend linearly on the tuning parameter JJ, we expect

U′​(Jc)=a​L1/ν∗+b​L1/νt+c​L1/νs.U^{\prime}(J_{c})=aL^{1/{\nu_{*}}}+bL^{1/{\nu_{t}}}+cL^{1/{\nu_{s}}}. (49)

We will test this three-length scaling form with data for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} and JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} models.

The derivatives can either be obtained from a set of closely spaced numerical values of the cumulants fitted to polynomials, by taking the derivative of the polynomials, or directly from an estimator in the SSE simulations. Typically, we find the latter to produce results with smaller statistical errors. In either case, results are interpolated at the crossing point of the AFM and VBS cumulants, or at the infinite-size critical point if it is known to sufficient precision. Alternatively, the maximum slopes (which occur at slightly different JJ values for the two cumulants) can be analyzed and should scale in the same way. Here we use the derivatives at the cumulant crossing point.

Fig. 34 shows results for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model, with insets showing raw data for the cumulants and the derivatives directly produced by the SSE simulations for each value of JJ. In practice, we find no significant differences between results obtained with the conventional cumulant definitions in Eqs. (22) and the SO(55) versions in Eq. (23), beyond some small shifts of the size dependent transition points and the values of the cumulants and their derivatives. The data presented below are for the SO(55) definitions, Eqs. (23), with the derivatives evaluated at the LL dependent point at which the two cumulants cross each other. We have also analyzed data at our most precisely determined infinite-size transition point J/Q2=0.04502​(1)J/Q_{2}=0.04502(1) (obtained in Sec. IX.1) and in addition studied the size behavior of the maximum slope (peak values in the right-bottom inset of Fig. 34). Both these definitions produce only small overall shifts of the data points relative to those in Fig. 34.

For system sizes roughly in the range L=30L=30 to 100100, the results in Fig. 34 are well described by the exponent νt\nu_{t}, while for larger sizes the behavior crosses over to a significantly faster growth with LL. The expected form with 1/ν∗≈2.401/\nu_{*}\approx 2.40 is fully consistent with the data only for the largest few system sizes (up to L=448L=448) but fits to the predicted form Eq. (49), shown as the continuous curves in Fig. 34, describe the data well for all sizes L∈[16,448]L\in[16,448]. This good fit is not trivial, since only the three factors a,b,ca,b,c in Eq. (49) are adjustable.

Next we study the cumulant derivatives in the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model, in order to examine the expected shift of the crossover from νt\nu_{t} to ν∗\nu_{*} scaling as we move deeper into the first-order line, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 4, where the generic parameter kk now corresponds to Q6−Q6​cQ_{6}-Q_{6c}. Fig. 35 shows results for three values of Q6Q_{6}, with the slopes extracted at the cumulant crossing points as before in Fig. 34 at Q6=0Q_{6}=0. In this case we only show results obtained from the AFM cumulants, but the VBS results look very similar. The expected shift of the crossover is seen clearly. At Q6=0.05Q_{6}=0.05, the behavior is still similar to the case Q6=0Q_{6}=0 in Fig. 34, with the data points up to L≈80L\approx 80 falling close to the line corresponding to νt\nu_{t} scaling. We do not have data for very large LL here, but the early stage of crossover to ν∗\nu_{*} scaling is seen at L≈80L\approx 80, somewhat smaller than at Q6=0Q_{6}=0 in Fig. 34. At the point furthest inside the first-order line, Q6=0.45Q_{6}=0.45, there is no regime for smaller sizes where the scaling is governed cleanly by νt\nu_{t}; instead, for L≳30L\gtrsim 30 the behavior is already well described by ν∗\nu_{*}. Thus, when moving further into the first-order line, the manifestations of the bubble scale are significant already on smaller length scales, as in the schematic illustration Fig. 4 for increasing kk. Finally, at a point between these extremes, Q6=0.2Q_{6}=0.2, we explicitly see the crossover taking place at L≈40L\approx 40.

A final crossover not seen clearly in Fig. 35 is expected that reflects the conventional aspects of the first-order transition. For a finite system, the scaled distance δ​La\delta L^{a} to the first-order point has a large exponent; a=da=d classically and likely a=4a=4 in the case at hand [34], which implies an ultimately faster large-LL growth of the cumulant derivatives with LL than L1/ν∗L^{1/\nu_{*}}. We expect this first-order finite-size scaling to hold also in the presence of two physical length scales, ξs\xi_{s} and ξ∗\xi_{*}, at the transition, and there are indeed signs of an onset of this faster growth for the largest systems at Q6=0.45Q_{6}=0.45 in Fig. 35.

To further elaborate on the ultimate first-order finite-size scaling, the effective correlation-length exponent reflects two different phases occupying different parts of the Hilbert space. Since a finite system can still tunnel between these subspaces, through the formation of system spanning domain walls, there are fluctuations on the length scale LL that are not present in the thermodynamic limit. It is well known from the classical literature that these finite-size fluctuations result in a scaling argument δ​L1/d\delta L^{1/d}, i.e., ν=1/d\nu=1/d in analogy with the correlation-length exponent at a critical point [207, 208, 209]. In the quantum case we should have 1/ν=d+z′1/\nu=d+z^{\prime}, with z′=2z^{\prime}=2 when at least one of the coexisting phases is long-range ordered and associated with a tower of Anderson rotor states (with states at energies 1/Ld1/L^{d}) in a finite-size system in which the spin-rotational symmetry is not broken [34]. For the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model this final stage of the transition cannot be observed with systems of practical size (Fig. 34), and even for the JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6} model at Q6=0.45Q_{6}=0.45 (Fig. 35) the slope taken with the largest 2-3 points corresponds to 1/ν≈31/\nu\approx 3. Values as large as 1/ν≈3.51/\nu\approx 3.5 were observed in a different model with emergent O(44) symmetry [34], where the first-order tendency is larger.

Here we have focused on the manifestation of the crossover in finite-size scaling of the exponent governing the correlation length. The physical bubble size at the first-order transition in the thermodynamic limit will eventually saturate at a value set by the field ss, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 4. Though it is the conventional correlation length ξt\xi_{t} that converges to the finite ξs∼s−νs\xi_{s}\sim s^{-\nu_{s}}, the growth of ξ∗\xi_{*} must also halt at the same point because the ground state does not evolve further until the first-order transition is crossed. The bubble size thus converges to a scale of order ξsν∗/νt\xi_{s}^{\nu_{*}/\nu_{t}} or s−νsν∗/νts^{-\nu_{s}\nu_{*}/\nu_{t}}, which was already used in Sec. VIII.2 and which is approximately s−0.90s^{-0.90} with our exponent values.

We have not computed the correlation length itself under the condition ξ≪L\xi\ll L, but exactly such a calculation for the 3D loop model was presented by Nahum et al. in Fig. 18 of Ref. [29] versus a distance gg to the transition. We expect the length ξ\xi studied there to be governed by the conventional exponent νt\nu_{t} for some g>g1∗g>g_{1}^{*} but then cross over to the slower growing bubble scale with exponent ν∗\nu_{*} for g<g1∗g<g_{1}^{*}. For convenience, we have re-graphed their data in Fig. 36 along with lines showing the predicted scaling with the inverse of the distance g=|J−Jc|g=|J-J_{c}| to the transition point. The behaviors ξ∼g−ν∗\xi\sim g^{-{\nu_{*}}} and ξ∼g−νt\xi\sim g^{-{\nu_{t}}} with our values of ν∗\nu_{*} and νt\nu_{t} are matched remarkably well for systems close to and far away, respectively, from the transition. Like in Fig. 34, the largest length scale here is barely enough to clearly follow the behavior ξ∼g−ν∗\xi\sim g^{-\nu_{*}} without any influence from νt\nu_{t}, but the crossover to the slower growth is still compelling, considering that only the amplitudes of the fitted lines are adjustable in Fig. 36. The behavior conforms with our assertion in Fig. 4, apart from the missing crossover to the eventual first-order behavior, which just means that the saturation value has not yet been reached at the minimum value of gg (and going to still smaller gg values would necessitate very large system sizes in order to satisfy L≫ξ∗L\gg\xi_{*}). This previously unexplained behavior serves as further confirmation of the pseudocritical crossover, as well as the close similarity of the JJ-QQ and loop models.

IX Anomalous finite-size scaling

The crossover behavior of the correlation length will impact also other physical observables—those that are directly related to the correlation length, in a way that will be made more precise in this section. In Ref. [41] it was already realized that a scaling form involving two length scales could explain some of the anomalous behaviors that had been observed in the lattice models. While those insights remain technically valid, the physical interpretation of the roles of the different length scales has to be revised in light of our current understanding of the exponent ν∗\nu_{*}. Previously this exponent was just called ν\nu, as it was assumed to be associated with the single relevant symmetric operator within the original DQCP scenario. Another exponent ν′>ν\nu^{\prime}>\nu was extracted that appeared to fit within the conventional DQCP scenario and its larger U(11) scale in the near-critical VBS phase, which was predicted [23, 24, 25] to also set the scale of spinon deconfinement. The numerical values of the exponents determined in Ref. [41] were ν=0.446​(8)\nu=0.446(8), extracted from cumulant slopes, and ν′=0.585​(18)\nu^{\prime}=0.585(18), from the scaling of the critical VBS domain wall energy density as well as an observable explicitly probing the size of a bound state of two spinons. These values agree reasonably well with our improved results (which benefit from larger systems and in many cases also smaller statistical errors) when we replace ν→ν∗\nu\to\nu_{*} and ν′→νt\nu^{\prime}\to\nu_{t}.

The quantitatively most important result of Ref. [41] was that the finite-size scaling forms for many physical observables depend on the ratio ν/ν′\nu/\nu^{\prime}. As we will see below, this ratio, now identified as ν∗/νt\nu_{*}/\nu_{t}, is indeed of crucial importance in finite-size scaling of a broad class of observables, but with ν∗\nu_{*} governing the bubble scale and νt\nu_{t} the conventional correlation length when approaching the SO(55) critical point. If indeed ν′≡νt\nu^{\prime}\equiv\nu_{t}, as it appears, the scale of spinon deconfinement is actually the correlation length and should then, presumably, exhibit crossover between νt\nu_{t} and ν∗\nu_{*} scaling when approaching the weak first-order line. Since it is hard to extract the size of a bound state for large systems—only lattices of size up to L=64L=64 were used in Ref. [41]—the crossover scale was likely not reached (though some weak tendencies are seen in Fig. 1 of Ref. [41]). We will not revisit the spinon scale directly here, but will discuss our updated view of the extended scaling hypothesis where ν∗/νt\nu_{*}/\nu_{t} appears. We first demonstrate the impact of more than one length scale in the drift of the AFM–VBS transition point in Sec. IX.1, then formulate an extended finite-size scaling ansatz for other observables in Sec. IX.2, and present an example of this ansatz applied to the spin stiffness in Sec. IX.3.

IX.1 Crossover scaling of the transition point

Based on the long-distance correlation functions of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model in Fig. 5, the AFM–VBS transition should be located somewhere between J/Q2=0.04500J/Q_{2}=0.04500 and J/Q2=0.04505J/Q_{2}=0.04505, which is slightly smaller than the value Jc/Q2=0.04510​(2)J_{c}/Q_{2}=0.04510(2) obtained by extrapolating the conventional cumulant crossings in Ref. [90]. Results based on the SO(55) crossing points and improved SSE data are shown in Fig. 37. At first sight, it again looks like the L→∞L\to\infty crossing point tends to about Jc/Q2=0.04510J_{c}/Q_{2}=0.04510, at odds with the results in Fig. 5, which indicates that the system at that coupling ratio is marginally inside the AFM phase. We therefore analyze the cumulant crossing points in more detail next.

Instead of fitting the data versus x=1/Lx=1/L to the form f⁡(x)=f0+a​xb+c​xdf(x)=f_{0}+ax^{b}+cx^{d} with five adjustable parameters (as was done in Ref. [90]), we here use a constrained form that should be expected in the presence of the three length scales governed by the already determined exponents νs\nu_{s}, νt\nu_{t}, and ν∗\nu_{*}:

Jc(L)=Jc(∞)+aL−1/νs+bL−1/νt+cL−1/ν∗,J_{c}(L)=J_{c}(\infty)+aL^{-1/\nu_{s}}+bL^{-1/\nu_{t}}+cL^{-1/\nu_{*}}, (50)

with only Jc​(∞)J_{c}(\infty) and the coefficients a,b,ca,b,c taken as fitting parameters. This form can be motivated by first considering a system approaching the critical point exactly, where ν∗\nu_{*} does not come into play. On the line t=0t=0, the condition of the two cumulants being equal to each other corresponds to some function h⁡(x)=h⁡(s​L1/νs)=0h(x)=h(sL^{1/\nu_{s}})=0, which has some solution x=x0x=x_{0}. Thus, the size dependent critical point scales as sc∼L−1/νss_{c}\sim L^{-1/\nu_{s}}. Similarly, on the line s=0s=0 we have tc∼L−1/νtt_{c}\sim L^{-1/\nu_{t}}. For a system tuned to the critical point on some line δ\delta such that s=ds​δs=d_{s}\delta and t=dt​δt=d_{t}\delta, with ds,dtd_{s},d_{t} arbitrary nonzero coefficients, both powers come into play for a finite-size shift of the form δc∼aL−1/νs+bL−1/νt\delta_{c}\sim aL^{-1/\nu_{s}}+bL^{-1/\nu_{t}}. In Eq. (50) we have posited that a similar term originating from the bubble scale appears when approaching the weak first-order line with small s≠0s\not=0.

Since 1/νs≈0.731/\nu_{s}\approx 0.73 is much smaller than the other exponents, it will eventually control the finite-size corrections for large systems. In fact, we find that the coefficients aa and bb have different signs, leading to nonmonotonic behavior that is not yet obvious with the SSE L≤448L\leq 448 data at hand but is a very stable feature of the fit. As shown in the inset of Fig. 37, for three data sets including different minimum system sizes, the fitted function consistently has a maximum at L≈500L\approx 500. The extrapolated value is stable (also when excluding additional small systems) and now agrees very well with the previous conclusion in Sec. IV (from the long-distance spin and dimer correlation functions) that the critical coupling ratio should be between J/Q2=0.04500J/Q_{2}=0.04500 and J/Q2=0.04505J/Q_{2}=0.04505. Based on the statistical quality of the fits and the variations among different LminL_{\min}, we conclude that the critical point is at (J/Q2)c=0.04502​(1)(J/Q_{2})_{c}=0.04502(1). The third correction in Eq. (50) is actually not very important for system size L≳50L\gtrsim 50, since the exponent 1/ν∗1/\nu_{*} is much larger than the other two exponents. Leaving out this term still produces a statistically good nonmonotonic fit and critical point consistent with the value stated above.

It should be noted that fitting two independent power laws does not produce the same exponents as the known ones imposed above. In fact, the best fit has two exponents very close to each other, both around 1.91.9, and with opposite signs of their coefficients. This behavior in itself indicates that the best fit mimics a different form. While the fit with fixed exponents 1/νs1/\nu_{s} and 1/νt1/\nu_{t} is not completely optimal (since other exponents give marginally lower χ2\chi^{2} values), it is still statistically good, as can even be judged visually in the inset of Fig. 37 (and χ2/dof≈1\chi^{2}/{\rm dof}\approx 1). The known exponents thus provide a good explanation for the nonmonotonic crossover behavior, the presence of which can also be inferred from our other indications (Sec. IV) of a transition point falling between J/Q2=0.04500J/Q_{2}=0.04500 and J/Q2=0.04505J/Q_{2}=0.04505. The extrapolated transition point (J/Q2)c≈0.04502​(1)(J/Q_{2})_{c}\approx 0.04502(1) also agrees very well with an estimate based on the AFM and VBS correlation lengths (in a combination that apparently cancels a correction) [166].

A similar nonmonotonic behavior of crossing points was observed in a dimerized 2D Heisenberg model [118], where the behavior is caused by a conventional scaling correction. An even more intricate (and harder to extrapolate) nonmonotonic behavior was observed in crossing points of the conventional [i.e., not SO(55)] version of the Binder ratio Eq. (21a) at a different ratio β/L\beta/L [41]. In principle there could be some further change in behavior for even larger LL than in Fig. 37. However, the very good agreement between the transition point extracted here and the bracketing values obtained from long-distance spin correlation in Sec. IV.2 suggests that any further change in (J/Q2)c(J/Q_{2})_{c} must be very small. Note that not all quantities are affected equally by the presence of more than one length scale, since the coefficients of the corresponding terms in the scaling function are specific to a given quantity [118].

IX.2 Extended finite-size scaling hypothesis

In standard finite-size scaling [192, 193, 194], a physical observable AA with scaling behavior A∼δκA\sim\delta^{\kappa} (with κ\kappa denoting a generic critical exponent) in the thermodynamic limit is first rewritten using the correlation length ξ∼δ−ν\xi\sim\delta^{-\nu}, i.e., A∼ξκ/νA\sim\xi^{\kappa/\nu}. Then at criticality ξ\xi is simply replaced by the system size LL. Thus, A(L)∼L−κ/νA(L)\sim L^{-\kappa/\nu}, which is valid in a window of size L−1/νL^{-1/\nu}, where the correlation length exceeds LL. Finite-size scaling effectively corresponds to the flow of observables with the length scale on which they are probed, motivating the sometimes used term “phenomenological renormalization” [192].

The easiest way [41] to construct a modified finite-size behavior in the presence of the bubble scale ξ∗\xi_{*} is to posit that it should be used in place of ξ\xi above, i.e., A∼ξ∗κ/νA\sim\xi_{*}^{\kappa/\nu}. Here we have only changed the relevant length scale that appears, without changing κ/ν\kappa/\nu (which is related to the scaling dimension of AA exactly at the critical point). Since ξ∗∼ξν∗/ν\xi_{*}\sim\xi^{\nu_{*}/\nu}, we can also write A∼ξ(κ/ν)​(ν∗/ν)A\sim\xi^{(\kappa/\nu)(\nu_{*}/\nu)}. If we now replace ξ\xi by LL we obtain A⁡(L)∼L−(κ/ν)​(ν∗/ν)A(L)\sim L^{-(\kappa/\nu)(\nu_{*}/\nu)}, or, more specifically when the AFM–VBS transition is crossed by tuning the tt field and ν\nu corresponds to νt\nu_{t},

A⁡(L)∼L−(κ/ν)​(ν∗/νt),A(L)\sim L^{-(\kappa/\nu)(\nu_{*}/\nu_{t})}, (51)

Here the exponent indeed differs by a factor ν∗/νt\nu_{*}/\nu_{t} from the conventional finite-size exponent κ/νt\kappa/\nu_{t}. The form should be valid at the transition point roughly in the range of system sizes corresponding to the window [g2∗​(k),g1∗​(k)][g_{2}^{*}(k),g_{1}^{*}(k)] of a tuning parameter gg in the schematic drawing of the crossover behavior in Fig. 4.

The physical interpretation of the steps leading to Eq. (51) was [41] that the shorter length scale ξ∗\xi_{*} ceases to grow when the larger scale ξ\xi reaches LL. If that is so, then it would appear that the two length scales are present at the same time (with the longer scale ξt\xi_{t} having been replaced by LL in finite-size scaling), which is not clear from the different finite-size analyses we have carried out and from the results for ξ\xi versus the distance to the transition by Nahum et al. [29] (data reproduced here in Fig. 36). Here we have explained this simultaneous presence of the length scales as originating from irrelevant repulsive interactions between the two order parameters, as illustrated in Fig. 3. The length scales physically correspond to the typical scale of amplitude fluctuations (ξt\xi_{t}) and the bubbles (ξ∗\xi_{*}). The shorter bubble scale should in practice be more prominently present in most observables, since a bubble in one phase represents an order parameter of the other phase; thus directly impacting the AFM and VBS correlation lengths.

A key question now is to what observables anomalous scaling involving ν∗\nu_{*} applies. Clearly, a form like Eq. (51) cannot apply to all operators, because the exponent κ/νt\kappa/\nu_{t} is the scaling dimension of the operator AA and we have presented numerous examples in the previous sections of scaling dimensions extracted from system size dependence. For instance, in Sec. V.2 we extracted the relevant scaling dimensions Δt\Delta_{t} from the correlation function of the ZZ operator at distance r=L/2r=L/2. If this correlation function CZ​(L)C_{Z}(L) takes the form where the exponent 2​Δt2\Delta_{t} is modified by the factor ν∗/νt\nu_{*}/\nu_{t}, then we would have to compensate by multiplying the exponent from the fit by the inverse ratio to obtain the true values of the two scaling dimensions. This would completely ruin the good agreement in Table 1 between the AFM–VBS transition and the SO(55) CFT and the fuzzy sphere model. Moreover, we considered both r=L/2r=L/2 and r≪Lr\ll L in Fig. 18, with full agreement between the decay exponents. A very strong confirmation of the correctness of the procedure is that the scaling dimension of the conserved current comes out very close to Δj=2\Delta_{j}=2 in Fig. 16.

The bubble size ξ∗\xi_{*} should be at the heart of the matter, and we propose that only those quantities are affected that relate explicitly to the order parameters through the conventional correlation lengths ξt\xi_{t} and ξs\xi_{s}. Such quantities would typically involve integration over the lattice and there should then also be similar anomalous scaling behaviors away from the transition point in the thermodynamic limit, related to the crossover of the correlation length illustrated in Fig. 4. For example, a squared order parameter (here VBS or AFM) scales with the distance to the critical point as m2=δ2​βm^{2}=\delta^{2\beta}, where 2​β=2​Δϕ​ν2\beta=2\Delta_{\phi}\nu, with ν=νt\nu=\nu_{t} if only the field tt is tuned at s=0s=0 and ν=νs\nu=\nu_{s} if ss is tuned with t=0t=0. Thus, m2m^{2} depends explicitly on an inverse correlation length, ξs\xi_{s} or ξt\xi_{t}. Another example is the spin stiffness ρs\rho_{s}, which scales as ρs∼δz​ν\rho_{s}\sim\delta^{z\nu}. This quantity as well is directly related to the (AFM) long-range order (as a response to a twist of the order parameter distributed over the entire system); since z=1z=1 here, the scaling should be identical (in terms of exponents, not the shape of the full scaling function) to that of the inverse correlation length. Then it is also plausibly affected by the crossover behavior. After presenting the general formalism here, we will study the important spin stiffness ρs\rho_{s} as an example below in Sec. IX.3.

The inverse correlation length of a system with a single tuned relevant field can be written as

ξ−1=δν​f​(δ​L1/ν),\xi^{-1}=\delta^{\nu}f(\delta L^{1/\nu}), (52)

where δν\delta^{\nu} is the form for L→∞L\to\infty and the function f⁡(x)f(x), x=δ​L1/νx=\delta L^{1/\nu}, accounts for the finite-size cut-off. The finite-size form ξ−1∼L−1\xi^{-1}\sim L^{-1} is obtained from the necessary condition (to eliminate δ\delta at criticality) that f⁡(x)→x−νf(x)\to x^{-\nu} when x→∞x\to\infty, i.e., for L→∞L\to\infty at x≠0x\not=0. An alternative, more common form of Eq. (52) for finite-size scaling including δ≠0\delta\not=0 is

ξ−1=L−1​f​(δ​L1/ν),\xi^{-1}=L^{-1}f(\delta L^{1/\nu}), (53)

with a different form of the scaling function f⁡(x)f(x). In practice, this form holds up to some value of xx, beyond which there is a finite-size peel-off from the scaling function, with that peel-off value increasing with LL. Here we will start from a generalized form of Eq. (52) with more than one scaling argument and derive a corresponding critical form with more than one power of LL.

Generalizing Eq. (52) to the case at hand, we have already argued that a scaling function depending on all the exponents νs\nu_{s}, νt\nu_{t}, and ν∗\nu_{*} is needed; Eq. (44). Further, we have in mind a situation where the bubble scale dominates the behavior for small values of ss in the thermodynamic limit and therefore start from the form

ξ−1=δν∗​f​(δ​L1/ν∗,δ​L1/νt,δ​L1/νs).\xi^{-1}=\delta^{\nu_{*}}f(\delta L^{1/{\nu_{*}}},\delta L^{1/{\nu_{t}}},\delta L^{1/{\nu_{s}}}). (54)

Here we have replaced all the factors in front of LL by just δ\delta, but it should be kept in mind that different arguments will dominate the behavior depending on how ss and tt are tuned by δ\delta. The last scaling argument should really be (δ+s0)​L1/νs(\delta+s_{0})L^{1/{\nu_{s}}}, with s0s_{0} the value of ss when we cross t=0t=0 (δ=0\delta=0). Then the system will eventually cross over to a first-order form that we do not consider here. The question is whether there is some range of LL where Eq. (54) can describe the finite-size behavior when the transition is weakly first-order, i.e., when scs_{c} is very small and there is a large range of length-scales governed by ξ∗\xi_{*} in the thermodynamic limit, as in Fig. 4 for small kk.

In the example of the cumulant derivative U′U^{\prime} in Sec. VIII.3 we already saw how the scaling function in Eq. (44) can, effectively, produce three different power laws. Since UU is a dimensionless quantity, there is no power of δ\delta in front of the scaling function and Eq. (49) is produced by the derivative. Such a form was able to reproduce the data in Fig. 34 very well from small to large systems. For the inverse correlation length of interest now, the asymptotic power of the arguments in Eq. (54) must be −1/ν∗-1/{\nu_{*}} in order to eliminate the overall δ\delta dependence, thus producing the form

ξ−1(L)=aL−1+bL−ν∗/νt+cL−ν∗/νs.\xi^{-1}(L)=aL^{-1}+bL^{-\nu_{*}/{\nu_{t}}}+cL^{-\nu_{*}/{\nu_{s}}}. (55)

This form is valid under the assumption that each argument, when large, produces its own power law to remove the δ\delta dependence at criticality. While we have not proved this property, Eqs. (54) and (55) are certainly mutually consistent. We will also see below that Eq. (55) is sufficient to describe numerical data without any cross terms or even more complicated crossover behavior.

According to Eq. (55), a conventional finite-size scaling term L−1L^{-1} will be produced in addition to the anomalous L−ν∗/νtL^{-\nu_{*}/{\nu_{t}}} term of the original two-length proposal [41]. The anomalous term decays slower and may dominate the behavior for large system sizes. In the last term, L−ν∗/νsL^{-\nu_{*}/{\nu_{s}}} decays even slower but here the coefficient cc should be small if the crossing value s0s_{0} of the ss field is small. Thus, it may only become important for very large system sizes, where the other terms have essentially decayed away. When the last term does become important, we also expect the first-order behavior to take over. In practice, only the L−1L^{-1} and L−ν∗/νsL^{-\nu_{*}/{\nu_{s}}} terms will likely reflect pseudocritical scaling.

IX.3 Spin stiffness

The spin stiffness ρs\rho_{s} provided the first hint of anomalous scaling in the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model [31] and has frequently been used to argue for a first-order transition [31, 46]. It is computed in SSE (and other QMC) simulations in terms of winding number fluctuations (of spin currents in systems with periodic boundary conditions) [210, 211]. The conventional critical form when z=1z=1 is ρs∼L−1\rho_{s}\sim L^{-1}, arising from ρs∼δνt\rho_{s}\sim\delta^{\nu_{t}} when crossing the transition by tuning tt at s=0s=0 in the thermodynamic limit. Thus, the modified LL dependent scaling form is identical to that for ξ−1\xi^{-1} in Eq. (55),

ρs(L)=ρs(∞)+aL−1+bL−ν∗/νt+cL−ν∗/νs,\rho_{s}(L)=\rho_{s}(\infty)+aL^{-1}+bL^{-\nu_{*}/{\nu_{t}}}+cL^{-\nu_{*}/{\nu_{s}}}, (56)

except for the added constant ρs​(∞)\rho_{s}(\infty), which reflects an expected nonzero value for L→∞L\to\infty because of the weak AFM order in the coexistence state, in analogy with how the non-vanishing order parameter itself was handled in correlation functions in Sec. IV. While the contribution originating from the ss field close to criticality may play some role, the crossover to the ultimate constant form for L→∞L\to\infty at the transition (or to other forms away from the transition) is likely more intricate. Moreover, even with high precision data it is not possible to reliably extract the relative contributions of the constant and the L−ν∗/νsL^{-\nu_{*}/{\nu_{s}}} term. We therefore leave out the ss contribution here.

We fit to SSE data for the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model generated at inverse temperature β=0.42​L\beta=0.42L, with the factor 0.420.42 being approximately the inverse of the critical spin wave velocity [164], thus representing cubic space-time geometry (which is not a prerequisite for scaling but may reduce some corrections). We have data for large systems, up to L=448L=448, at two coupling ratios, J=0.0450J=0.0450 and J=0.0451J=0.0451 (Q2=1Q_{2}=1), and interpolated in those data sets to the estimated transition point J=0.04502J=0.04502.

The data are graphed versus 1/L1/L in Fig. 38 and have been fitted to the expected form for L≥12L\geq 12, shown with the red curve. The dashed black line shows the form L−ν∗/νt=L−0.66L^{-\nu_{*}/{\nu_{t}}}=L^{-0.66}, where the exponent is slightly smaller than in Ref. [41] (ν∗/νt≈0.715\nu_{*}/{\nu_{t}}\approx 0.715). While this term indeed governs the large-LL data very well, the L−1L^{-1} term is important to match the results for the smaller systems and also to improve the fit overall before the asymptotic behavior sets in. The L−1L^{-1} term corresponds almost exactly to a correction term with optimized exponent used in Ref. [41]. Thus, the results of the two fits are almost the same (but here we also have data for larger systems), with the main difference being the added constant ρs​(∞)\rho_{s}(\infty) in Eq. (56), which has a value ≈0.0003\approx 0.0003 in our fit and plays only a minor role in the available range of system sizes. There are still, not unexpectedly, further corrections for the smaller system sizes that are not included in Eq. (56). Overall, the extended scaling ansatz works well here.

X Conclusions and Discussion

The many past efforts to elucidate the nature of the DQCP and its adjacent phases can be likened to the ancient Indian parable of a group of blind men examining an elephant, an entity that they have never before encountered. Feeling different parts of the animal without access to the whole, they present their individual findings and theories but, given the conflicting observations, they cannot reach any consensus on what they are dealing with. In the case of the putative DQCP, many models and methods have been applied to study the AFM–VBS transition in different ways. Individually, most of these studies present plausible and coherent scenarios for exotic critical phenomena, but, taken together, no consistent unified picture has emerged. Here we have reconstructed the entire elephant—a multicritical point with emergent SO(55) symmetry at the end of a line of weak first-order transitions—which explains previously irreconcilable observations and scenarios.

X.1 Multicritical SO(5) point

We have analyzed our numerical results in a space of two scaling fields (contained in ratios of model parameters) and extracted scaling dimensions compatible with results for an SO(55) CFT. The CFT results of main interest here [65, 56] are strictly speaking only boundaries of allowed values in the space of scaling dimensions. However, it is believed that the true exponents should fall at or very close to the boundaries, as is the case for O(NN) models [63]. Our relevant scaling dimensions listed in Table 1 fall within about 1-2% from the boundaries, read off of graphs available for the combinations (Δϕ,Δs)(\Delta_{\phi},\Delta_{s}) and (Δϕ,Δt)(\Delta_{\phi},\Delta_{t}) [65]. While Δ4\Delta_{4}, as well as the other dimensions, is in less good agreement with Ref. [56], the discrepancies can likely be explained by the input value Δϕ=0.63\Delta_{\phi}=0.63 used in that calculation. Our value is lower, Δϕ=0.607​(4)\Delta_{\phi}=0.607(4), and once this is taken into account the agreement is improved for all scaling dimensions [56]. Overall, the remarkably good agreement between two very different calculations represents strong support for the multicritical SO(55) CFT.

The multicritical point is inaccessible (with our current models) in QMC simulations, because of sign problems (e.g., a negative Q6Q_{6} interaction would be needed, according to Fig. 23). However, in our view the point is not fundamentally inaccessible, in contrast to the complex CFT scenario [48, 60]. Methods such as DMRG and machine learning approaches can be used to study models like the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-Q2Q_{2} Hamiltonian, but on much smaller lattices than those accessed here or with infinite-size approaches that require other cut-offs. Useful results may still be obtained, because the scaling behavior will not be contaminated by the effects from the weak first-order transition. Based on previous results for frustrated spin models [69, 70, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, 79], which can be continuously deformed into the JJ-QQ model studied here, there is also most likely a gapless QSL phase adjacent to the parameter regime accessible to efficient (sign problem free) QMC simulations. The simplest scenario then is that the phase diagram is of the type in Fig. 2(b), where the multicritical point (which then is bicritical) is also the tip of the QSL phase. A QSL connected to a direct AFM–VBS transition was actually observed in a tensor-network study of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} model [77], but it was not possible to determine the nature of the special point and the direct transition.

In principle, there could also be a line of generic DQCPs, as in Fig. 2(a), with the spin liquid only opening for still smaller ss values. However, N=2N=2 is a special case [27] of the more general SU(NN) theory [23], being the only case for which the emergent SO(55) symmetry is expected—at least for large NN, where the anomalous dimensions for the spin and dimer order parameters become different, thus prohibiting a unified order parameter. The multicritical scenario without generic DQCP transition may therefore also be unique to this case. The generic line of DQCPs between the first-order end point and the tip of the spin liquid would then have to emerge for N>2N>2. It is already known that some first-order signatures weaken with increasing NN [178] and some of the critical exponents have been extracted for different values of NN [127, 38, 39, 151]. With our new insights on the nature of the transition for N=2N=2 and the associated complications in extracting scaling dimensions, further work on SU(NN) spin models with N>2N>2 is also called for.

X.2 Emergent pseudocriticality and excitations

Beyond the nature of the critical point that we have now resolved, we have also demonstrated that the emergent SO(55) symmetry leads to previously not understood pseudocritical scaling behaviors when the weak first-order transition is approached. While previous works found evidence of two length scales and related anomalous scaling behaviors [41], here we have clarified the origin of the emergent length scale and its consequences. We have presented concrete evidence for the presence of an effectively repulsive irrelevant interaction between the AFM and VBS order parameters, which leads to a specific deformation of the SO(55) symmetry that we have observed. We have argued that the CFT operator responsible for the observed behavior is the lowest irrelevant rank-22 CFT operator t′t^{\prime}, with all other quantum numbers the same as the traceless symmetric tensor tt driving the AFM–VBS transition. Such an operator with reasonably similar scaling dimension was identified with the fuzzy sphere approach [60] but not ascribed any particular significance.

The symmetry deformation leads to two different length scales of fluctuations of the symmetry-breaking phases in the neighborhood of the weak (nearly critical) first-order transition. The size of defects (bubbles) formed by fluctuations of one of the ordered phases into the other phase is governed by the pseudocritical exponent ν∗\nu_{*}, for which we have derived a relationship, Eq. (1), to scaling dimensions of the multicritical point. This relationship is obeyed by our numerical results for the JJ-QQ models. The conventional correlation length is associated with the amplitude fluctuations of the order parameter, and there are also two (in the AFM phase) or one (in the VBS phase) gapless Goldstone modes left. The various crossovers and symmetry considerations are summarized in Fig. 3. It should be noted that the length scale ξ∗\xi_{*} is different from the conventional length scale generated inside an ordered phase (specifically here in the VBS phase) by a dangerously irrelevant perturbation, which we have also discussed and in some cases studied quantitatively. Importantly, while the conventional emergent U(11) and SO(55) length scales are larger than the conventional correlation lengths governed by the exponents νt\nu_{t} (when crossing between the AFM and VBS phases) and νs\nu_{s} (on the coexistence line), the pseudocritical length ξ∗\xi_{*} is actually smaller; ν∗<νt<νs\nu_{*}<\nu_{t}<\nu_{s}. The pseudocritical crossover is also different from the conventional “walking” scenario of pseudocriticality [48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53], where no emergent length scale ξ∗\xi_{*} has been discussed.

The pseudocriticality can be regarded as a “beyond Landau” phenomenon, since it relies on the emergent SO(55) symmetry. Classical NN-component spin models cannot have emergent O(N>2N>2) (unless all relevant perturbations are tuned away) [80, 81]. Thus, the proposed topological θ\theta term [27, 26] is likely needed in the field theory, which in the most well known incarnation would be the 2+1 dimensional WZW k=1k=1 theory with SO(55) symmetry (which has to be properly regularized, e.g., within the fuzzy sphere approach [60] or with lattice simulations [105]). It has been believed that this theory has no relevant SO(55) singlet, contrary to what we have found here at the AFM–VBS transition. Interestingly, the emergent bubbles are somewhat akin to the topological defects in the original DQCP proposal, where a defect in one phase can be considered as having the order of the other phase [23], though the origin of this phenomenon is different in our scenario and requires multicriticality with an irrelevant repulsive interaction between the two order parameters.

We have not investigated excitations explicitly here, but the amplitude and bubble excitations of course correspond to vacuum fluctuations of excitations; particles whose masses can in principle be extracted from correlation functions in imaginary time, from which spectral functions can also be extracted [180]. Such calculations have already been employed with JJ-QQ models to investigate the expected spectrum of (almost) deconfined spinons [42, 43], whose dispersion relation turned out to be in remarkable agreement with the fermionic π\pi-flux state, one of the effective descriptions of the AFM–VBS transition that is also related to the SO(55) WZW theory [26]. More recently, spin-charge separation was detected for a hole injected into the host system [43] and this type of fractionalization can also be described within the π\pi-flux framework.

An important question now is how the bubble excitations discussed here fit into the picture of deconfined spinons. On the VBS side of the weak first-order transition, the AFM bubbles can be understood as bound states of spinons [180], with ξ∗\xi_{*} being the size of such a state. In order to account for the four states of two almost deconfined spinons, there must be a triplet and a singlet bubble, and these two types will only become completely degenerate exactly at the multicritical point (where the concept of bubble excitation also breaks down). On the AFM side, the VBS bubbles carry U(11) charge q=±1q=\pm 1 (vorticity, assuming only minor effects of the ultimate ℤ4\mathbb{Z}_{4} symmetry) and the total spin SS label does not apply because of the weak SO(33) symmetry breaking (though nevertheless the VBS bubbles can be regarded as S=0S=0). It is not clear to what degree all these excitations (including the amplitude modes and the remaining gapless Goldstone modes) can be separated in QMC calculations with analytic continuation, though steps in this direction have already been taken in studies at the very nearly critical transition point [42, 43, 212]. In order for the separation of the length scales (and thereby the mass scales) to be sufficiently large, the best approach may be to stay very close to the first-order line, where ξt\xi_{t} and ξ∗\xi_{*} have converged, but ideally not exactly at the transition point. Since the system size LL also has to be larger than both of the two length scales, the plain JJ-Q2Q_{2} or JJ-Q3Q_{3} models are likely not ideal. The separation of the amplitude-mode and bubble scales should be clearer in JJ-QnQ_{n} models with larger nn or extended models like JJ-Q2Q_{2}-Q6Q_{6}. In the case of the latter, Fig. 35 shows that ξ∗\xi_{*} can apply already from 2020 (or even less), but the larger ξs\xi_{s} (ξt→ξs\xi_{t}\to\xi_{s} when converged) may still make it challenging to satisfy L≫ξsL\gg\xi_{s} (to approach the thermodynamic limit). In any case, the scenario presented here should motivate such calculations.

X.3 Higgs-like mass generation

A very interesting aspect of the two different massive excitations is the functional resemblance to the Higgs mechanism in particle physics, in which a SO(44) Higgs field and a unified electroweak SU(22)×\timesU(11) gauge field constitute different gauge-coupled sectors. The Higgs potential drives the spontaneous symmetry breaking of the SO(44) field, producing the massive Higgs boson (amplitude mode), and the gauge coupling causes the three would-be Goldstone modes to combine with the gauge fields, forming the massive W±W^{\pm} and ZZ bosons and leaving the gapless U(11) photon. The analogy between the near-multicritical SO(55) quantum magnet with its amplitude mode (Higgs), bubble excitations (massive soliton-like configurations of the five-vector), and remaining Goldstone (photon) mode(s) is actually closer to alternatives to the standard Higgs mechanism. Such theories often start from a unified field with higher symmetry instead of the separate Higgs field [91, 92, 93], similar to the SO(55) critical order parameter of the quantum magnet, and the spontaneous symmetry breaking of this field leads to the same Higgs, W±W^{\pm} and ZZ bosons, and photon as in the standard theory, but with possibly different mass scales.

In our scenario for the weak first-order AFM–VBS transition the irrelevant repulsive order-parameter interaction remaining when the relevant tt field has been tuned very small is what causes the separation between the Higgs and bubble scales. In the absence of this interaction, they are both controlled by the exponent νt\nu_{t} of the tuning field tt, but in the presence of the interaction the energetically costly domain walls between the order parameter components and the bubble components cause a larger bubble mass controlled by ν∗<νt\nu_{*}<\nu_{t}. The separation of the scales and the eventual convergence of the lengths (and their inverses corresponding to masses) very close to the first-order line is illustrated in Fig. 3, where the number of bubble excitations is two on the AFM side (VBS bubbles) and three on the VBS side (AFM bubbles). There is a single gapless Goldstone mode in the VBS phase and two in the AFM phase, though the one in the VBS phase is also strictly gapped because of its eventual ℤ4\mathbb{Z}_{4} crossover. That gap is, however, smaller than the bubble gap, with the emergent U(11) length scale being larger than ξ∗\xi_{*}.

Although the analogy to the hierarchy problem in particle physics is clearly only suggestive, especially since the number of space dimensions is two instead of three and the massive bubble excitations are scalars (at least at first sight) instead of ℓ=1\ell=1 vector bosons, it would be interesting to explore further whether the crossover mechanism with the emergent length scale ξ∗\xi_{*} (and related mass scale of order ξ∗−1\xi_{*}^{-1} that we have not explored directly here), driven by a dangerously irrelevant interaction (in an unconventional manner), could have some counterpart in field theories of interest in the context of mass hierarchies in particle physics. Our scenario essentially corresponds to the WZW k=1k=1 SO(55) theory to which the irrelevant repulsive order-parameter interaction has to be added in order to generate the pseudocritical ξ∗\xi_{*} scale governed by an effective exponent ν∗\nu_{*} in a regime close to the transition. This is reminiscent of the soft mass scales that arise in near-conformal (walking) Higgs alternatives, e.g. the light dilaton, where proximity to a fixed point sets a mass parametrically below the natural scale [213, 214, 215, 216, 217]. Whether the specific pseudocritical mass separation mechanism and structure that we have found have counterparts there is an intriguing question.

To make the analogy with particle physics formally clearer (i.e., beyond the functional analogy discussed above), the original CP1 gauge field theory of deconfined quantum criticality [23] could be considered. Since it is believed to be related to the SO(55) WZW theory through the web of dualities [48] it should be possible to analyze the effects of the irrelevant interaction also there and elucidate the possible relationship to the electroweak gauge-field theories and proposed alternative Higgs mechanisms in particle physics. The CP1 theory may also reveal whether the bubble excitations couple to the emergent gauge field and thereby carry hidden vector content, which would imply a more literal electroweak correspondence.

X.4 JJ-QQ model extensions

It is also possible to study JJ-QQ type models with emergent O(44) symmetry, either by having a two-fold degenerate plaquette-singlet (PS) phase transitioning into an SO(33) breaking AFM state [218], or by four-fold degenerate VBS transitioning into an O(22) AFM state [101]. Previous work on a “checker-board” JJ-QQ model with AFM–PS transition showed emergent O(44) symmetry up to the largest system sizes studied (L=96L=96) even though the transition was rather obviously first-order [34] (a related classical loop model found similar behaviors [35]). An XY anisotropic (planar) JJ-QQ model with O(22) deformed AFM state has also been studied [218, 42]. It also has a first-order transition but signatures of deconfined spinons were seen in the dynamic spectral functions [42]. These models should be further studied in light of our results presented here.

Ising symmetric versions of the JJ-QQ models have not been considered so far. Such models would be interesting in light of recent work on 1D analogues of the DQCP separating two Ising-type ordered phases [219, 145, 220, 221]. While these order-order transitions fall into the well known Luttinger liquid classification and have been studied in that context previously [222, 223, 224], 2D Ising-like JJ-QQ models could shed further light on the higher-dimensional DQCP phenomenon. In the 1D models considered, the two Ising-type order parameters vanish continuously and there is emergent O(44) symmetry at the common critical point. Recent work [225] has introduced an additional tuning parameter—a spin-phonon coupling—that eventually causes the line of critical points to terminate at a tricritical point in the 4-state Potts universality class, after which the transition is of first order. This scenario is also very similar to the symmetrically equivalent stripe-AFM transition in classical J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Ising model [226, 227], through a simple mapping between the phase diagram and transitions by adding a field favoring vertical or horizontal stripes in the classical Ising model.

The Ising anisotropy contrasts with isotropic quantum spin chains with long-range interactions [228, 229], which retain the critical WZW level k=1k=1 phase of the standard Heisenberg chain (a 1D gapless QSL, sometimes referred to as a quasi long-range ordered state in the context of this model) but also have an adjacent true long-range ordered AFM phase (circumventing the Mermin-Wagner theorem) and a two-fold degenerate VBS phase. There is a direct AFM–VBS transition ending at the tip of the critical phase. In one variant of the model—the frustrated J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} chain with long-range unfrustrated interactions Jr>2J_{r>2} [228]—the direct AFM–VBS transition is strongly first-order, while in a JJ-QQ chain with likewise unfrustrated long-range JrJ_{r} couplings [229] it was believed to be continuous. However, in light of the present knowledge of the 2D case, the direct transition likely also is weakly first-order, with only a bicritical point with emergent O(44) symmetry at the tip of the critical phase.

The introduction of Ising anisotropy in the long-range interacting 1D models should destroy the critical phase and lead to a similar diagram with tricritical point as in the spin-phonon model. The QSL phase should also be destroyed by Ising anisotropy in 2D systems, and one can reasonably speculate that systems like the Ising-anisotropic JJ-QQ models should then also have a line of direct AFM–VBS transitions replacing the extended QSL phase. However, this Ising-AFM to VBS transition will unlikely be continuous in 2D, and there is then the possibility of two first-order lines meeting at a special multicritical point, likely associated with a duality. A line of continuous transitions can perhaps not be completely excluded, as a higher-dimensional analogy of “classical deconfined criticality” at finite temperature in 2D [230], or possibly a weak first-order transition in the complex CFT scenario could apply here.

An important question is whether the generic DQCP could appear with electronic model Hamiltonians [159, 148, 231] [i.e., beyond the fuzzy sphere approach of directly regularizing the SO(55) field theory]. A candidate is the transition between an AFM ground state and a dd-wave superconductor, which was found to be continuous within the resolution of early QMC studies [104] and for which further evidence of excitations expected at the DQCP was presented very recently [105]. At finite doping, the AFM–VBS DQCP may evolve into an exotic spin-charge separated “holon metal” [232], and the spectral function of a single injected fermionic hole in a JJ-QQ model is indeed consistent with spin-charge separation [43]. More detailed comparisons between the AFM–dd-wave and AFM–VBS transitions are called for, especially as concerns the question of generic versus multicritical DQCP in the fermionic models, which would require high-precision values of the scaling dimensions also in those models.

X.5 Recent developments

After the first version of this paper appeared online (arXiv:2405.06607v1) two significant works addressing the complex CFT [233] and the multicriticality DQCP scenarios [234] for the DQCP have appeared. Ref. [233] constructed a non-Hermitian version of the planar JJ-QQ model and demonstrated that the first-order discontinuity could be increased by turning on the imaginary coupling. However, as also noted by the authors, the results cannot be taken as a demonstration of the conventional JJ-QQ model realizing the complex CFT scenario. Ref. [233] made significant progress on the numerical conformal bootstrap approach, going beyond the previous SO(55) works [65, 56] in how much of the space of scaling dimensions can be excluded by the symmetries of the CFT. In particular, a multicritical cone in the space was found where the several scaling dimensions considered all agree very closely with the results presented here in Table 1. These calculations are also claimed to be inconsistent with the complex CFT scenario, but still roughly consistent with the numerical fuzzy sphere results [60]—not just the scaling dimensions (which are less precise than those presented here) but also other CFT data.

Ref. [234] together with the results presented here can be taken as a rather definite proof of the multicritical SO(55) CFT scenario, which now is being further explored in the context of models that contain gapless QSL phases with SO(55) tips in their phase diagrams (beyond the previous works [74, 77]) [235, 236]. It would still be useful to further improve the QMC calculations, e.g., implementing the recently proposed operator covariance method [237, 238] and constructing models with interactions beyond the JJ and QnQ_{n} terms [239], which may potentially reach closer to the multicritical point without sign problems. Even in cases where the sign problem cannot be avoided, the fact that the multicritical point in the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model is so close to the sign free region (and perhaps even closer in models yet to be constructed) offers hope that some QMC calculations may still be possible there. One approach would be to add a second PQMC stage after projecting to the transition in the sign-free regime; technically an imaginary-time quench from the transition point of the JJ-Q2Q_{2} model H0H_{0} into the ground state of a JJ-Q2Q_{2}-KK model HKH_{K}, where KK is an appropriate small term (e.g., negative Q6Q_{6}, negative JJ, positive J2J_{2}, etc.), so that the ground state is now at or closer to the multicritical point.
